options: He met that boy at the party.
She met that boy at the party.
He met that girl at the party.
He met that man at the party.
mcqs.why: The notes change every feminine word to its masculine form: 'she' becomes 'he' and 'girl' becomes 'boy', giving 'He met that boy at the party.'

mcqs.q: Change the gender: 'The hen is a useful bird.' becomes:
options: The ox is a useful bird.
The cock is a useful bird.
The man is a useful bird.
The boy is a useful bird.
mcqs.why: The notes give the masculine of 'hen' as 'cock', so the changed sentence is 'The cock is a useful bird.'

lessons.title: Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Writing A — Write a composition of three or more paragraphs on 'Causes of Floods and Risk reduction'

  • Q: Write a composition of three or more paragraphs on 'Causes of Floods and Risk reduction' following the conventions of essay writing (introductory paragraph, body paragraph, concluding paragraph).
    Ans: Causes of Floods and Risk Reduction Floods are among the most destructive natural hazards in Pakistan. The devastating floods of July 2010 affected approximately 20 million people, claimed about 2,000 lives and rendered about 1.6 million people homeless. Such a disaster shows that we must understand the causes of floods and learn how their risks can be reduced. Floods occur when heavy rainfall leads to the unfettered flow of large quantities of water that the soil is unable to absorb. Monsoon rains were the chief cause of the floods of 2010. Moreover, the soil loses its ability to absorb water in areas where people have chopped down trees without planting new ones. However, the damage of a flood can be greatly reduced if we plan and prepare in time. People should be warned about an imminent flood through announcements on loudspeakers and helped to move to safe places, and livestock and valuable household items should also be shifted to safety. In addition, houses should be built at safe locations, mud walls and rooftops should be repaired before the rainy season, river embankments should be properly secured, and drains should be dug to channelize floodwater. The government should work closely with the communities, provide timely information about imminent hazards, and schools should have safety plans and evacuation drills. In conclusion, we cannot stop natural hazards like floods from happening, but we can certainly make them less damaging. If communities, schools and the government prepare together and take the steps described above, the risks of flood disasters can be mitigated and many lives and homes can be saved.

Writing B — Write a formal dialogue between a flood victim and a news reporter on 'The Relief Measures by the Government'

  • Q: Write a formal dialogue between a flood victim and a news reporter on 'The Relief Measures by the Government'.
    Ans: Reporter: Good morning, sir. I am reporting from the flood-affected area. May I ask you a few questions about the relief measures by the government? Flood Victim: Good morning. Yes, please ask. I will be glad to share our experience. Reporter: How has the flood affected your family and your village? Flood Victim: The flood destroyed our homes and crops. We lost our household items, and many families had to leave their houses and move to safe places. Reporter: What relief has the government provided to the affected people so far? Flood Victim: The government has set up relief camps for the homeless families. We are being provided with food, tents and clean drinking water, and medical teams are treating the sick and protecting us from waterborne diseases. Reporter: Are the announcements and rescue arrangements satisfactory? Flood Victim: Yes, to a large extent. We were warned about the imminent flood through announcements on loudspeakers, and rescue teams helped us and shifted our livestock to safe places. However, more help is still needed for rebuilding our homes. Reporter: What do you expect from the government in the future? Flood Victim: We request the government to secure the river embankments, repair the damaged roads and help us rebuild our houses at safe locations, so that such a disaster does not destroy our lives again. Reporter: Thank you very much for your time, sir. We shall convey your message to our viewers and to the authorities. Flood Victim: Thank you for visiting us and for raising our voice.

mcqs.q: According to the model essay, what were the chief cause of the floods of 2010?
mcqs.why: The model essay in the notes states clearly that monsoon rains were the chief cause of the devastating floods of 2010, which affected approximately 20 million people.

mcqs.q: According to the model essay, why does soil lose its ability to absorb water?
options: Because embankments are built too high
Because drains are dug near rivers
In areas where people have chopped down trees without planting new ones
Because houses are built at safe locations
mcqs.why: The model essay in the notes says the soil loses its ability to absorb water in areas where people have chopped down trees without planting new ones, which contributes to floods.

mcqs.q: According to the model essay, when should mud walls and rooftops be repaired?
options: Only when the government orders it
mcqs.why: The model essay in the notes lists repairing mud walls and rooftops before the rainy season as one of the steps that reduce the damage of a flood.

mcqs.q: According to the model essay, how should floodwater be directed away?
options: By digging drains to channelize floodwater
By blocking all the drains in a town
mcqs.why: The model essay in the notes says drains should be dug to channelize floodwater, alongside securing river embankments and building houses at safe locations.

mcqs.q: What does the concluding paragraph of the model essay say about floods?
options: Floods can be stopped completely by the government
We cannot stop natural hazards like floods, but we can make them less damaging by preparing together
Floods cause no damage if people stay calm
Only schools are responsible for reducing flood risks
mcqs.why: The conclusion in the notes says we cannot stop natural hazards like floods from happening, but we can make them less damaging if communities, schools and the government prepare together.

mcqs.q: In the model dialogue, how did the flood affect the victim's family and village?
options: It destroyed their homes and crops, and they lost their household items
It only damaged the roads slightly
It improved the fertility of their fields
It forced the school to close for a week
mcqs.why: In the model dialogue in the notes, the flood victim says the flood destroyed their homes and crops, they lost their household items, and many families had to move to safe places.

mcqs.q: In the model dialogue, what relief has the government provided, according to the victim?
options: Only cash payments to every family
Relief camps with food, tents and clean drinking water, and medical teams treating the sick
New houses for every affected family
Free boats for all the villagers
mcqs.why: In the model dialogue in the notes, the victim says the government set up relief camps and provided food, tents and clean drinking water, while medical teams treated the sick and protected people from waterborne diseases.

mcqs.q: In the model dialogue, how were the people warned about the flood, according to the victim?
options: Through announcements on loudspeakers, and rescue teams shifted their livestock to safe places
Through messages painted on the embankments
They received no warning at all

mcqs.q: In the model dialogue, what does the victim request from the government for the future?
options: To build a dam in his village only
To secure the river embankments, repair damaged roads and help rebuild houses at safe locations
To provide free seeds for the next crop only
To shift his village to another province
mcqs.why: In the model dialogue in the notes, the victim requests the government to secure the river embankments, repair the damaged roads and help them rebuild their houses at safe locations.

mcqs.q: How does the reporter end the model dialogue?
options: By refusing to publish the victim's story
By thanking the victim and promising to convey his message to the viewers and the authorities
By asking the victim for money
By announcing a new relief camp himself
mcqs.why: In the model dialogue in the notes, the reporter ends by thanking the victim for his time and saying, 'We shall convey your message to our viewers and to the authorities.'

lessons.title: Practice Activities
lessons.notes_html:
Listening and Speaking — Formal and Informal Dialogues

  • Q: Note the difference between the formal dialogue (Admission to a School) and the informal dialogue (Rina and Lubna) given in the unit.
    Ans: The formal dialogue is polite, respectful and purpose-based. Mr. Afzal greets the Principal with 'Good morning, sir. May I come in?', uses full and careful sentences, addresses him as 'Sir' throughout, and thanks him formally at the end: 'Thank you, Sir! I am extremely grateful for the time you have given us.' The informal dialogue between Rina and Lubna is relaxed and friendly. It begins with 'Hi, Lubna. Good to see you.', uses short sentences, contractions and everyday expressions such as 'It was simply fabulous' and 'I hope so.' In short, the formal dialogue uses respectful vocabulary, complete sentences and a serious tone, while the informal dialogue uses casual vocabulary, short forms and a friendly tone.

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-reading

  • Q: Look at the pictograph and predict what the lesson is about.
    Ans: The pictograph shows computers being used to watch a movie, chat with a friend, listen to the news, type a document, use the internet, send e-mail, draw a picture and play games. From these pictures we can predict that the lesson is about the computer and the internet, their different types and parts, and the many ways they are used in our daily life at home, in school and in the office.

Glossary — Word Meanings

  • Q: What does 'brilliant' mean?
    Ans: Extremely clever or impressive.
  • Q: What does 'invention' mean?
    Ans: A thing or idea that has been invented.
  • Q: What does 'amazing' mean?
    Ans: Very surprising, especially in a way that makes one full of pleasure.
  • Q: What does 'activities' mean?
    Ans: A situation in which something is happening or a lot of things are being done.
  • Q: What does 'forecast' mean?
    Ans: A statement about what will happen in future based on information that is available now.
  • Q: What does 'carry out' mean?
    Ans: To put into execution; to complete a task.
  • Q: What does 'manually' mean?
    Ans: By hand rather than a machine.
  • Q: What does 'multiple' mean?
    Ans: More than one.
  • Q: What does 'accuracy' mean?
    Ans: The state of being exact or correct.
  • Q: What does 'enormous' mean?
    Ans: Extremely large.
  • Q: What does 'software' mean?
    Ans: The programs, etc. used to operate a computer.
  • Q: What does 'prototype' mean?
    Ans: The first design of something from which other forms are copied or developed.
  • Q: What does 'transistor' mean?
    Ans: A small electronic device used in computers, radios, televisions, etc. for controlling an electric current as it passes along a circuit.
  • Q: What does 'innovation' mean?
    Ans: The introduction of new things, ideas or ways of doing something.
  • Q: What does 'handier' mean?
    Ans: Easy to use or to do.
  • Q: What does 'navigation' mean?
    Ans: The skill or the process of planning a route for a ship or other vehicle and taking it there; also, the way that you move around a website or the Internet when you are looking for information.

Comprehension A — Answer the following questions

  • Q: Q1. How many paragraphs are there in this essay?
    Ans: There are eight paragraphs in this essay. The first describes the computer and Charles Babbage's first mechanical computer, the second tells about the completion of the Babbage Engine, the third explains hardware and software, the fourth describes the uses of computers and personal computers such as desktops and laptops, the fifth is about handheld computers like iPads and tablets, the sixth is about smart phones and smart TV, the seventh is about the internet, and the last paragraph advises the responsible use of the internet.
  • Q: Q2. What is the main idea of the second last paragraph?
    Ans: The main idea of the second last paragraph is that the internet is a global computer network that connects us to the whole world from our homes. Through the internet we can perform many functions which were initially performed manually, such as making payments online for utility bills, social networking around the world, and browsing websites through search engines for information and education.
  • Q: Q3. Why is a 'program' essential for a computer?
    Ans: A program is essential for a computer because a computer works only by following instructions given to it. These instructions are given through various programs called software. The ability of computers to follow generalized sets of operations, called programs, enables them to perform an extremely wide range of tasks, and software tells the hardware what to do and how to do it. Without a program, the computer cannot perform any task.
  • Q: Q4. What are the different uses of a computer?
    Ans: A computer can perform a variety of tasks very easily. It is used for typing documents, sending emails, playing games and browsing the web. It is also a tool to edit or create spreadsheets, presentations and even videos. According to the pictograph, it is also used to watch movies, chat with friends, listen to the news, draw pictures and use the internet. Even when we withdraw cash from an ATM, wait at a traffic signal or use a calculator, we are using some form of computer.
  • Q: Q5. How has internet facilitated human beings?
    Ans: The internet has greatly facilitated human beings. It is a global computer network providing a variety of information and communication facilities, so we can sit at home and be connected to the whole world. Through the internet we can perform many functions sitting at home which were initially performed manually; for example, we can make payments online for utility bills. The internet has opened doors for social networking around the world, we can browse websites of our interest for information and education through search engines, and we can communicate with friends and family across the globe. Thus, computers and the internet have made access to information, knowledge and entertainment very easy.
  • Q: Q6. How is computer useful for students?
    Ans: A computer is very useful for students because through the internet they can browse websites of their interest for information and education and use search engines to find material for their studies. Students can type their documents and assignments, prepare presentations and spreadsheets, and send and receive emails. In this way, the computer and the internet make learning easier and give students quick access to knowledge from all over the world.

lessons.title: Language Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary A — Use the following phrases in sentences of your own

  • Q: Use 'by virtue of' in a sentence of your own.
    Ans: By virtue of his hard work and honesty, he won the respect of the whole village.
  • Q: Use 'by far' in a sentence of your own.
    Ans: This is by far the most useful machine of modern science.
  • Q: Use 'global village' in a sentence of your own.
    Ans: The internet has turned the whole world into a global village.
  • Q: Use 'brilliant gift' in a sentence of your own.
    Ans: The computer is a brilliant gift of modern science.
  • Q: Use 'store house' in a sentence of your own.
    Ans: A library is a store house of knowledge for students.
  • Q: Use 'every walk of life' in a sentence of your own.
    Ans: People from every walk of life use computers and mobile phones today.
  • Q: Use 'around the globe' in a sentence of your own.
    Ans: Through the internet, we can communicate with our friends and family around the globe.
  • Q: Use 'carry out' in a sentence of your own.
    Ans: The students were asked to carry out the experiment carefully in the laboratory.
  • Q: Use 'useful application' in a sentence of your own.
    Ans: Typing documents is a useful application of the computer in every office.
  • Q: Use 'open doors' in a sentence of your own.
    Ans: Education can open doors to success and a better future.

Vocabulary B — Find the meaning of the following words from the dictionary and identify the part of speech through abbreviation used. Also find guide words and entry words

  • Q: Find the meaning, part of speech, guide words and entry word for 'information'.
    Ans: Meaning: facts or details about somebody or something. Part of speech: noun (abbreviation 'n.'). The entry word is 'information'. Note: guide words are the first and last words printed at the top of a dictionary page, so they differ from dictionary to dictionary; the word is looked up alphabetically in the 'in-' section of the dictionary being used.
  • Q: Find the meaning, part of speech, guide words and entry word for 'harmful'.
    Ans: Meaning: causing damage, injury or danger. Part of speech: adjective (abbreviation 'adj.'). The entry word is 'harmful'. Note: guide words are the first and last words printed at the top of a dictionary page, so they differ from dictionary to dictionary; the word is looked up alphabetically in the 'ha-' section of the dictionary being used.
  • Q: Find the meaning, part of speech, guide words and entry word for 'encounter'.
    Ans: Meaning: to meet somebody or face something unexpectedly; in the lesson, to come across websites while using the internet. Part of speech: verb (abbreviation 'v.'), also used as a noun for an unexpected meeting. The entry word is 'encounter'. Note: guide words are the first and last words printed at the top of a dictionary page, so they differ from dictionary to dictionary; the word is looked up alphabetically in the 'en-' section of the dictionary being used.
  • Q: Find the meaning, part of speech, guide words and entry word for 'website'.
    Ans: Meaning: a place on the internet where a person or organization puts information. Part of speech: noun (abbreviation 'n.'). The entry word is 'website'. Note: guide words are the first and last words printed at the top of a dictionary page, so they differ from dictionary to dictionary; the word is looked up alphabetically in the 'we-' section of the dictionary being used.
  • Q: Find the meaning, part of speech, guide words and entry word for 'payment'.
    Ans: Meaning: the act of paying money for something, or an amount of money paid. Part of speech: noun (abbreviation 'n.'). The entry word is 'payment'. Note: guide words are the first and last words printed at the top of a dictionary page, so they differ from dictionary to dictionary; the word is looked up alphabetically in the 'pa-' section of the dictionary being used.
  • Q: Find the meaning, part of speech, guide words and entry word for 'laptop'.
    Ans: Meaning: a small portable computer that is battery-powered and can be carried and used almost anywhere. Part of speech: noun (abbreviation 'n.'). The entry word is 'laptop'. Note: guide words are the first and last words printed at the top of a dictionary page, so they differ from dictionary to dictionary; the word is looked up alphabetically in the 'la-' section of the dictionary being used.

Vocabulary C — Use internet to find what the following abbreviations stand for

  • Q: What does the abbreviation 'USB' stand for?
    Ans: Universal Serial Bus.
  • Q: What does the abbreviation 'DVD' stand for?
    Ans: Digital Versatile Disc (also called Digital Video Disc).
  • Q: What does the abbreviation 'CD' stand for?
    Ans: Compact Disc.
  • Q: What does the abbreviation 'TV' stand for?
    Ans: Television.
  • Q: What does the abbreviation 'ATM' stand for?
    Ans: Automated Teller Machine.
  • Q: What does the abbreviation 'CPU' stand for?
    Ans: Central Processing Unit.

Grammar — Subject and Object Pronouns: Fill in the blanks with an appropriate subject or object pronoun

  • Q: I met _____ at the party but _____ didn't recognize _____.
    Ans: him, he, me
  • Q: I think I have seen _____ before.
    Ans: him
  • Q: You shouldn't have done this to _____.
    Ans: me
  • Q: Where could _____ have gone at this hour of the night?
    Ans: he
  • Q: He took _____ with _____.
    Ans: me, him
  • Q: All of _____ arrived on time.
    Ans: us

Grammar — Possessive Pronouns: Fill in the blanks with appropriate possessive pronoun

  • Q: Maria has already eaten her lunch, but I'm saving _____ until later.
    Ans: mine
  • Q: My computer is a Mac, but _____ is a PC.
    Ans: yours
  • Q: We gave them our telephone number, and they gave us _____.
    Ans: theirs
  • Q: My pencil is broken. Can I borrow _____?
    Ans: yours
  • Q: Our car is cheap, but _____ is expensive.
    Ans: yours
  • Q: You can't have any chocolate! It's all _____.
    Ans: mine

Grammar — Reflexive Pronouns: Fill in the blanks with appropriate reflexive pronoun

  • Q: Rashid made this T-shirt _____.
    Ans: himself
  • Q: Lubna did the homework _____.
    Ans: herself
  • Q: We helped _____ to some cola at the party.
    Ans: ourselves
  • Q: Samina, did you take the photo by _____?
    Ans: yourself
  • Q: I wrote this poem _____.
    Ans: myself
  • Q: He cut _____ with the knife while he was doing the dishes.
    Ans: himself

Grammar — Emphatic Pronouns

  • Q: What is an emphatic pronoun? Give examples from the unit.
    Ans: An emphatic pronoun is a reflexive pronoun used to emphasize another noun or pronoun in the sentence. For example, in 'Asma will do it herself', the emphatic pronoun 'herself' emphasizes that Asma will do it. Similarly, in 'The scouts cooked these cakes themselves', the emphatic pronoun 'themselves' emphasizes that the scouts cooked the cakes.

Grammar — Relative Pronouns: Fill in the blanks with relative pronouns who, which or that

  • Q: Mr. Asim, _____ is a taxi driver, lives on the corner.
    Ans: who
  • Q: We often visit our aunt in Charsadda _____ is in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
    Ans: which
  • Q: That's Adnan, the boy _____ has just arrived at the airport.
    Ans: who
  • Q: Thank you very much for your e-mail _____ was very interesting.
    Ans: which

Grammar — Indefinite Pronouns: Fill in the blanks with indefinite pronouns

  • Q: Would you like _____ to eat?
    Ans: something
  • Q: It was really dark and I couldn't see _____.
    Ans: anything
  • Q: Does _____ live in that house?
    Ans: anyone
  • Q: It doesn't matter where we go. We can go _____ we want to.
    Ans: anywhere
  • Q: This is boring. There's _____ to do.
    Ans: nothing

Grammar — Pronoun-Antecedent Agreement: Fill in the pronoun that agrees with its antecedent

  • Q: A person needs to see _____ dentist twice a year.
    Ans: his
  • Q: The committee members put _____ signatures on the document.
    Ans: their
  • Q: If any one of the sisters needs a ride, _____ can call me.
    Ans: she
  • Q: Each of these companies had _____ books audited.
    Ans: its
  • Q: Some of the crockery has lost _____ shine.
    Ans: its

Grammar — Question Words: Make questions for the following sentences using question words (who, why, how, what, when etc.)

  • Q: Make a question for the sentence using a question word: Bashir designed this house.
    Ans: Who designed this house?
  • Q: Make a question for the sentence using a question word: The weather is fine.
    Ans: How is the weather?
  • Q: Make a question for the sentence using a question word: She walks home from school because she does not have transport facility.
    Ans: Why does she walk home from school?
  • Q: Make a question for the sentence using a question word: The children are solving the sum.
    Ans: What are the children doing?
  • Q: Make a question for the sentence using a question word: Palwasha runs with her dog on Sundays.
    Ans: When does Palwasha run with her dog?

lessons.title: Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Writing A — Complete the mind map and write a unified paragraph on 'Computer'

  • Q: Complete the mind map on 'Computer' after brainstorming.
    Ans: Mind map on 'Computer' — Centre: Computer. Branch 1 (What it is): an electronic machine; one of the most brilliant gifts of modern science; solves problems by following instructions called programs. Branch 2 (Parts): hardware — keyboard, mouse, monitor, computer case, wires, transistors and circuits; software — programs such as web browsers, games and word processors that tell the hardware what to do. Branch 3 (Types): desktop computers, laptop computers, handheld computers such as iPads and tablets, smart phones and smart TV. Branch 4 (Uses): typing documents, sending emails, playing games, browsing the web, making spreadsheets, presentations and videos, paying utility bills online and withdrawing cash from ATMs.
  • Q: Write a unified paragraph on 'Computer' using specific words, vivid verbs and modifiers, with appropriate supporting details and transitional devices.
    Ans: The computer is one of the most brilliant gifts of modern science. It is an electronic machine that solves various problems by following instructions given to it through programs called software. A modern computer comprises hardware and software: the keyboard, mouse, monitor and circuits form the hardware, while programs such as web browsers, games and word processors form the software that tells the hardware what to do. Computers perform a variety of tasks very easily; for example, we use them for typing documents, sending emails, playing games, browsing the web and preparing spreadsheets, presentations and videos. Moreover, they come in many forms, such as desktops, portable laptops, handy tablets and smart phones. Through the internet, a global computer network, we can even pay our utility bills online and communicate with people around the globe. In short, computers have become a part of our everyday lives at home, in school and in the office, and life without them is now unimaginable.

lessons.title: Practice Activities
lessons.notes_html:
Listening and Speaking — Conversation on the telephone

  • Q: Work in pairs and develop a dialogue to demonstrate appropriate expressions and etiquettes for a telephonic conversation.
    Ans: Kamal: Hello, this is Kamal on the line. Is that Nabeel? Nabeel: Hello, Kamal. Yes, this is Nabeel speaking. How are you? Kamal: I am fine, thank you. I called to ask about our computer class tomorrow. Will Sir take the test on hardware and software? Nabeel: I am sorry, I am not sure about it. Rashid may know. Rashid is not in at the moment. Would you like to leave a message for him? Kamal: Yes, please. Please tell him to call me back this evening. Could you please repeat your number, so that I note it correctly? Nabeel: Certainly. It is 0345-1234567. Can you speak a little louder, please? The line is not very clear. Kamal: Of course. Is it clear now? Nabeel: Yes, it is fine now. I will surely give your message to Rashid. Kamal: Thank you for your time, Nabeel. It was nice speaking to you. I must hang up now. Nabeel: You are welcome, Kamal. I'll speak to you again. Do call again. Goodbye. Kamal: Goodbye.

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Reading — Deduce the meaning of the following words

  • Q: Deduce the meaning of the word: awake
    Ans: In the poem awake means having woken up and become active. The dawn is spoken of as if it has woken up from sleep, so a new day and a new hope have begun.
  • Q: Deduce the meaning of the word: flame
    Ans: A flame is the hot, bright, burning part of a fire. In the poem the first red and golden light of the rising sun in the east is compared to a smouldering flame and fire.
  • Q: Deduce the meaning of the word: higher
    Ans: Higher means at a greater height above the ground. In the poem the golden light of the sun rises higher and higher over the whole grey sky.
  • Q: Deduce the meaning of the word: light
    Ans: Light means the brightness that comes from the sun and makes things visible. In the poem the boon of light also stands for hope and freedom, which the people had longed for and waited for a long time.

Glossary

  • Q: What does the word 'forlorn' mean?
    Ans: Forlorn means pitifully sad and abandoned or lonely, and unlikely to succeed or come true.
  • Q: What does the word 'paean' mean?
    Ans: A paean is a song of praise or triumph.
  • Q: What does the word 'smouldering' mean?
    Ans: Smouldering means burning slowly without a flame.
  • Q: What does the word 'dawn' mean?
    Ans: Dawn is the time of day when light first appears.
  • Q: What does the word 'ignites' mean?
    Ans: Ignites means to start to burn, or to make something start to burn.
  • Q: What does the word 'fragrance' mean?
    Ans: Fragrance is a pleasant smell.
  • Q: What does the word 'borne' mean?
    Ans: In the glossary, borne is explained as the start of an idea or feeling. In the line 'The torch of gold is borne', the golden torch of the sun is carried up into the sky.
  • Q: What does the word 'pent-up' mean?
    Ans: Pent-up describes a feeling that cannot be expressed or released.
  • Q: What does the word 'eternal' mean?
    Ans: Eternal means without an end, existing or continuing forever.
  • Q: What does the word 'boon' mean?
    Ans: A boon is something that is very helpful and makes life easier for you.
  • Q: What does the word 'mingled' mean?
    Ans: Mingled means combined, or made to combine with another thing.
  • Q: What does the word 'numb' mean?
    Ans: Numb means unable to feel, think or react in the normal way.

Comprehension A — Answer the following questions

  • Q: Q1. What is the mood of the poem? How does the use of figurative language by poet contribute to the mood of the poem?
    Ans: The mood of the poem is joyful, hopeful and triumphant, although it also remembers past suffering. Figurative language makes this mood strong and lively: the dawn is personified as a person who is awake, the sun is a metaphorical torch of gold, and music is shown singing in the hills. These bright and living images fill the poem with hope, energy and happiness.
  • Q: Q2. What is the theme of the poem?
    Ans: The theme of the poem is awakening and freedom after a long period of slavery, suffering and darkness. Just as dawn ends the night and brings golden light, a new age of hope, dreams and spring has come for the people who had waited for it for a long time.
  • Q: Q3. Do you like the poem 'The Dawn's Awake'? Why?
    Ans: Yes, I like the poem because it gives a message of hope after hardship. Its beautiful images of golden light, singing hills, fragrance and eternal spring show that sorrow does not last forever and that a bright and free future comes at last.
  • Q: Q4. Reread first and second stanza of the poem. What natural item is described as having human characteristics and what human characteristics does this item have?
    Ans: The natural item is the dawn. It is personified in the repeated line 'The Dawn's awake!', which gives it the human characteristic of waking up from sleep. The dawn is treated like a living person who wakes up and becomes active at the start of the new day.
  • Q: Q5. Identify the rhyming words in the poem.
    Ans: The main rhyming pairs in the poem are: fire and higher, forlorn and borne, thrills and hills, and song and long. These rhyming words give the poem music and rhythm.
  • Q: Q6. Identify an example of metaphor in the poem, explain which two things are being compared.
    Ans: An example of metaphor is 'The torch of gold is borne'. Here the rising sun is directly compared to a torch of gold carried up into the sky. The two things compared are the sun and a golden torch, and the comparison shows the brightness and glory of the sunrise.

Comprehension B — Choose the correct option

  • Q: Read these lines from the poem: 'A paean of eternal spring / Voices the new awakening.' What does this mean in the poem?
    Options: The spring season has arrived after months of autumn. / The spring season is singing a song after years of silence. / It is time of freedom and victory after years of slavery. / The voice of spring can be heard after years of silence.
    Ans: It is time of freedom and victory after years of slavery.
  • Q: Read these lines from the poem: 'Faint snatches of half-forgotten song — Fathers! Torn and numb, — The boon of light we craved, awaited long,' What is the tone of these lines?
    Options: These lines are sad and express suffering. / These lines are gloomy and express joy. / These lines are joyful and express pleasure. / These lines are cheerful and express enjoyment.
    Ans: These lines are sad and express suffering.
  • Q: Read this line from the last stanza of the poem: 'The boon of light we craved, awaited long,' What does the phrase 'awaited long' mean?
    Options: something that someone has been waiting for a long time / something that someone has not been anticipating / something that someone has unlooked for / something that someone has not been waiting for a long time
    Ans: something that someone has been waiting for a long time
  • Q: What feature of 'The Dawn's Awake' tells the reader that it is a poem?
    Options: It tells a story. / It is about nature. / It is written in stanzas. / It has personification.
    Ans: It is written in stanzas.
  • Q: Which line from the poem supports the idea that an early or flourishing stage of development is everlasting?
    Options: The dawn of a thousand dreams and thrills. / And music singing in the hills. / A paean of eternal spring. / Voices the new awakening.
    Ans: A paean of eternal spring.

lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary B — Use dictionary to find word definition, pronunciation, syllable division and stress pattern

  • Q: Give the definition, syllable division and stress pattern of the word: flash
    Ans: Flash means a sudden bright burst of light or fire. It has one syllable: flash, and the stress falls on the whole word.
  • Q: Give the definition, syllable division and stress pattern of the word: crave
    Ans: Crave means to long for something very strongly. It has one syllable: crave, and the stress falls on the whole word.
  • Q: Give the definition, syllable division and stress pattern of the word: torch
    Ans: A torch is a flame or light that is carried, or a device that gives light. It has one syllable: torch, and the stress falls on the whole word.
  • Q: Give the definition, syllable division and stress pattern of the word: gold
    Ans: Gold is a precious yellow metal, and also its shining yellow colour. It has one syllable: gold, and the stress falls on the whole word.
  • Q: Give the definition, syllable division and stress pattern of the word: dream
    Ans: A dream is a hope or wish for the future, or pictures seen in sleep. It has one syllable: dream, and the stress falls on the whole word.
  • Q: Give the definition, syllable division and stress pattern of the word: spring
    Ans: Spring is the season after winter when plants begin to grow again. It has one syllable: spring, and the stress falls on the whole word.
  • Q: Give the definition, syllable division and stress pattern of the word: thrill
    Ans: A thrill is a sudden strong feeling of excitement and pleasure. It has one syllable: thrill, and the stress falls on the whole word.
  • Q: Give the definition, syllable division and stress pattern of the word: harmony
    Ans: Harmony is a pleasing combination of musical notes, or peaceful agreement. It has three syllables: har-mo-ny, and the stress falls on the first syllable, HAR.
  • Q: Give the definition, syllable division and stress pattern of the word: faint
    Ans: Faint means weak and not clear or strong. It has one syllable: faint, and the stress falls on the whole word.
  • Q: Give the definition, syllable division and stress pattern of the word: torn
    Ans: Torn means pulled apart or ripped, and in the poem it describes people worn out by suffering. It has one syllable: torn, and the stress falls on the whole word.
  • Q: Give the definition, syllable division and stress pattern of the word: whisper
    Ans: A whisper is a very soft, low voice or sound. It has two syllables: whis-per, and the stress falls on the first syllable, WHIS.
  • Q: Give the definition, syllable division and stress pattern of the word: snatch
    Ans: A snatch is a short part or small piece of something, such as a few lines of a song. It has one syllable: snatch, and the stress falls on the whole word.
  • Q: Give the definition, syllable division and stress pattern of the word: east
    Ans: East is the direction from which the sun rises. It has one syllable: east, and the stress falls on the whole word.
  • Q: Give the definition, syllable division and stress pattern of the word: await
    Ans: Await means to wait for something or someone. It has two syllables: a-wait, and the stress falls on the second syllable, WAIT.

lessons.title: Language Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary A — Poetic Devices: Metaphor, Simile and Personification

  • Q: 1. Metaphor is present in the first stanza: 'The torch of gold is borne.' This is a metaphor because _____
    Ans: This is a metaphor because the rising sun is directly called a torch of gold, without using like or as. One thing, the sun, is said to be another unlike thing, a golden torch, to show its bright golden light.
  • Q: 2. Personification is present in the first line: 'The Dawn's awake!' This is personification because _____
    Ans: This is personification because the dawn, which is not a human being, is given the human quality of waking up from sleep. The dawn is shown as if it were a person who has awoken.
  • Q: 3. Personification is present in the line: 'And music singing in the hills.' This is personification because _____
    Ans: This is personification because music, which cannot really sing, is given the human action of singing. The sweet sounds in the hills are described as if music itself were a singer.
  • Q: 4. Personification is present in the line: 'Voices the new awakening.' This is personification because _____
    Ans: This is personification because the paean of eternal spring is given a human voice and the human power of speaking. Spring is shown as if it could voice, or speak out, the new awakening.

Vocabulary C — Find three nouns from the poem then change those adverbs into adjectives

  • Q: Note: about the wording of this task
    Ans: As printed, the task asks for three nouns from the poem and then speaks of changing adverbs into adjectives. It is solved here in the only way that fits the poem: three nouns from the poem are given with their adjective forms.
  • Q: Give a noun from the poem and change it into an adjective: gold
    Ans: Gold is a noun in the line 'The torch of gold is borne'. Its adjective form is golden, as in 'the golden light of the sun'.
  • Q: Give a noun from the poem and change it into an adjective: music
    Ans: Music is a noun in the line 'And music singing in the hills'. Its adjective form is musical, as in 'a musical voice filled the hills'.
  • Q: Give a noun from the poem and change it into an adjective: dream
    Ans: Dream is a noun in the line 'The dawn of a thousand dreams and thrills'. Its adjective form is dreamy, as in 'a dreamy morning sky'.

Grammar — Helping Verbs: Identify the helping verb(s) in each sentence

  • Q: Identify the helping verb(s): 1. My sister has promised to come with us to Bunair.
    Ans: The helping verb is 'has'. It helps the main verb 'promised'.
  • Q: Identify the helping verb(s): 2. Samina and Dawood will prepare a presentation for the class.
    Ans: The helping verb is 'will'. It helps the main verb 'prepare'.
  • Q: Identify the helping verb(s): 3. We should read another story book.
    Ans: The helping verb is 'should'. It helps the main verb 'read'.
  • Q: Identify the helping verb(s): 4. We should not waste our time watching TV.
    Ans: The helping verb is 'should'. It helps the main verb 'waste'.
  • Q: Identify the helping verb(s): 5. My brother will be flying out of Karachi tomorrow morning.
    Ans: The helping verbs are 'will' and 'be'. They help the main verb 'flying'.
  • Q: Identify the helping verb(s): 6. We have been studying all week for the final exam.
    Ans: The helping verbs are 'have' and 'been'. They help the main verb 'studying'.
  • Q: Identify the helping verb(s): 7. I can help you tonight if you will drive me home later.
    Ans: The helping verbs are 'can' and 'will'. 'Can' helps 'help', and 'will' helps 'drive'.
  • Q: Identify the helping verb(s): 8. I know that I must make a decision soon, but first I may ask my teacher for advice.
    Ans: The helping verbs are 'must' and 'may'. 'Must' helps 'make', and 'may' helps 'ask'.
  • Q: Identify the helping verb(s): 9. Maria could not start her car this morning, so she will probably not go to work today.
    Ans: The helping verbs are 'could' and 'will'. 'Could' helps 'start', and 'will' helps 'go'.

Grammar — Linking Verbs: Make use of following verbs as linking verbs in your own sentences

  • Q: Use 'seem' as a linking verb in your own sentence.
    Ans: The sky seems clear and bright this morning. Here 'seems' links the subject 'sky' with its description.
  • Q: Use 'become' as a linking verb in your own sentence.
    Ans: After hard work, he became a successful lawyer. Here 'became' links the subject 'he' with what he turned into.
  • Q: Use 'is / are / am' as a linking verb in your own sentence.
    Ans: I am a student, and my teachers are kind and helpful. Here 'am' and 'are' link the subjects with their descriptions.
  • Q: Use 'was / were' as a linking verb in your own sentence.
    Ans: The morning was cold, but the children were happy. Here 'was' and 'were' link the subjects with their past states.

Grammar — Modal Verbs: Rewrite the sentences and use the verbs can, may or must

  • Q: She will return tonight. She _____ return tonight.
    Ans: must
  • Q: Don't stand up! You _____ stand up!
    Ans: must not
  • Q: I'm sure they will finish it in a minute. They _____ finish it in a minute.
    Ans: can
  • Q: Please, do it for me. _____ you do it for me?
    Ans: Can
  • Q: I'd like to see your children. _____ I see your children?
    Ans: May

Grammar — Fill in the blanks with modal verbs i.e. could / couldn't, should / shouldn't, must / mustn't, may / may not, can / can't

  • Q: 1. I didn't feel very well yesterday. I _____ eat anything.
    Ans: couldn't
  • Q: 2. You _____ look at me when I am talking to you.
    Ans: should
  • Q: 3. I was using my pencil a minute ago. It _____ be here somewhere!
    Ans: must
  • Q: 4. You _____ forget your sun cream. It's going to be very hot!
    Ans: mustn't
  • Q: 5. _____ I go to the bathroom, please?
    Ans: May
  • Q: 6. His excuse _____ be true, but I don't believe.
    Ans: may

Grammar — Infinitives: Use the following verb as infinitives in your own sentences

  • Q: Use 'eat' as an infinitive in your own sentence.
    Ans: We went to the market to eat fresh fruit. Here 'to eat' is the infinitive.
  • Q: Use 'speak' as an infinitive in your own sentence.
    Ans: She stood up to speak before the class. Here 'to speak' is the infinitive.
  • Q: Use 'smash' as an infinitive in your own sentence.
    Ans: The boy tried to smash the old pot with a stone. Here 'to smash' is the infinitive.
  • Q: Use 'talk' as an infinitive in your own sentence.
    Ans: I called my friend to talk about our homework. Here 'to talk' is the infinitive.
  • Q: Use 'help' as an infinitive in your own sentence.
    Ans: He came early to help his teacher in the classroom. Here 'to help' is the infinitive.

options: The sky seems clear and bright this morning.

options: We went to the market to eat fresh fruit.

options: He came early to help his teacher in the classroom.

lessons.title: Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Writing A — Paraphrase the second stanza of the poem

  • Q: What is paraphrasing?
    Ans: Paraphrasing is re-writing the poet's words or ideas in your own words without altering the meaning. In a paraphrase a stanza takes the shape of prose and stays about the same length as the original, because the purpose is to re-phrase without leaving out any important point.
  • Q: Paraphrase the second stanza of the poem: 'The Dawn's awake! / The dawn of a thousand dreams and thrills / And music singing in the hills / A paean of eternal spring / Voices the new awakening.'
    Ans: Paraphrase: The dawn has come at last. This new dawn brings with it a thousand hopes, dreams and feelings of joy and excitement. Sweet sounds are heard in the hills, as if music itself were singing there. It is like a song of praise for an everlasting spring, and this song announces and gives voice to the new awakening of the people after their long suffering.

Writing B — Write the summary of the poem

  • Q: Write the summary of the poem 'The Dawn's Awake'.
    Ans: Summary: In 'The Dawn's Awake', Otto Leland Bohanan celebrates the coming of dawn as a symbol of freedom after long slavery and suffering. The golden sun rises like a torch over the grey sky, sweet music sings in the hills, and a song of eternal spring announces a new awakening full of dreams and thrills. At the end the poet joyfully declares that the blessing of light, which the suffering fathers had longed for and awaited for so long, has come at last.

mcqs.q: What is paraphrasing, according to the notes?
options: Copying the poet's words exactly as they are
Re-writing the poet's words or ideas in your own words without altering the meaning

Changing the meaning of a stanza completely
mcqs.why: The notes define paraphrasing as re-writing the poet's words or ideas in your own words without altering the meaning.

options: It becomes a much longer poem in verse
It takes the shape of prose and stays about the same length as the original

mcqs.why: The notes say that in a paraphrase a stanza takes the shape of prose and stays about the same length as the original.

options: Only silence and darkness for the people
A long winter of suffering and slavery

mcqs.why: The paraphrase says this new dawn brings with it a thousand hopes, dreams and feelings of joy and excitement.

options: Loud drums are beaten by the farmers in the hills
Sweet sounds are heard in the hills, as if music itself were singing there

The hills echo with the noise of a market

mcqs.q: In the paraphrase, the paean of eternal spring is described as what?
options: A cry of sorrow for the lost fathers

chapters.title: Unit 6: The Founding Father of Pakistan

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-reading

  • Q: Pre-reading: Look at the title and predict what the lesson is all about.
    Ans: From the title 'The Founding Father of Pakistan' and the picture of the Mazar-e-Quaid, we can predict that the lesson is about Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah. It tells how he was born and educated, how he became a great lawyer and leader, and how, through his wise and untiring leadership, he created Pakistan for the Muslims of the Sub-continent.

Glossary

  • Q: What does the word 'concerted' mean?
    Ans: Concerted means done in a planned and determined way, especially by more than one person, government, country, etc.
  • Q: What does the word 'reconciliation' mean?
    Ans: Reconciliation is an end to a disagreement and the start of a good relationship again.
  • Q: What does the word 'ebb' mean?
    Ans: Ebb is the period of time when the sea flows away from the land. In the lesson, 'at its lowest ebb' means at its weakest and lowest point.
  • Q: What does the word 'ignited' mean?
    Ans: Ignited means to start to burn, or to make something start to burn. In the lesson it is used for kindling new inspiration among the Muslims.
  • Q: What does the word 'consciousness' mean?
    Ans: Consciousness is the state of being able to use your senses and mental powers to understand what is happening.
  • Q: What does the word 'channelized' mean?
    Ans: Channelized means directed money, feelings, ideas, etc. towards a particular thing or purpose.
  • Q: What does the word 'visionary' mean?
    Ans: Visionary means original and showing the ability to think about or plan the future with great imagination and intelligence.
  • Q: What does the word 'noble' mean?
    Ans: Noble means having fine personal qualities that people admire, such as courage, honesty and care for others.
  • Q: What does the word 'ambassador' mean?
    Ans: An ambassador is an official who lives in a foreign country as the senior representative there of his or her own country.
  • Q: What does the word 'span' mean?
    Ans: Span is the length of time that something lasts or is able to continue.
  • Q: What does the word 'inspiration' mean?
    Ans: Inspiration is the process that takes place when somebody sees or hears something that causes them to have exciting new ideas or makes them want to create something.
  • Q: What does the word 'tenacity' mean?
    Ans: Tenacity is the quality of not giving up something easily; the quality of being determined.

Comprehension A — Answer the following questions

  • Q: Q1. Why was Jinnah called the Ambassador of Hindu-Muslim Unity?
    Ans: Jinnah was called the Ambassador of Hindu-Muslim Unity because he brought about reconciliation between the Congress Party and the Muslim League in the form of the Lucknow Pact of 1916. It was Sarojini Naidu who gave him this title for his great work for unity between Hindus and Muslims.
  • Q: Q2. What great qualities did M. A. Jinnah show when he was a school boy?
    Ans: As a school boy, M. A. Jinnah was keenly devoted to his studies. He was disciplined and punctual and strictly observed the rules of the school. These habits were signs of his future greatness, and his teachers loved him dearly for his outstanding qualities.
  • Q: Q3. What disillusioned Quaid-e-Azam at the beginning of his political career?
    Ans: At the beginning of his political career, Quaid-e-Azam firmly believed in the concerted struggle of all communities for the freedom of the Sub-continent. He was disillusioned when he realized that the ambition of the Congress was to establish Hindu rule in India. So he left the Congress in 1920 and devoted his services to the uplift of the Muslim League.
  • Q: Q4. Why did Gandhi call Quaid-e-Azam as 'an impossible man'?
    Ans: Gandhi called Quaid-e-Azam 'an impossible man' because Quaid-e-Azam would never compromise on his principles. He stood like a rock against his opponents, so no one could move him from his stand for the rights of the Muslims.
  • Q: Q5. Why do the people call M. A. Jinnah, the father of the nation?
    Ans: People call M. A. Jinnah the father of the nation because he turned the dream of the Muslims of India into reality by creating Pakistan. His untiring labour, missionary zeal and exemplary leadership gave the Muslims a separate homeland of their own, so the whole nation honours him as its father.
  • Q: Q6. Describe the qualities of the Quaid-e-Azam in four sentences.
    Ans: Quaid-e-Azam was a highly intelligent, strictly disciplined and hardworking man. He was supremely self-confident and a man of very strong determination. His integrity was beyond reproach, and he never compromised on his principles. He led his movement with great skill and tenacity until Pakistan came into being.
  • Q: Q7. Read the third paragraph fast and give its theme.
    Ans: The theme of the third paragraph is Quaid-e-Azam's early belief in joint struggle and Hindu-Muslim unity, followed by his disillusionment with the Congress. It shows how he first worked for the freedom of all communities together and brought about the Lucknow Pact, but then, realizing the real aim of the Congress, he left it in 1920 and devoted himself to the Muslim League.

mcqs.q: What does the word 'concerted' mean in the lesson on Quaid-e-Azam?
options: Done in a planned and determined way, especially by more than one person
Done quietly by a single person alone
Done without any plan or purpose
Done only in time of war
mcqs.why: The glossary defines concerted as done in a planned and determined way, especially by more than one person, government or country.

mcqs.q: What does 'reconciliation' mean in the notes?
options: A strong wish to succeed in life

The length of time something lasts
A state of being able to use the senses

options: At its strongest and highest point
At the time when the sea flows in

At the start of a new movement

mcqs.why: The notes state that it was Sarojini Naidu who gave Jinnah this title for his great work for unity between Hindus and Muslims.

mcqs.why: Comprehension Q3 says he was disillusioned when he realized the Congress aimed at Hindu rule, so he left it in 1920 for the Muslim League.

options: Because Quaid-e-Azam often changed his decisions

mcqs.why: Comprehension Q4 explains that Gandhi used these words because Quaid-e-Azam never compromised on his principles and stood like a rock.

lessons.title: Sounds and Speaking
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary A — Use dictionary to identify word definition, syllable division, stress pattern and part of speech

  • Q: Give the definition, syllable division, stress pattern and part of speech of the word: keenly
    Ans: Keenly means in an eager and strongly interested way. It is an adverb. It has two syllables, keen-ly, with the stress on the first syllable, KEEN.
  • Q: Give the definition, syllable division, stress pattern and part of speech of the word: devoted
    Ans: Devoted means giving a lot of time and love to something or someone. It is an adjective. It has three syllables, de-vot-ed, with the stress on the second syllable, VOT.
  • Q: Give the definition, syllable division, stress pattern and part of speech of the word: punctual
    Ans: Punctual means arriving or doing something at the right time, not late. It is an adjective. It has three syllables, punc-tu-al, with the stress on the first syllable, PUNC.
  • Q: Give the definition, syllable division, stress pattern and part of speech of the word: sincerely
    Ans: Sincerely means in a true and honest way, without pretending. It is an adverb. It has three syllables, sin-cere-ly, with the stress on the second syllable, CERE.
  • Q: Give the definition, syllable division, stress pattern and part of speech of the word: ambition
    Ans: Ambition is a strong wish to succeed or to achieve something. It is a noun. It has three syllables, am-bi-tion, with the stress on the second syllable, BI.
  • Q: Give the definition, syllable division, stress pattern and part of speech of the word: untiring
    Ans: Untiring means never becoming tired and never stopping one's effort. It is an adjective. It has three syllables, un-tir-ing, with the stress on the second syllable, TIR.
  • Q: Give the definition, syllable division, stress pattern and part of speech of the word: zeal
    Ans: Zeal is great energy, eagerness and enthusiasm for a cause. It is a noun. It has one syllable, zeal, and the stress falls on the whole word.

options: A noun, with stress on the second syllable, BI
An adjective, with stress on the first syllable, AM
An adverb, with stress on the last syllable, TION

options: Three syllables, and it is an adjective

lessons.title: Language Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary B — Complete analogous pairs below

  • Q: Complete the analogy: Evening is to morning as dinner is to _____
    Options: breakfast / soup / coffee / supper
    Ans: breakfast
  • Q: Complete the analogy: Left is to right as horizontal is to _____
    Options: below / middle / down / vertical
    Ans: vertical
  • Q: Complete the analogy: All is to many as few is to _____
    Options: some / never / none / always
    Ans: some
  • Q: Complete the analogy: Butcher is to knife as hairdresser is to _____
    Options: scissors / hair / curls / blond
    Ans: scissors
  • Q: Complete the analogy: warm is to hot as old is to _____
    Options: oldest / young / years / antique
    Ans: antique

Grammar — Regular and Irregular Verbs: Complete each sentence with the appropriate past form of the regular / irregular verbs in brackets

  • Q: Last weekend my friend and I _____ (go) to a very nice party.
    Ans: went
  • Q: Afzal, my friend, _____ (buy) a very big present
    Ans: bought
  • Q: and _____ (keep) it in our car;
    Ans: kept
  • Q: then we _____ (drive) for two hours
    Ans: drove
  • Q: and _____ (reach) a very big house.
    Ans: reached
  • Q: We _____ (get) very confused
    Ans: got
  • Q: and a little _____ (scare).
    Ans: scared
  • Q: I _____ (ask) Afzal to go back home,
    Ans: asked
  • Q: but he _____ (insist) on staying.
    Ans: insisted
  • Q: When we _____ (knock) on the door,
    Ans: knocked
  • Q: I _____ (realize) it was open.
    Ans: realized
  • Q: I _____ (hear) a little noise
    Ans: heard
  • Q: and when we _____ (walk) in the house
    Ans: walked
  • Q: most of my friends and family _____ (shout): 'HAPPY BIRTHDAY SAAD!'
    Ans: shouted
  • Q: We _____ (eat) delicious food
    Ans: ate
  • Q: and _____ (enjoy) all night long.
    Ans: enjoyed

Grammar — Transitive and Intransitive Verbs: Use the following words in sentences of your own

  • Q: Use 'stopped' in sentences of your own to show whether it acts transitively, intransitively, or as both.
    Ans: Stopped can be both. Transitive: The driver stopped the bus at the gate. Intransitive: The bus stopped at the gate.
  • Q: Use 'broke' in sentences of your own to show whether it acts transitively, intransitively, or as both.
    Ans: Broke can be both. Transitive: The boy broke the window with a ball. Intransitive: The glass broke into pieces.
  • Q: Use 'melted' in sentences of your own to show whether it acts transitively, intransitively, or as both.
    Ans: Melted can be both. Transitive: The sun melted the snow on the roof. Intransitive: The snow melted in the warm sun.
  • Q: Use 'fell' in sentences of your own to show whether it acts transitively, intransitively, or as both.
    Ans: Fell is intransitive, because it does not take an object. Example: The old tree fell in the storm.
  • Q: Use 'won' in sentences of your own to show whether it acts transitively, intransitively, or as both.
    Ans: Won can be both. Transitive: Our team won the match. Intransitive: Our team won easily.
  • Q: Use 'walk' in sentences of your own to show whether it acts transitively, intransitively, or as both.
    Ans: Walk can be both. Transitive: He walks his younger brother to school every day. Intransitive: We walk to school every morning.
  • Q: Use 'read' in sentences of your own to show whether it acts transitively, intransitively, or as both.
    Ans: Read can be both. Transitive: She read an interesting story last night. Intransitive: He likes to read in the evening.

mcqs.q: How does the verb 'stopped' act, according to the notes?

It is intransitive only and never takes an object
It is neither transitive nor intransitive

mcqs.q: How does the verb 'fell' act, according to the notes?
options: It can be both transitive and intransitive

It is intransitive, because it does not take an object

mcqs.q: How does the verb 'won' act, according to the notes?
options: It can be both transitive and intransitive
It never acts as a verb
mcqs.why: The notes show won as both: transitive in 'Our team won the match' and intransitive in 'Our team won easily'.

mcqs.q: How does the verb 'read' act, according to the notes?
options: It is intransitive only, as in reading in the evening
It is transitive only, as in reading a story

It acts only as a helping verb
mcqs.why: The notes show read as both: transitive in 'She read an interesting story' and intransitive in 'He likes to read in the evening'.

mcqs.q: How does the verb 'melted' act, according to the notes?
options: It can be both transitive and intransitive
It is transitive only, as in the sun melting snow
It is intransitive only, as in snow melting
It is neither, because it is an adjective
mcqs.why: The notes show melted as both: transitive in 'The sun melted the snow' and intransitive in 'The snow melted in the warm sun'.

lessons.title: Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Writing A — Proof read and edit the following text for errors

  • Q: Proof read and edit the following text for errors: 'the beach — do you no what riaz did last weekend. he goed to the beach with his family. First, riaz builded a huge sand castle. then, he collect seashell's and rock's after that, he goed swimming with his brother. riaz has a wonderful time at the beach.' Write the corrected text in full.
    Ans: Corrected text: The Beach. Do you know what Riaz did last weekend? He went to the beach with his family. First, Riaz built a huge sand castle. Then, he collected seashells and rocks. After that, he went swimming with his brother. Riaz had a wonderful time at the beach.
  • Q: List the errors corrected in the proof-reading text about Riaz at the beach.
    Ans: The main corrections are: the title and names begin with capital letters (The Beach, Riaz); 'no' is changed to 'know'; the question ends with a question mark; 'goed' is changed to 'went' and 'builded' to 'built' because go and build are irregular verbs; 'collect' is changed to 'collected' to keep the past tense; the wrong apostrophes in 'seashell's' and 'rock's' are removed because these are simple plurals, seashells and rocks; sentences begin with capital letters (He, Then, After); and 'has' is changed to 'had' to agree with the past time of the story.

mcqs.q: In the proof-reading passage about Riaz, 'goed' is corrected to 'went' because:
options: Go is a regular verb that takes -ed
Go is an irregular verb, so its past form is 'went', not 'goed'
Every verb in the passage must end with -t
'Went' is the present tense of go
mcqs.why: The notes explain that goed is changed to went and builded to built because go and build are irregular verbs.

mcqs.q: In the corrected text, what did Riaz build at the beach?
mcqs.why: The corrected text says: First, Riaz built a huge sand castle at the beach with his family.

mcqs.q: Why are the apostrophes removed from 'seashell's' and 'rock's' in the corrected text?
options: Because they are names of people
Because they are verbs in the past tense
Because these are simple plurals, seashells and rocks, which need no apostrophe
mcqs.why: The notes say the wrong apostrophes are removed because seashells and rocks are simple plurals, not possessives.

mcqs.q: In the proof-reading passage, the word 'no' is corrected to what?
mcqs.why: The notes list this correction: 'no' is changed to 'know' in the question 'Do you know what Riaz did last weekend?'

mcqs.q: Why is 'collect' changed to 'collected' in the corrected text?
options: To make the word a plural noun
To keep the past tense of the story
To turn it into a question
To make it a present continuous verb
mcqs.why: The notes say collect is changed to collected to keep the past tense, since the whole story is about last weekend.

mcqs.q: Why is 'has' changed to 'had' at the end of the corrected text?

  • Q: In groups of three, practice and develop a dialogue to use polite forms to negotiate and reach conclusions. Give a model dialogue.
    Ans: Model dialogue: Student A: Good morning! Shall we decide where to hold our class function? Student B: Good morning. In my opinion, the school hall would be the best place. What do you think? lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-reading

  • Q: Q1. What are handicrafts?
    Ans: Handicrafts are useful and decorative things made by hand by skilled workers, called artisans or craftsmen, instead of being made by machines in factories. Examples are pottery, brassware, wood carving, embroidery, baskets and carpets, and each region makes them in its own designs and patterns.
  • Q: Q2. Can you name handicrafts of your region?
    Ans: The handicrafts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa include brass work of Peshawar, such as household utensils and decoration pieces, marble carving, thread embroidery of Swat, and the Chitrali Patti woven on handlooms and Kadhai done on the Chitrali Chugha. Cane work of the northern areas and hill stations is also famous among tourists.

Comprehension — Answer the following questions

  • Q: Q1. How are the artisan and craftsmen the cultural recognition of Pakistan?
    Ans: The artisans and craftsmen are the cultural recognition of Pakistan because the fascinating handicrafts they produce depict the rich cultural heritage of Pakistan and its glorious history. Their creative designs, colours and attractive texture are famous all over the world, so wherever these handicrafts go, they introduce Pakistan and its culture to the world.
  • Q: Q2. Which are the famous handicrafts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa?
    Ans: The famous handicrafts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa are the brass work of Peshawar, done on household utensils of daily use and decoration pieces, marble carving, and cane work in the northern areas and hill stations. Swat is well-known for thread embroidery, and the Chitrali Patti woven on handlooms and the Kadhai done on the Chitrali Chugha are also very famous.
  • Q: Q3. Which handicrafts is Multan famous for?
    Ans: Multan is famous for its exotic blue pottery, made of the special clay found in the area and noted for its elegance, delicacy of design and decorative patterns. Multan, the city of saints, is also famous for camel-skin lamps and shades decorated in colourful floral patterns.
  • Q: Q4. Which handicraft of Balochistan is dated back to the Palaeolithic age?
    Ans: Marble carving of Balochistan is dated back to the Palaeolithic age. The utility articles of Balochistan include marble carved in decorative patterns, which represent a rare craftsmanship of the area, and the onyx-made show pieces are really eye-catching.
  • Q: Q5. What are the handicrafts of Sialkot and what is it famous for?
    Ans: Sialkot is famous for its predominantly handmade sports goods based on indigenous raw materials, and its sports goods, especially the footballs, have gained worldwide recognition for several decades. Besides sports goods, Sialkot also produces surgical goods and tableware, which are a class of their own, and musical instruments including bagpipes, which are exported to Scotland.
  • Q: Q6. How can handicrafts contribute to the economic growth of the country?
    Ans: Handicrafts contribute to the economic growth of the country because they provide jobs to a large number of people who earn their living by sheer hard work. Many handicrafts, such as carved wooden furniture, sports goods and bagpipes, are exported in huge quantities to other countries, and tourists buy them eagerly, so they bring valuable income and foreign exchange into the country.

Glossary — Word Meanings

  • Q: What does 'heritage' mean?
    Ans: The history, traditions and qualities that a country or society has had for many years and that are considered an important part of its character.
  • Q: What does 'imprints' mean?
    Ans: To have a great effect on something so that it cannot be forgotten, changed, etc.
  • Q: What does 'successive' mean?
    Ans: Following immediately one after the other.
  • Q: What does 'civilization' mean?
    Ans: A society, its culture and its way of life during a particular period of time or in a particular part of the world.
  • Q: What does 'dialect' mean?
    Ans: The form of a language that is spoken in one area with grammar, words and pronunciation that may be different from other forms of the same language.
  • Q: What does 'folklore' mean?
    Ans: The traditions and stories of a country or community.
  • Q: What does 'connoisseur' mean?
    Ans: An expert on matters involving the judgement of beauty, quality or skill in art, food or music.
  • Q: What does 'wrought' mean?
    Ans: Caused something to happen, especially a change; to shape or mould something.
  • Q: What does 'reminiscent' mean?
    Ans: Reminding you of somebody or something from the past.
  • Q: What does 'carving' mean?
    Ans: An object or a pattern made by cutting away material from wood or stone.
  • Q: What does 'ivory' mean?
    Ans: A hard yellowish-white substance like bone that forms the tusks (long teeth) of elephants and some other animals.
  • Q: What does 'inlaid' mean?
    Ans: Of furniture, floors, etc., decorated with designs of wood, metal, etc. that are set into the surface.
  • Q: What does 'pattern' mean?
    Ans: The regular way in which something happens or is done.
  • Q: What does 'exotic' mean?
    Ans: From or in another country, especially a tropical one; seeming exciting and unusual because it is connected with foreign countries.
  • Q: What does 'quilt' mean?
    Ans: A decorative cover for a bed, made of two layers with soft material between them.
  • Q: What does 'glorious' mean?
    Ans: Deserving or bringing great fame and success.
  • Q: What does 'distinctive' mean?
    Ans: Having a quality or characteristic that makes something different and easily noticed.
  • Q: What does 'elegance' mean?
    Ans: The quality of being attractive and showing a good sense of style.
  • Q: What does 'delicacy' mean?
    Ans: The quality of being, or appearing to be, easy to damage or break.
  • Q: What does 'exquisite' mean?
    Ans: Extremely beautiful or carefully made.
  • Q: What does 'woven' mean?
    Ans: To make cloth, a carpet, a basket, etc. by crossing threads or strips across, over and under each other by hand or on a machine called a loom.
  • Q: What does 'boast' mean?
    Ans: To talk with too much pride about something that you have or can do.
  • Q: What does 'bagpipe' mean?
    Ans: A musical instrument.
  • Q: What does 'coveted' mean?
    Ans: To want something very much, especially something that belongs to somebody else.
  • Q: What does 'indigenous' mean?
    Ans: Belonging to a particular place rather than coming to it from somewhere else.

lessons.title: Language Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary B — Find synonyms and antonyms of the following words using thesaurus

  • Q: Give a synonym and an antonym of 'delicacy'.
    Ans: Synonym: fineness / daintiness. Antonym: coarseness / roughness. In the lesson, delicacy means the quality of being easy to damage or break, as in the delicacy of design of the blue pottery.
  • Q: Give a synonym and an antonym of 'decorative'.
    Ans: Synonym: ornamental / beautifying. Antonym: plain / undecorated. Brassware and pottery in the lesson carry decorative patterns painted on them.
  • Q: Give a synonym and an antonym of 'patterns'.
    Ans: Synonym: designs / models. Antonym: disorder / jumble (patterns mean a regular, repeated design or way, so they have no single exact opposite). The artisans paint decorative patterns on the pottery.
  • Q: Give a synonym and an antonym of 'elegant'.
    Ans: Synonym: graceful / stylish. Antonym: clumsy / ungraceful. Cane articles are made in elegant designs decorated with floral patterns.
  • Q: Give a synonym and an antonym of 'indigenous'.
    Ans: Synonym: native / local. Antonym: foreign / imported. The glossary defines indigenous as belonging to a particular place rather than coming to it from somewhere else, as Sialkot's sports goods are based on indigenous raw materials.
  • Q: Give a synonym and an antonym of 'covet'.
    Ans: Synonym: desire / long for. Antonym: dislike / not want. Cane articles are coveted owing to their exquisite craftsmanship, that is, people want them very much.
  • Q: Give a synonym and an antonym of 'floral'.
    Ans: Synonym: flowery / flower-patterned. Antonym: plain / unpatterned (floral has no single exact opposite). Camel-skin lamps and cane articles are decorated in colourful floral patterns.

Grammar A — State whether the following groups of words are phrases, independent clauses or subordinate clauses

  • Q: 1. 'Over my head' — phrase, independent clause or subordinate clause?
    Ans: Phrase. It is a group of words without a subject and a verb, so it cannot stand alone as a complete thought.
  • Q: 2. 'Because I was afraid' — phrase, independent clause or subordinate clause?
    Ans: Subordinate clause. It has a subject 'I' and a verb 'was', but it begins with 'because' and cannot stand alone; it needs an independent clause to complete its meaning.
  • Q: 3. 'I didn't get very much sleep' — phrase, independent clause or subordinate clause?
    Ans: Independent clause. It has a subject 'I' and a predicate 'didn't get very much sleep' and gives a complete thought, so it can stand alone as a sentence.
  • Q: 4. 'That night' — phrase, independent clause or subordinate clause?
    Ans: Phrase. It has neither a subject nor a verb and does not express a complete thought.
  • Q: 5. 'I knew what happened' — phrase, independent clause or subordinate clause?
    Ans: Independent clause. 'I knew what happened' has the subject 'I' and the predicate 'knew what happened' and can stand alone as a complete sentence.
  • Q: 6. 'So that I could get some rest' — phrase, independent clause or subordinate clause?
    Ans: Subordinate clause. It has a subject 'I' and a verb 'could get', but 'so that' makes it dependent, so it cannot stand alone.
  • Q: 7. 'I heard the cat's meow' — phrase, independent clause or subordinate clause?
    Ans: Independent clause. It has a subject 'I' and a predicate 'heard the cat's meow' and expresses a complete thought.
  • Q: 8. 'Sitting by the broken plate licking the crumbs' — phrase, independent clause or subordinate clause?
    Ans: Phrase. It has no subject and no finite verb, so it is only a group of words that must become part of a sentence.
  • Q: 9. 'When I finally got up' — phrase, independent clause or subordinate clause?
    Ans: Subordinate clause. It has a subject 'I' and a verb 'got up', but it begins with 'when' and leaves the thought incomplete, so it must be joined to an independent clause.
  • Q: 10. 'I got so tired' — phrase, independent clause or subordinate clause?
    Ans: Independent clause. It has a subject 'I' and a predicate 'got so tired' and can stand alone as a complete sentence.

Grammar B — Read and analyse each sentence: subjects, predicates and clauses

  • Q: 1. Analyse: 'My sister and I were at my grandma's house when the phone rang.'
    Ans: Subject 1: 'My sister and I'; Predicate 1: 'were at my grandma's house'. Subject 2: 'the phone'; Predicate 2: 'rang'. Clauses: 'My sister and I were at my grandma's house' is an independent clause, and 'when the phone rang' is a subordinate clause.
  • Q: 2. Analyse: 'My sister almost fainted because she was hungry.'
    Ans: Subject 1: 'My sister'; Predicate 1: 'almost fainted'. Subject 2: 'she'; Predicate 2: 'was hungry'. Clauses: 'My sister almost fainted' is an independent clause, and 'because she was hungry' is a subordinate clause.
  • Q: 3. Analyse: 'I love learning, so I spend a lot of time reading.'
    Ans: Subject 1: 'I'; Predicate 1: 'love learning'. Subject 2: 'I'; Predicate 2: 'spend a lot of time reading'. Clauses: the sentence has two independent clauses, 'I love learning' and 'I spend a lot of time reading', joined by the conjunction 'so'.
  • Q: 4. Analyse: 'After working late into the night, Amir fell asleep on his desk.'
    Ans: Subject: 'Amir'; Predicate: 'fell asleep on his desk'. Clauses: the sentence has one independent clause, 'Amir fell asleep on his desk', and 'After working late into the night' is a phrase, not a clause, because it has no subject and no finite verb.
  • Q: 5. Analyse: 'I took the dog to the park.'
    Ans: Subject: 'I'; Predicate: 'took the dog to the park'. Clauses: the sentence has only one independent clause, 'I took the dog to the park', which is a complete sentence by itself.
