lessons.title: Practice Activities
lessons.notes_html:
Listening and Speaking — In groups of four discuss 'Peaceful Co-existence' with reference to the current world scenario and summarize the main points of discussion

  • Q: Summarize the main points of a group discussion on 'Peaceful Co-existence' with reference to the current world scenario.
    Ans: Model summary: Our group discussed that peaceful coexistence is the need of the present world, where people of different religions, colours, languages and countries live together. The main points of our discussion were: first, everyone should be respected regardless of social class, religion, colour or creed. Second, disputes should be solved through patience, forgiveness and dialogue instead of anger and violence. Third, we should help others in the hour of need, as Asfandyar helped Jack, because selfless service creates love and trust between people. Fourth, no one should be ridiculed for his simplicity, poverty or different way of life. In conclusion, our group agreed that if individuals, societies and countries adopt these principles, the world will become peaceful and harmonious, just as Islam teaches us to live with others in peace and harmony.

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-reading

  • Q: Q1. Can you name a few festivals of Pakistan?
    Ans: The important festivals of Pakistan include Eid-ul-Fitr, Eid-ul-Adha, Eid Milad-un-Nabi, Shab-e-Barat, the Urs of famous saints, and national days such as Independence Day on 14th August and Pakistan Day on 23rd March. People also celebrate local and seasonal festivals such as Basant in some areas and the Sindhi and other regional cultural days.
  • Q: Q2. What is your favourite festival? How does your family celebrate it?
    Ans: Model answer: My favourite festival is Eid-ul-Fitr, which we celebrate at the end of the holy month of Ramadan. On this day my family wears new clothes, offers the Eid prayer together, and visits relatives and neighbours. My mother prepares sweet dishes such as sheer khurma, we give Eidi to the children, and we also remember the poor and needy by giving them food and money so that they can share our happiness.

Glossary — Word Meanings

  • Q: What does 'feast' mean?
    Ans: A large or special meal, especially for a lot of people and to celebrate something.
  • Q: What does 'lanterns' mean?
    Ans: A lamp in a transparent case, often a metal case with glass sides, that has a handle, so that you can carry it outside.
  • Q: What does 'mythical' mean?
    Ans: Connected with stories from ancient times, especially ones that were told to explain natural events or to describe the early history of a people.
  • Q: What does 'parade' mean?
    Ans: A public celebration of a special day or event, usually with bands in the streets and decorated vehicles.
  • Q: What does 'manipulating' mean?
    Ans: To control or influence somebody or something, often in a dishonest way so that they do not realize it. In the lesson, it is used for handling and moving the dragon in the dragon dance, where one person manipulates the head and the rest move the body.
  • Q: What does 'intricate' mean?
    Ans: Having a lot of different parts and small details that fit together.
  • Q: What does 'symbolize' mean?
    Ans: A person, an object, an event, etc. that represents a more general quality or situation. As a verb, to symbolize means to represent such a quality.
  • Q: What does 'lunar' mean?
    Ans: Connected with the moon.
  • Q: What does 'phase' mean?
    Ans: A stage in a process of change or development.
  • Q: What does 'inserted' mean?
    Ans: To put something into something else or between two things.
  • Q: What does 'zodiac' mean?
    Ans: The imaginary area in the sky in which the sun, moon and planets appear to lie, and which has been divided into twelve equal parts, each with a special name and symbol.
  • Q: What does 'revenge' mean?
    Ans: Something that you do in order to make somebody suffer because they have made you suffer.
  • Q: What does 'insane' mean?
    Ans: Seriously mentally ill and unable to live in normal society.
  • Q: What does 'firecrackers' mean?
    Ans: A small firework that explodes with a loud noise.
  • Q: What does 'scroll' mean?
    Ans: A decoration cut in stone or wood with a curved shape like a roll of paper. In the lesson, red spring scrolls are hung on windows and doors at the New Year.
  • Q: What does 'longevity' mean?
    Ans: Long life; the fact of lasting a long time.
  • Q: What does 'vitality' mean?
    Ans: Energy and enthusiasm.
  • Q: What does 'supernatural' mean?
    Ans: That cannot be explained by the laws of science and that seems to involve gods or magic.
  • Q: What does 'solar' mean?
    Ans: Of or connected with the sun.
  • Q: What does 'festival' mean?
    Ans: A series of performances of music, plays, films, etc., usually organized in the same place once a year; a series of public events connected with a particular activity or idea.

Comprehension A — Answer the following questions

  • Q: Q1. How is the date fixed for the Chinese New Year?
    Ans: The Chinese New Year is the first day of the first month in the traditional Chinese calendar. It is based on a traditional Chinese lunisolar calendar, whose date indicates both the moon phase and the time of the solar year. A lunar month is around 2 days shorter than a solar month, so in order to catch up with the solar calendar, an extra month is inserted every few years. This is why, according to the solar calendar, the Chinese New Year falls on a different date each year.
  • Q: Q2. Why do Chinese use red colour and fireworks on New Year?
    Ans: According to the legend, the mythical beast Nian was afraid of the red colour and loud noises. The old man put red papers up and set off firecrackers, and the Nian did not harm the village. Since then, the Chinese wear red clothes, hang red lanterns and red spring scrolls, and use firecrackers to frighten away the Nian and evil spirits. Red also represents power, happiness and vitality and is used to bring good fortune, while the noise of fireworks is also believed to wake up the dragon that brings the spring rain for the crops.
  • Q: Q3. How is the Chinese New Year connected to the mythical beast called the Nian?
    Ans: According to tales and legends, the beginning of the Chinese New Year started with a mythical beast called the Nian. The Nian would eat villagers, especially children, so one year all the villagers decided to hide from the beast. An old man stayed back in the village, put red papers up and set off firecrackers to take revenge on the Nian. The next day the villagers returned and saw that nothing was destroyed. They assumed the old man was a deity who had come to save them, and they understood that the Nian was afraid of the red colour and loud noises. From then on, they used red clothes, lanterns, scrolls and firecrackers every New Year, and the Nian never came to the village again.
  • Q: Q4. Do you like the lesson? Why?
    Ans: Yes, I like the lesson very much. It gives interesting information about the most important festival of another nation and its old legends, traditions and beliefs. It tells us how the Chinese clean their houses, exchange gifts, enjoy feasts, perform the dragon dance and celebrate the Lantern Festival. Reading it helps us understand and respect the culture of other people.
  • Q: Q5. What is the most interesting event of the Chinese New Year?
    Ans: The most interesting event of the Chinese New Year is the dragon dance in the large parade down the city streets. People dress up in dragon costumes made of brightly coloured silk, decorated very extravagantly, and some of the dragons are 100 feet long. Men and boys perform intricate dragon dances, with one person manipulating the head of the dragon and the rest moving the body, while firecrackers are thrown at the feet of the dragons to keep them awake for the celebration.

Comprehension B — State whether the following statements are facts or opinion

  • Q: State whether the statement is a fact or an opinion: 'Chinese New Year starts a new animal's zodiac year.'
    Ans: Fact. The lesson states that Chinese years are grouped in sets of 12, with each year being represented by an animal, that is, a zodiac sign, so a new animal's zodiac year begins with the New Year.
  • Q: State whether the statement is a fact or an opinion: 'The noise of fireworks wakes up the dragon that will fly across the sky to bring the spring rain for the crops.'
    Ans: Opinion. The lesson presents this only as one of the beliefs about fireworks: 'One is that the noise wakes up the dragon that will fly across the sky to bring the spring rain for the crops.' It is a traditional belief, not a proven fact.
  • Q: State whether the statement is a fact or an opinion: 'The celebration lasts for 15 days till Lantern Festival.'
    Ans: Fact. The lesson states that New Year's Eve and the first three days are officially observed as holidays, people return to work between the fifth and eighth day, and the spirit of celebration lasts through the Festival of Lanterns on the 15th day of the New Year.
  • Q: State whether the statement is a fact or an opinion: 'The dragon is another popular symbol for Chinese New Year.'
    Ans: Fact. The lesson directly states that the dragon is another popular symbol for Chinese New Year and that it is a symbol of strength, goodness, good luck and supernatural forces.
  • Q: State whether the statement is a fact or an opinion: 'The red colour is used to bring good fortune, and the money inside is used by the children to buy holiday treats.'
    Ans: Fact. The lesson directly states that the red colour of the envelopes is used to bring good fortune and that the money inside is used by the children to buy holiday treats.

Comprehension C — Complete the cloze exercise

  • Q: One very important tradition of the Chinese _____ Year is exchanging gifts.
    Ans: New
  • Q: A traditional gift _____ is given is small red envelopes filled with 'lucky money'.
    Ans: that
  • Q: A traditional gift that is given is small red envelopes filled _____ 'lucky money'.
    Ans: with
  • Q: These envelopes are given to _____ by their family and friends.
    Ans: children
  • Q: The red _____ is used to bring good fortune, and the money inside is used by the children to buy holiday treats.
    Ans: colour
  • Q: The red colour is used to bring good fortune, and _____ money inside is used by the children to buy holiday treats.
    Ans: the
  • Q: The money inside is used by the children _____ buy holiday treats.
    Ans: to
  • Q: These envelopes symbolize the _____ of good fortune.
    Ans: giving

options: It is the first day of the first month in the traditional Chinese lunisolar calendar, so it falls on a different solar date each year
It is fixed by the Lantern Festival

lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary A — Use the following phrases in sentences of your own

Grammar A — Now choose the correct preposition in each sentence

  • Q: 1. Stay _____ the dog. It bites.

    Ans: away from
  • Q: 2. Please get _____ the stage, the performance is about to start.
    Options: off / at / up / in

  • Q: 3. Quick! Get the ball before it rolls _____ the hill.

  • Q: 5. I haven't seen her _____ June.
    Options: in / since / for / on

  • Q: 6. We will next meet _____ the middle of next month.

Grammar B — Complete the following sentences with the correct preposition: to, toward, on, onto, in, or into

  • Q: The dog jumped _____ the lake.
    Ans: into
  • Q: Are the boys still swimming _____ the pool?

  • Q: The plane landed _____ the runway.

  • Q: We drove _____ the river for an hour but turned north before we reached it.

Grammar — Compound Prepositions: Identify the compound preposition in each sentence below

  • Q: 2. In our solar system, one planet next to Earth is Venus. Identify the compound preposition.
    Ans: The compound preposition is 'next to'. Venus is the planet next to Earth.
  • Q: 3. According to old theories, Venus was much like Earth. Identify the compound preposition.
    Ans: The compound preposition is 'according to'. The sentence begins with it: According to old theories.

Grammar — Use of Since and For: Complete the following sentences with since and for

  • Q: Laiba has lived here _____ ten years.
    Ans: for
  • Q: I haven't seen you _____ last March.
    Ans: since
  • Q: We sat and talked _____ 30 minutes.

  • Q: Saman has been learning English _____ March 1999.

  • Q: We haven't had an earthquake _____ 23 years.

  • Q: I haven't heard from you _____ Saturday.

  • Q: Maria hasn't eaten _____ 7:00 this morning.

  • Q: He played basketball _____ over 20 years.

Grammar — Prepositional Phrase: Choose a prepositional phrase to complete each sentence

  • Q: 1. There are lots of birds nesting _____.

  • Q: 2. After school, the children played cricket _____.

  • Q: 5. I gave the children pizza _____ pancakes for breakfast today.

lessons.title: Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Writing — Write two paragraphs of comparison between Chinese New Year and Eid-ul-Fitar

  • Q: Write two paragraphs of comparison between Chinese New Year and Eid-ul-Fitar. Use appropriate similes for comparison and correct connectors of comparison.
    Ans: Paragraph 1: The Chinese New Year and Eid-ul-Fitr are both the most important festivals of their people, and they are celebrated with great joy and preparation. Like the Chinese, who clean their houses, pay off debts, purchase new clothes and even get new haircuts to welcome the New Year, Muslims also clean their homes, wear new clothes and prepare special dishes for Eid. Similarly, both festivals bring families and friends together for large feasts, just as relatives gather at one table on Eid. In the same way, gifts are exchanged on both occasions: the Chinese give children small red envelopes filled with lucky money, and likewise elders give Eidi to children on Eid, as sweet as the love it carries. Paragraph 2: However, the two festivals are different in their basis and meaning. The Chinese New Year is based on a traditional lunisolar calendar and is linked with legends such as the beast Nian, red decorations, fireworks, the dragon dance and the Lantern Festival, whereas Eid-ul-Fitr is a religious festival that comes after the fasting month of Ramadan and is based on the Islamic lunar calendar. Unlike the Chinese New Year, whose celebration lasts for about fifteen days, Eid-ul-Fitr is mainly celebrated for three days. In contrast to the Chinese customs of scaring away evil spirits, Eid is marked by the Eid prayer, thankfulness to Allah and charity to the poor, so that everyone, rich and poor alike, can share its happiness.

mcqs.q: What do the two comparison paragraphs say both festivals are?
options: Both the most important festivals of their people, celebrated with great joy and preparation
mcqs.why: Paragraph 1 in the notes opens by saying Chinese New Year and Eid-ul-Fitr are both the most important festivals of their people, celebrated with joy.

mcqs.why: The notes compare Chinese red envelopes filled with lucky money with elders giving Eidi to children on Eid, using the connector 'likewise'.

options: As sweet as the love it carries
Like a dragon in a parade
mcqs.why: Paragraph 1 in the notes describes Eidi as 'as sweet as the love it carries', a simile comparing Eidi with the love behind it.

mcqs.q: How do the festivals differ in their basis, according to paragraph 2?
options: Chinese New Year follows a lunisolar calendar with legends like Nian, whereas Eid-ul-Fitr follows Ramadan and the Islamic lunar calendar
Eid follows the solar calendar only
mcqs.why: Paragraph 2 contrasts the lunisolar, legend-linked Chinese New Year with Eid-ul-Fitr, a religious festival after Ramadan on the Islamic lunar calendar.

Eid lasts fifteen days and Chinese New Year three
mcqs.why: Paragraph 2 states unlike the Chinese New Year lasting about fifteen days, Eid-ul-Fitr is mainly celebrated for three days.

options: The Eid prayer, thankfulness to Allah and charity to the poor
mcqs.why: Paragraph 2 contrasts Chinese scaring of evil spirits with Eid's prayer, thankfulness to Allah and charity so rich and poor share happiness.

mcqs.why: The notes use 'Similarly' to show likeness — both festivals bring families together — while whereas, unlike and in contrast show difference.

Listening and Speaking — Interview your parents about traditions that you have in your families

  • Q: Interview your parents about a tradition that you have in your family. Ask how the tradition started and what special meanings it has, and share the responses with the class.

My father told me that the tradition was started by his grandfather, who believed that the whole family must begin the day of Eid together. chapters.title: Unit 13: Ibn-e-Sina, A Great Muslim Scientist

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-reading

  • Q: Look at the pictures and predict the content of the lesson.
    Ans: The pictures show Muslim scholars of old times studying books, working with scientific instruments and discussing knowledge in libraries and courts. So the lesson is likely to be about a great Muslim scientist of the past, his education, his studies and his contribution to science.

Glossary

  • Q: What does 'transmission' mean?
    Ans: Transmission means the act or process of passing something from one person, place or thing to another.
  • Q: What does 'feather to cap' mean?
    Ans: It means an achievement to be proud of, an act or deed to one's credit; a distinctive achievement.
  • Q: What does 'credit' mean?
    Ans: As printed in the glossary, credit means an arrangement that you make, with a shop or store for example, to pay later for something you buy. In the lesson, 'to his credit' means to his honour and achievement.
  • Q: What does 'pioneer' mean?
    Ans: A pioneer is a person who is the first to study and develop a particular area of knowledge, culture, etc. that other people then continue to develop.
  • Q: What does 'metaphysics' mean?
    Ans: Metaphysics is the branch of philosophy that deals with the nature of existence, truth and knowledge.
  • Q: What does 'philosophy' mean?
    Ans: Philosophy is the study of the nature and meaning of the universe and of human life.
  • Q: What does 'discoveries' mean?
    Ans: Discoveries mean an act or the process of finding somebody or something, or learning about something that was not known about before.
  • Q: What does 'graphic' mean?
    Ans: Graphic means very clear and full of details, especially about something unpleasant.
  • Q: What does 'encyclopaedia' mean?
    Ans: An encyclopaedia is a book or set of books giving information about all areas of knowledge or about different areas of one particular subject, usually arranged in alphabetical order.
  • Q: What does 'Latin' mean?
    Ans: Latin is the language of ancient Rome and the official language of its empire.
  • Q: What does 'contagious' mean?
    Ans: If a person is contagious, they have a disease that can be spread to other people by touch.
  • Q: What does 'anatomy' mean?
    Ans: Anatomy is the scientific study of the structure of human or animal bodies.

Comprehension A: Answer the following questions

  • Q: Q1. Why is Ibn-e-Sina still remembered today? What is the major work of Ibn-e-Sina and what does it contain?
    Ans: Ibn-e-Sina is still remembered today because his contribution to the world of science was enormous. He was the first to detect the contagious nature of tuberculosis and that diseases spread by water, he showed the close relationship between psychology and health, he worked on anatomy and child health, and he discussed the inter-relationship between time and motion in physics. His great medical work is al-Qanun (The Canon), which contains the medical knowledge of his time and remained a reference book in European universities for centuries. His other great work, Kitab-Al-Shifa, is a philosophical encyclopaedia which covers a wide range of fields like philosophy, science, physics, mathematics, metaphysics, ethics, economics and politics.
  • Q: Q2. What type of training and education do you think Ibn-e-Sina received?
    Ans: Ibn-e-Sina received a broad and deep education in many branches of knowledge. His mother tongue was Persian, so he first studied Arabic under Abu Bakr Ahmad bin Muhammad al-Barqi al-Khwarizmi. After mastering Arabic, his father arranged a teacher of the Qur'an and another for literature for him, and before he was ten years old he knew the Qur'an and a considerable amount of literature. Next he turned to philosophy, geometry and mathematics, and then to medical science, in which he soon surpassed all the scholars of his age. Later, in the great libraries of Bukhara, he read many great books, so that by the age of eighteen he had learned all branches of knowledge of his time.
  • Q: Q3. What was the position of al-Qanun (The Canon) in the western countries?
    Ans: Al-Qanun (The Canon) held a very high position in the western countries. It was translated into Latin towards the end of the twelfth century and became a reference source for medical studies in the universities of Europe until the end of the seventeenth century. In this way, European students of medicine learned from Ibn-e-Sina's book for about five hundred years.
  • Q: Q4. How would you describe Ibn-e-Sina?
    Ans: Ibn-e-Sina was a brilliant, hard-working and curious scholar with an excellent memory. He learned very quickly: he knew the Qur'an and much literature before the age of ten and had mastered all branches of knowledge of his time by eighteen. He was a skilful physician whom other physicians recommended to the ruler of Bukhara, and a deep thinker whose philosophical views engaged the attention of Western thinkers for several centuries. In his own words, his stock of knowledge remained the same as in his youth, but his knowledge became more exact with age.
  • Q: Q5. Write down the theme of the second paragraph.
    Ans: The theme of the second paragraph is the early education of Ibn-e-Sina at the peak of Islamic Arabic culture. It tells that Arabic was the accepted language for the transmission of knowledge in that era, that Ibn-e-Sina, whose mother tongue was Persian, mastered Arabic, and that his father then arranged teachers of the Qur'an and literature for him, so that he learned very rapidly as a young pupil.

Comprehension B: Respond to each statement by writing an explanation as to why you agree or disagree

  • Q: 1. Ibn-e-Sina was a great Muslim Scientist. I agree / disagree because:
    Ans: I agree because Ibn-e-Sina made original contributions in many fields. He detected the contagious nature of tuberculosis, worked on anatomy and child health, discussed time and motion in physics, and wrote famous books on medicine and philosophy that were used in Europe for centuries.
  • Q: 2. His philosophical views have engaged the attention of Western thinkers. I agree / disagree because:
    Ans: I agree because the lesson itself states that his philosophical views have engaged the attention of Western thinkers over several centuries, and his books have been among the most important sources in philosophy. His encyclopaedia Kitab-Al-Shifa covered philosophy, metaphysics, ethics, economics and politics.
  • Q: 3. Muslim world has produced great scientists who had made remarkable contribution to science and technology. I agree / disagree because:
    Ans: I agree because, as the lesson says, Muslim scientists made tireless and valuable research and provided a stronger foundation to the present day science and technology. Ibn-e-Sina is one shining example of this galaxy of Muslim scientists.

lessons.title: Sounds and Speaking
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar: Intonation — practice the following expressions (identify the intonation pattern)

  • Q: Where is the degree college?
    Ans: Falling intonation, because it is a wh-question and the voice falls on the final stressed syllable.
  • Q: What time does the game finish?
    Ans: Falling intonation, because it is a wh-question, like 'What time does the play finish?' in the lesson.
  • Q: I suppose we have completed the book.
    Ans: Fall-rise intonation, because 'I suppose' shows that the speaker is not fully sure and may have more to add.
  • Q: Oh! Here is the newspaper you wanted.
    Ans: Falling intonation, because it is a definite statement, said clearly, like 'OK, here's the magazine you wanted' in the lesson.
  • Q: Are you hungry?
    Ans: Rising intonation, because it is a yes-no question and the voice rises at the end of the sentence.
  • Q: I don't think they will reach tomorrow.
    Ans: Fall-rise intonation, because the speaker is not sure about what he says and may have more to add.

lessons.title: Language Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar: Punctuation — Commas after Introductory Phrase and Colon (rules from the lesson)

  • Q: When do we use a comma after an introductory phrase?
    Ans: When an introductory prepositional phrase is very short (less than four words), the comma is usually optional. But if the phrase is longer than four words, we use a comma. Examples from the lesson: 'Before the match starts, let's get some popcorn.' and 'After riding his bike around the neighborhood twice, Rasheed was sweating profusely.'
  • Q: When do we use a colon to introduce a list of items?
    Ans: We use a colon to introduce an item or a series of items, and we do not capitalize the first item after the colon unless it is a proper noun. Example: 'I want the following items: butter, sugar, and flour.' We must avoid using a colon before a list if it directly follows a verb or preposition, so 'I want butter, sugar, and flour' is correct and 'I want: butter, sugar, and flour' is incorrect.
  • Q: When do we use a colon to introduce a quote?
    Ans: We use a colon to introduce a quotation if the introduction is an independent clause, and we start the quotation with a capital letter. Example from the lesson: The guides always gave the same advice: 'Leave them alone, and they will leave you alone.'

Grammar A: Rewrite each given sentence, adding a colon where necessary

  • Q: 1. These are my favorite colors purple, turquoise, pink and yellow.
    Ans: These are my favorite colors: purple, turquoise, pink and yellow.
  • Q: 2. I bought a lot of grocery at the store bread, meat, chicken and fish.
    Ans: I bought a lot of grocery at the store: bread, meat, chicken and fish.

Grammar B: Rewrite each of the following sentences using a colon

  • Q: 1. I can't believe Jane said, 'I'm not coming.'

lessons.title: Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Writing A: Complete the mind map and write down the summary of the lesson 'Ibn-e-Sina, the Great Muslim Scientist'

  • Q: Complete the mind map of 'Ibn-e-Sina, the Great Muslim Scientist'. The given boxes are: childhood, education, discoveries. Complete the remaining boxes.
    Ans: Mind map — Centre: Ibn-e-Sina, the Great Muslim Scientist. Childhood: born in 980 AD at Afsana near Bukhara; mother tongue Persian; a very quick and intelligent pupil. Education: learned Arabic, the Qur'an and literature before the age of ten; then philosophy, geometry, mathematics and medical science; read the great books in the libraries of Bukhara and by eighteen had learned all branches of knowledge of his time. Discoveries: first detected the contagious nature of tuberculosis and diseases spread by water; close relationship between psychology and health; work on anatomy and child health; in physics, the inter-relationship between time and motion. Major works (remaining box): al-Qanun (The Canon) on medicine and Kitab-Al-Shifa, a philosophical encyclopaedia. Fields of contribution (remaining box): medicine, philosophy, physics, mathematics, geography and chemistry.
  • Q: Write down the summary of the lesson 'Ibn-e-Sina, the Great Muslim Scientist'.
    Ans: Summary: The Muslim world has produced great scientists whose research laid a stronger foundation for present day science, and Abu Ali Hussain Ibn-e-Abdullah Ibn-e-Sina was one of its shining stars. He was born in 980 AD at Afsana near Bukhara and died in Hamdan in 1047. His mother tongue was Persian, but he mastered Arabic, and before the age of ten he knew the Qur'an and a considerable amount of literature. He then studied philosophy, geometry, mathematics and medical science, and soon surpassed all the scholars of his age in medicine. When the ruler of Bukhara, Nuh bin Mansur Samani, fell ill and his physicians failed to cure him, Ibn-e-Sina helped in his treatment and won his favour, gaining permission to study in the ruler's great libraries. By the age of eighteen he had learned all branches of knowledge of his time. His most famous works are on philosophy and medicine. His medical book al-Qanun (The Canon) was translated into Latin in the twelfth century and remained a reference source in European universities until the end of the seventeenth century, while Kitab-Al-Shifa is a philosophical encyclopaedia covering many fields. He was the first to detect the contagious nature of tuberculosis and the spread of diseases by water, he showed the link between psychology and health, and he also contributed to anatomy, child health, physics, geography and chemistry.

Writing B: Write a descriptive essay on 'A Great Muslim Scientist'

  • Q: Write a descriptive essay on 'A Great Muslim Scientist'.
    Ans: A Great Muslim Scientist — Ibn-e-Sina was a great Muslim scientist whose real name was Abu Ali Hussain Ibn-e-Abdullah Ibn-e-Sina. He was born in 980 AD at Afsana near Bukhara in Central Asia, at a time when Muslim civilization was at the climax of its scientific growth. As a person, he was exceptionally intelligent, keen and hard-working. He had a wonderful memory and learned everything quickly: before he was ten years old he knew the Qur'an and much literature, and by eighteen he had mastered all the branches of knowledge of his time, including Arabic, literature, philosophy, geometry, mathematics and medicine. In character he was humble and truthful about himself; he said that his stock of knowledge stayed the same as in his youth, but it became more exact. As a physician he was so skilful that other physicians recommended him to the ruler of Bukhara, and as a thinker he was deep and original. His famous medical book al-Qanun and his encyclopaedia Kitab-Al-Shifa show the width of his mind. Truly, Ibn-e-Sina was a shining star in the galaxy of Muslim scientists, and the world still remembers him for his enormous contribution to science.

lessons.title: Practice Activities
lessons.notes_html:
Listening and Speaking: Making Plans

  • Q: Make pairs and make plans for different events. Practice the expressions in the dialogue between Ahmad and Wajid. What plan do Ahmad and Wajid finally make?
    Ans: Ahmad and Wajid greet each other and ask about each other's health. Ahmad asks if Wajid is free the next morning, but Wajid has a class. Wajid is free in the afternoon from 1 to 5, so Ahmad suggests going out for lunch. Wajid agrees and asks where to go. He does not like Chinese food, but Italian food is fine with him. Finally they decide to meet at the Italian restaurant on the Mall at half past one the next day. Model expressions for making plans: 'Are you free tomorrow morning?' 'How about going out for lunch?' 'Sure, sounds good.' 'What about Italian?' 'Let's meet at ... at half past one.' 'Great! See you tomorrow.'

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-reading

  • Q: Look at the title / picture and predict the content of the lesson.
    Ans: The title and the pictures show a brightly coloured kingfisher sitting by the water, diving into the water and catching a fish in its long beak. So the poem is likely to describe the kingfisher, its beautiful colours, its life near still water and its skill in catching fish.
  • Q: Kingfisher fact 1: Where are kingfishers found?
    Ans: Kingfishers are found by still or slow flowing water such as lakes, canals and rivers in lowland areas.
  • Q: Kingfisher fact 2: What do these kingfishers look like?
    Ans: These kingfishers are powder blue above with fine, white spotting on the wings and tail.
  • Q: Kingfisher fact 3: Why can kingfishers judge the distance of moving prey in water?
    Ans: Kingfishers have very keen eyesight, therefore they have the ability to judge the distance of moving prey in water.
  • Q: Kingfisher fact 4: Why is the bird named kingfisher?
    Ans: The kingfisher has elegance in catching fish, so it is named as king fisher.

Reading: Deduce the meaning of the following words

  • Q: What does 'thee' mean?
    Ans: 'Thee' is an old word meaning 'you', used for the person spoken to as the object of a sentence.
  • Q: What does 'thy' mean?
    Ans: 'Thy' is an old word meaning 'your', used before a noun, as in 'clap thy wings' — clap your wings.
  • Q: What does 'thou' mean?
    Ans: 'Thou' is an old word meaning 'you', used for the person spoken to as the subject of a sentence.
  • Q: What does 'art' mean?
    Ans: 'Art' is an old form meaning 'are', as in 'thou art not vain' — you are not vain.
  • Q: What does 'proud' mean?
    Ans: 'Proud' means full of pride; feeling pleased and satisfied about one's own beauty, qualities or achievements, and showing it to others.
  • Q: What does 'shining' mean?
    Ans: 'Shining' means bright and smooth, giving out or reflecting light, as in 'lawns as smooth as shining glass'.
  • Q: What does 'mankind' mean?
    Ans: 'Mankind' means all human beings; the whole human race.

Glossary

  • Q: What does 'haunt' mean?
    Ans: A haunt is a place visited frequently by a particular or specific person. In the poem, the kingfisher's haunts are the lonely pools.
  • Q: What does 'hues' mean?
    Ans: Hues mean a colour; a particular shade of a colour.
  • Q: What does 'glorious' mean?
    Ans: Glorious means deserving or bringing great fame and success; splendid and magnificent.
  • Q: What does 'bough' mean?
    Ans: A bough is a large branch of a tree.
  • Q: What does 'vain' mean?
    Ans: As printed in the glossary, vain means that does not produce the result you want. In the poem, 'thou art not vain' means the bird is not full of pride about its own beauty.
  • Q: What does 'hast' mean?
    Ans: Hast is a way of saying 'you have', as in 'Thou hast no proud, ambitious mind'.
  • Q: What does 'sigh' mean?
    Ans: To sigh means to take and then let out a long deep breath that can be heard, to show that you are disappointed, sad, tired, etc.
  • Q: What does 'ambitious' mean?
    Ans: Ambitious means determined to be successful, rich, powerful, etc.
  • Q: What does 'bosom' mean?
    Ans: Bosom is the front of a person's chest especially when thought of as centre of human feelings.
  • Q: What does 'nay' mean?
    Ans: Nay is an old-fashioned word used to emphasize something you have just said by introducing a stronger word or phrase; it means 'no'.

Comprehension A: Answer the following questions

  • Q: Q1. Why does the poet connect the rainbow with the kingfisher?
    Ans: The poet connects the rainbow with the kingfisher because the kingfisher has all the lovely colours of the rainbow. He imagines that it was the Rainbow who gave birth to the kingfisher and left it all her lovely hues, so the bird's bright and glorious colours come from the rainbow.
  • Q: Q2. What characteristics does the poet share with the kingfisher?
    Ans: The poet shares the kingfisher's love of loneliness and quiet nature. Like the kingfisher, it runs in his blood to choose the lonely pools as his haunts and to keep company with the weeping trees. He says, 'I also love a quiet place that's green, away from all mankind', so both the poet and the bird love a green, quiet and lonely place away from people.
  • Q: Q3. Why does the poet say that 'And, as her mother's name was Tears'?
    Ans: The poet says this because the rainbow appears with rain, and rain is like tears falling from the sky. As the rainbow's mother was Tears, the kingfisher, born of the rainbow, inherits a love of sadness and loneliness. That is why it runs in his blood to choose the lonely pools and to live with trees that weep.
  • Q: Q4. Why does the poet want the kingfisher to live with the peacocks?
    Ans: In the second stanza the poet first suggests a grand life for the bird: with such glorious hues, the kingfisher could go and live with proud peacocks in green parks, show every feather's marks on lawns as smooth as shining glass, and clap its wings on boughs before the windows of proud kings. He says this to bring out the bird's beauty, before rejecting this proud life in the last stanza.
  • Q: Q5. What according to the poet, is the difference between the peacock and the kingfisher?
    Ans: According to the poet, the peacock is proud and showy: it lives in green parks and displays its feathers before people and kings. The kingfisher, in spite of its glorious hues, is not vain and has no proud, ambitious mind. It loves a quiet, green and lonely place, away from all mankind, by a lonely pool.
  • Q: Q6. Why does the poet say, 'Nay, lovely Bird, thou art not vain;'?
    Ans: The poet says this because, although the kingfisher has the most beautiful and glorious colours, it does not show off its beauty. It has no proud, ambitious mind and does not go to parks and kings to display itself. Instead, it stays quietly at the lonely pools, so it is lovely but not vain.
  • Q: Q7. Write down the theme of the poem 'The Kingfisher'.
    Ans: The theme of the poem is the beauty of humble and quiet living in nature. The kingfisher has all the lovely hues of the rainbow, yet it is not proud or ambitious and loves a green, quiet and lonely place away from mankind. The poet, who shares this love of solitude, praises the bird and teaches that true beauty does not need show and pride.
  • Q: Q8. Do you like this poem? Why?
    Ans: Yes, I like this poem because it describes the kingfisher in beautiful and simple words. The picture of the bird with the rainbow's hues, the lonely pools and the weeping trees is very pleasing. I also like its message that one should be beautiful in character but humble, quiet and free from pride and ambition, like the kingfisher.
  • Q: Q9. Describe the objects being personified in the poem.
    Ans: The main objects personified in the poem are the Rainbow, the trees and the kingfisher itself. The Rainbow is given human qualities: she gives birth to the kingfisher, leaves it her hues, and has a mother whose name was Tears. The trees are personified as human beings who weep and sigh with their bosom over the poet. The kingfisher is addressed like a person who can choose its haunts, go to live with peacocks, clap its wings before kings, and who has a mind that is not proud or ambitious.

Comprehension B: Read the poem and fill in the blanks

  • Q: The rainbow gave all the lovely _____ to the kingfisher.
    Ans: hues
  • Q: The kingfisher lives on _____.
    Ans: lonely pools
  • Q: Lawns are smooth as _____.
    Ans: shining glass
  • Q: The kingfisher _____ its wings.
    Ans: claps
  • Q: The kingfisher is neither proud nor _____.
    Ans: ambitious
  • Q: The kingfisher loves _____ place.
    Ans: quiet
  • Q: Common point between poet and kingfisher is _____.
    Ans: their love of a quiet, green and lonely place away from all mankind

lessons.title: Sounds and Speaking
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary E: Use dictionary to locate entry and guide words, identify pronunciation, syllable division and stress pattern

  • Q: Give the syllable division and stress pattern of 'feather'.
    Ans: feather: feath-er — 2 syllables, stress on the first syllable (FEATH-er).
  • Q: Give the syllable division and stress pattern of 'rainbow'.
    Ans: rainbow: rain-bow — 2 syllables, stress on the first syllable (RAIN-bow).
  • Q: Give the syllable division and stress pattern of 'mother'.
    Ans: mother: moth-er — 2 syllables, stress on the first syllable (MOTH-er).
  • Q: Give the syllable division and stress pattern of 'haunt'.
    Ans: haunt: haunt — 1 syllable, the whole word is stressed.
  • Q: Give the syllable division and stress pattern of 'glorious'.
    Ans: glorious: glo-ri-ous — 3 syllables, stress on the first syllable (GLO-ri-ous).
  • Q: Give the syllable division and stress pattern of 'ambitious'.
    Ans: ambitious: am-bi-tious — 3 syllables, stress on the second syllable (am-BI-tious).
  • Q: Give the syllable division and stress pattern of 'windows'.
    Ans: windows: win-dows — 2 syllables, stress on the first syllable (WIN-dows).

Grammar: Strong form and weak form — pronounce the grammatical words (personal pronouns, modal / auxiliary verbs, articles, prepositions and conjunctions in weak form)

  • Q: What is the difference between a strong form and a weak form?
    Ans: Grammatical words such as articles, prepositions, conjunctions and auxiliary verbs help us construct a sentence but carry little meaning of their own, so they have no stress and are weakened in speech. This weakened pronunciation is called the weak form, often pronounced with a schwa sound. The strong form is the full form of the word pronounced with stress, used when the word is pronounced alone or when we emphasize it.
  • Q: Give the weak forms of the auxiliary (modal) verbs: am, are, be, been, can, could, do, does, has, had, shall, should, was, were, would.
    Ans: In connected speech these auxiliary verbs are normally unstressed and weak: am becomes 'm (I'm), are becomes a weak 'er' sound, can becomes a weak 'kn' sound, could becomes a weak 'kd' sound, has becomes 's (he's), had becomes 'd (he'd), should becomes a weak 'shd' sound, was and were become weak forms with a schwa, and would has two weak forms, as the lesson shows: would can be pronounced weakly and even weaker as 'd (I'd like). Example from the lesson: 'I would like some fish and chips' with weak forms sounds natural, while the full strong forms sound unnatural.
  • Q: Give the weak forms of the personal pronouns: he, her, him, his, me, she, them, us, we, you.
    Ans: Personal pronouns are usually unstressed in a sentence and take weak forms: him loses its 'h' and becomes a weak 'im' sound, as in the lesson's example 'Tell him to go', where the strong forms of 'him' and 'to' become weak in natural speech. Similarly her, them, us and you are pronounced weakly with a schwa sound when they are not emphasized, and he, she, we and me are shortened in contractions such as he's, she's and we're.
  • Q: Give the weak forms of the articles: a, the, an.
    Ans: The articles a, an and the are almost always unstressed and weak in conversation: a and an are pronounced with a weak schwa sound, and the is pronounced weakly before consonant sounds. They take a strong form only when they are emphasized or pronounced alone.
  • Q: Give the weak forms of the prepositions (at, for, from, of, to) and conjunctions (for, and, but, or, than, that) listed in the lesson.
    Ans: Prepositions and conjunctions are grammatical words, so they are normally weak in a sentence: to becomes a weak 'tuh' sound (as in 'Tell him to go'), at, for, from and of are pronounced with a schwa, and is very often reduced to a weak 'n' sound, but has the weak form shown in the lesson, and than and that are also pronounced weakly with a schwa when unstressed.

Grammar: Minimal Pairs for Consonants

  • Q: What are minimal pairs? Give examples from the lesson table for /b/ and /p/.
    Ans: Minimal pairs are words that are exactly the same in phonetic transcription but contrast in only one speech sound, and that one sound changes the meaning. Examples from the lesson: beach (/b/) — peach (/p/), bored — poured, bull — pull, nibble — nipple, carb — carp.
  • Q: Give the minimal pair examples from the lesson for /v/ and /w/.
    Ans: Examples from the lesson table: vet (/v/) — wet (/w/), vest — west, valt — walt, vary — wary, roving — rowing. The lesson also lists /v/ words such as volley, van, marvel, curve and jive, contrasted with /b/ words such as bali, ban, marble, curb and jibe.

Vocabulary A: Find rhyming words from the poem

Vocabulary B: Find words in the poem which mean the same as

  • Q: Find a word in the poem which means the same as 'silent'.

  • Q: Find a word in the poem which means the same as 'determined'.

Vocabulary C: Choose the describing words used in the poem for the following nouns

  • Q: What describing word is used in the poem for 'peacock'?

  • Q: What describing word is used in the poem for 'park'?

Vocabulary D: Figurative language in the poem 'The Kingfisher'

  • Q: 'On lawns as smooth as shining glass,' — There is a simile because _____.

lessons.title: Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Writing A: Paraphrase the third stanza of the poem

  • Q: Paraphrase the third stanza of the poem: 'Nay, lovely Bird, thou art not vain; / Thou hast no proud, ambitious mind; / I also love a quiet place / That's green, away from all mankind; / A lonely pool, and let a tree / Sigh with her bosom over me.'
    Ans: Paraphrase: No, beautiful bird, you are not vain at all. You have no proud or ambitious mind, and you do not show off your beauty. I, too, like you, love a quiet and green place far away from all people. I wish to sit by a lonely pool, where a tree bends over me and sighs softly above my head. In simple words, both the bird and the poet love peace, solitude and nature, and both stay away from pride and the crowd of people.

Writing B: Write the summary of the poem

  • Q: Write the summary of the poem 'The Kingfisher' by William Henry Davies.
    Ans: Summary: In this poem William Henry Davies praises the kingfisher. He imagines that the Rainbow gave birth to the bird and left it all her lovely colours, and because the rainbow's mother was Tears, it is in the bird's blood to choose lonely pools and the company of weeping trees. The poet then imagines a grand life for it: with its glorious hues it could live with proud peacocks in green parks, display its feathers on lawns as smooth as shining glass, and clap its wings before proud kings. But at once he corrects himself: the lovely bird is not vain and has no proud, ambitious mind. Like the poet himself, it loves a quiet, green place away from all mankind, a lonely pool where a tree sighs over it. The poem thus praises beauty joined with humility and a love of quiet nature.

Writing C: Develop a dialogue between the kingfisher and the peacock (at least ten sentences)

  • Q: Imagine both the kingfisher and the peacock are claiming to be the King of the bird's world. Develop a dialogue between the kingfisher and the peacock, starting with: Kingfisher: I am so colorful, I have every right to be the King of birds. Peacock: Oh! You small bird, ...
    Ans: Kingfisher: I am so colourful, I have every right to be the King of birds. Peacock: Oh! You small bird, how can you be the King? Look at my large and shining feathers; every eye in the park turns towards me. Kingfisher: Size is not greatness, Peacock. The Rainbow herself gave me birth and left me all her lovely hues. Peacock: But I live in green parks and display my beauty before proud kings, while you hide at lonely pools. Kingfisher: I do not hide; I love a quiet place away from all mankind, and I am not vain like you. Peacock: You call it quietness, I call it fear. A king must be seen and admired by all. Kingfisher: A true king does not need show and pride. I have no proud, ambitious mind, yet I catch my fish with such elegance that men have named me the king fisher. Peacock: Hmm, you are small, but your colours are truly glorious, and your words are wise. Kingfisher: Then let us agree: you may be the king of the parks, but by the lonely pools and rivers, I am the Kingfisher. Peacock: Agreed! Pride is mine, but the name of King truly belongs to you.

mcqs.q: In the paraphrase of the third stanza, what does the poet first say about the lovely bird?

mcqs.why: The paraphrase begins 'No, beautiful bird, you are not vain at all', and adds that it does not show off its beauty.

mcqs.why: The paraphrase ends with the wish to sit by a lonely pool where a tree bends over him and sighs softly above his head.

mcqs.why: Writing B in the notes is the summary of the poem 'The Kingfisher' by William Henry Davies, who praises the kingfisher in the poem.

options: Because its mother, the Rainbow, had Tears as her mother

mcqs.why: The summary says the Rainbow gave birth to the bird and, because the rainbow's mother was Tears, it is in its blood to choose lonely pools and weeping trees.

mcqs.q: What grand life does the poet first imagine for the kingfisher in the summary?
options: Catching fish quietly at a lonely pool
Living with proud peacocks in green parks and displaying its feathers
Sighing with a tree over a lonely pool
Staying away from all mankind forever
mcqs.why: The summary says that with its glorious hues it could live with proud peacocks in green parks, display its feathers and clap its wings before proud kings.

mcqs.q: In that imagined grand life, on what would the bird display its feathers?
options: On boughs beside a lonely pool

mcqs.why: The summary describes it displaying its feathers on lawns as smooth as shining glass, in the grand life the poet imagines before correcting himself.

options: By saying it hides at lonely pools because it is afraid

mcqs.why: The dialogue in the notes starts with the kingfisher claiming, 'I am so colourful, I have every right to be the King of birds.'

mcqs.q: What does the peacock boast about in the dialogue?
options: Its elegance in catching fish at rivers
Its love of a quiet place away from mankind
Its large and shining feathers, with every eye in the park turning towards it
Its rainbow hues inherited from Tears
mcqs.why: In the dialogue the peacock boasts of its large and shining feathers and says every eye in the park turns towards it, unlike the small kingfisher.

mcqs.q: How does the dialogue between the kingfisher and the peacock end?
options: The peacock drives the kingfisher away from the park

The kingfisher agrees to display its feathers before kings
They agree that pride is better than quietness
mcqs.why: The dialogue ends in agreement: the peacock may be king of the parks, but by the lonely pools and rivers the name of King truly belongs to the kingfisher.

chapters.title: Unit 15: A Family Trip to Naran

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-reading — Informal Letters: The Format

  • Q: What are informal letters?
    Ans: Informal letters are social or friendly letters. They are usually written to people we know personally, for example members of our family, relatives, friends or pen friends.
  • Q: What is the format of an informal letter as shown in the book?
    Ans: An informal letter has these parts in order: (1) the writer's or sender's address at the top, for example 'House # 15B, Near BHU Mira, Besham'; (2) the date below it, for example '1st March 2017'; (3) the salutation, for example 'Dear Farah,'; (4) the opening remarks; (5) the contents or main body of the letter; (6) the closing remarks, for example 'Do write to me again after your examinations. Until then, good luck in the exam!'; (7) the ending, for example 'Yours affectionately,'; and (8) the signature, for example 'Sadia'.
  • Q: How is an informal letter different from a formal letter?
    Ans: An informal letter is written in a friendly, personal tone to family, relatives and friends, and it uses simple, warm language and a loving ending such as 'Yours affectionately'. A formal letter is written for official or business purposes to people we do not know personally, and it uses polite, serious language, a subject line and a formal ending such as 'Yours faithfully'.

Comprehension A — Answer the following questions

  • Q: Q1. Who is the narrator of the lesson?
    Ans: The narrator of the lesson is Salma Khan. The whole lesson is her informal letter to her friend Sara, written from House # 166A, Phase V, Hayatabad, Peshawar, and signed 'Your loving friend, Salma Khan'.
  • Q: Q2. What does Naran present to the tourist?
    Ans: Naran presents wonderful picnic spots along the noisy River Kunhar, very cold river water, honey bee boxes along the roadside and rich flora because of which it is called 'the botanist's paradise'. It also offers the majestic Lake Saif-ul-Malook, tasty food in Naran Bazar and a pleasant, beautiful atmosphere, so the narrator calls it a heaven on earth.
  • Q: Q3. Describe the beauty of Lake Saif-ul-Malook?
    Ans: Lake Saif-ul-Malook is 10 km away from Naran and is reached by jeep because the road is rough. The lake has a majestic and mesmerizing natural beauty and a pleasant atmosphere. The local people narrate the tale of fairies and the history associated with it. It is famous as the habitat of large brown Trout fish which weigh up to 7 kilograms, and it provides a marvellous view of Malika Parbat, the highest peak of Kaghan Valley.
  • Q: Q4. What is the main idea of the letter?
    Ans: The main idea of the letter is to describe Salma's family trip to Naran after her examinations and to share the natural beauty of Naran, River Kunhar and Lake Saif-ul-Malook with her friend Sara. Through the trip she also shows that Pakistan is an amazing country with all seasons and all terrains, including mountains, deserts, sea, glaciers and fertile plains.
  • Q: Q5. How is the narrator's opinion about the people of Naran?
    Ans: The narrator's opinion about the people of Naran is favourable and appreciative. She happily records how the local people narrated the tale of fairies and the history of Lake Saif-ul-Malook for the visitors, and the whole visit, including the food at Tikka House in Naran Bazar and the stay at the PTDC motels, left her so pleased that she advises Sara to visit Naran and calls it a heaven on earth.

Comprehension B — Choose the correct option

  • Q: 1. 'I hope this letter finds you in good health and lots of happiness.' In this sentence the phrase 'finds you' refers to _____
    Options: the time when the letter discovers you are in good health / arrival of letter at a time when you are in good health / the time when the letter loses you as being present / the time when the letter looks at you in good health
    Ans: arrival of letter at a time when you are in good health
  • Q: 2. 'The noisy River Kunhar passes through city of Balakot.' In this sentence 'noisy river' refers to _____
    Options: talkative and lively river / loud and fast flowing river / slow and gently flowing river / unhurried and smoothly flowing river
    Ans: loud and fast flowing river
  • Q: 3. 'As soon as my examinations finished, my father arranged a family trip to Naran.' In this sentence 'my' refers to _____
    Options: Sara / Sara's father / Salma's father / Salma
    Ans: Salma
  • Q: 4. 'The taste of food was marvelous and mouth-watering.' In this sentence 'mouth-watering' is a _____
    Options: hyphenated compound adjective / hyphenated compound noun / hyphenated compound verb / hyphenated compound adverb
    Ans: hyphenated compound adjective
  • Q: 5. Lake Saif-ul-Malook provides a marvellous view of _____
    Options: Malika Parbat / Mount K-2 / Mount Everest / Malam Jabba
    Ans: Malika Parbat

Glossary — Word Meanings

  • Q: What does 'marvellous' mean?
    Ans: Extremely good; wonderful.
  • Q: What does 'glaciers' mean?
    Ans: A large mass of ice, formed by snow on mountains, that moves very slowly down a valley.
  • Q: What does 'habitat' mean?
    Ans: The place where a particular type of animal or plant is normally found.
  • Q: What does 'fertile' mean?
    Ans: (Of land or soil) that plants grow well in.
  • Q: What does 'majestic' mean?
    Ans: Impressive because of size or beauty.
  • Q: What does 'deft' mean?
    Ans: Skilful and quick.
  • Q: What does 'terrains' mean?
    Ans: Used to refer to an area of land when you are mentioning its natural features, for example, if it is rough, flat, etc.
  • Q: What does 'check out' mean?
    Ans: To pay your bill and leave a hotel, etc.
  • Q: What does 'pleasant' mean?
    Ans: Enjoyable, pleasing or attractive.
  • Q: What does 'narrated' mean?
    Ans: To tell a story.
  • Q: What does 'cultivated' mean?
    Ans: To prepare and use land for growing plants or crops.
