lessons.title: Language Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary A — Use dictionary to locate guide and entry words, choose definition, identify part of speech and pronunciation

  • Q: Word: 'journey' — give its dictionary information.
    Ans: Entry word: journey. It is found in a dictionary under the guide words for 'J', between words beginning with 'jou-' and 'jud-'. Part of speech: noun (also used as a verb). Pronunciation: 'jur-nee'. Meaning: an act of travelling from one place to another, especially a long distance. In the lesson, Salma's family started their journey towards Naran in the morning.
  • Q: Word: 'curve' — give its dictionary information.
    Ans: Entry word: curve. It is found under the guide words for 'C', among words beginning with 'cur-'. Part of speech: noun (also used as a verb). Pronunciation: 'kurv'. Meaning: a line or surface that bends gradually without sharp angles. The road to Naran bends in many curves along the River Kunhar.
  • Q: Word: 'suspend' — give its dictionary information.
    Ans: Entry word: suspend. It is found under the guide words for 'S', among words beginning with 'sus-'. Part of speech: verb. Pronunciation: 'sus-pend'. Meaning: to hang something from above; also to stop something for a time. In the lesson, the family crossed the River Kunhar over a suspended bridge at Balakot.
  • Q: Word: 'maize' — give its dictionary information.
    Ans: Entry word: maize. It is found under the guide words for 'M', among words beginning with 'mai-'. Part of speech: noun. Pronunciation: 'mayz'. Meaning: a tall plant grown for its large yellow grains, also called corn, which are eaten as food.
  • Q: Word: 'habitat' — give its dictionary information.
    Ans: Entry word: habitat. It is found under the guide words for 'H', among words beginning with 'hab-'. Part of speech: noun. Pronunciation: 'hab-i-tat'. Meaning (as given in the glossary): the place where a particular type of animal or plant is normally found. Lake Saif-ul-Malook is the habitat of large brown Trout fish.
  • Q: Word: 'peak' — give its dictionary information.
    Ans: Entry word: peak. It is found under the guide words for 'P', among words beginning with 'pea-'. Part of speech: noun. Pronunciation: 'peek'. Meaning: the pointed top of a mountain. Malika Parbat is the highest peak of Kaghan Valley.

Vocabulary B — Consult a thesaurus and find out the synonyms of the following words

  • Q: Give synonyms of 'amazing'.
    Ans: Synonyms of amazing: astonishing, surprising, wonderful, remarkable, incredible. The lesson calls Pakistan an amazing country.
  • Q: Give synonyms of 'severe'.
    Ans: Synonyms of severe: harsh, intense, extreme, serious, strict. The lesson mentions a severe heat wave in Peshawar.
  • Q: Give synonyms of 'marvellous'.
    Ans: Synonyms of marvellous: wonderful, excellent, splendid, superb, fantastic. The glossary defines it as extremely good; wonderful.
  • Q: Give synonyms of 'majestic'.
    Ans: Synonyms of majestic: grand, magnificent, impressive, splendid, stately. The glossary defines it as impressive because of size or beauty.
  • Q: Give synonyms of 'pleasant'.
    Ans: Synonyms of pleasant: enjoyable, pleasing, attractive, delightful, agreeable. The glossary defines it as enjoyable, pleasing or attractive.
  • Q: Give synonyms of 'livelihood'.
    Ans: Synonyms of livelihood: living, income, means of support, occupation, earning. It means the way a person earns money to live.
  • Q: Give synonyms of 'paradise'.
    Ans: Synonyms of paradise: heaven, Eden, bliss, perfect place. Naran is called 'the botanist's paradise' and 'a heaven on earth' in the lesson.

Vocabulary C — Look up the meaning and make sentences to bring out the difference between the following words

  • Q: 1. Difference between 'hotel' and 'motel'.
    Ans: A hotel is a building, usually inside a town or city, where travellers pay to stay, eat and sleep, often with many facilities. A motel is a small hotel on or near a main road for motorists, where rooms open towards a parking area so travellers can park near their rooms. Sentences: We stayed in a comfortable hotel in the city during our tour. On the long highway journey, we stopped at a motel for the night and parked our car outside our room. In Naran, Salma's family stayed at the PTDC motels.
  • Q: 2. Difference between 'lake' and 'stream'.
    Ans: A lake is a large area of water surrounded by land, while a stream is a small, narrow river that flows continuously. Sentences: Lake Saif-ul-Malook is a famous lake near Naran, famous for its brown Trout. A clear stream flows down the mountainside into the River Kunhar.
  • Q: 3. Difference between 'snow' and 'glacier'.
    Ans: Snow is the soft white flakes of frozen water that fall from the sky in cold weather and cover the ground for a short time. A glacier is a large mass of ice, formed by snow on mountains, that moves very slowly down a valley and stays for a very long time. Sentences: Soft snow covered the mountain tops around Naran. The family witnessed glacial ice alongside the Naran-Kaghan road.
  • Q: 4. Difference between 'fauna' and 'floral'.
    Ans: Fauna means all the animals of a particular region or period, while floral means relating to flowers, or made of flower patterns; the plant life of a region is called its flora. Sentences: The fauna of Naran includes the brown Trout of Lake Saif-ul-Malook. Because of its rich flora, Naran is known as the botanist's paradise, and its floral beauty attracts tourists.
  • Q: 5. Difference between 'valley' and 'village'.
    Ans: A valley is a low area of land between hills or mountains, usually with a river running through it, while a village is a small group of houses and homes in a rural area, smaller than a town. Sentences: Malika Parbat is the highest peak of Kaghan Valley. Many small villages are situated along the River Kunhar in the valley.
  • Q: 6. Difference between 'mountain' and 'hill'.
    Ans: A mountain is a very high area of land with steep sides and a peak, much higher than a hill, while a hill is a raised area of land that is smaller and lower than a mountain and easier to climb. Sentences: The snow-covered mountains around Naran look majestic. Green hills surround the picnic spots near the river.

Grammar — Hyphen: Divide the following words at the end of a line following rules of hyphen

  • Q: Divide 'instruction' at the end of a line.
    Ans: instruc- / tion. The word is divided between syllables (in-struc-tion) and the hyphen goes at the end of the line.
  • Q: Divide 'television' at the end of a line.
    Ans: tele- / vision. The word is divided between syllables (tel-e-vi-sion).
  • Q: Divide 'father-in-law' at the end of a line.
    Ans: father- / in-law. A hyphenated word is divided only at the hyphen already in the word.
  • Q: Divide 'footsteps' at the end of a line.
    Ans: foot- / steps. The compound word is divided between its syllables (foot-steps).
  • Q: Divide 'elderly' at the end of a line.
    Ans: elder- / ly. The word is divided between syllables (el-der-ly).
  • Q: Divide 'Peshawar' at the end of a line.
    Ans: Peshawar cannot be divided. Rule: proper nouns and proper adjectives are never divided at the end of a line, so the whole word is written on the next line.
  • Q: Divide 'dry-cleaning' at the end of a line.
    Ans: dry- / cleaning. A hyphenated word is divided only at the hyphen already in the word.
  • Q: Divide 'security' at the end of a line.
    Ans: secu- / rity. The word is divided between syllables (se-cu-ri-ty).
  • Q: Divide 'butterfly' at the end of a line.
    Ans: butter- / fly. The compound word is divided between syllables (but-ter-fly).
  • Q: Divide 'successful' at the end of a line.
    Ans: success- / ful. The word is divided between syllables (suc-cess-ful).
  • Q: Divide 'well-being' at the end of a line.
    Ans: well- / being. A hyphenated word is divided only at the hyphen already in the word.
  • Q: Divide 'full moon' at the end of a line.
    Ans: 'Full' and 'moon' are both one-syllable words, and one-syllable words are never divided. So neither word can be split at the end of a line.
  • Q: Divide 'ginger' at the end of a line.
    Ans: gin- / ger. The word is divided between syllables (gin-ger).
  • Q: Divide 'traffic' at the end of a line.
    Ans: traf- / fic. The word is divided between syllables (traf-fic).
  • Q: Divide 'Shahid' at the end of a line.
    Ans: Shahid cannot be divided. It is a proper noun, and proper nouns are never divided at the end of a line.
  • Q: What is a dash and how is it used?
    Ans: A dash is a punctuation mark similar in appearance to a hyphen or minus sign, but it is longer and has different functions. A dash denotes a break in a sentence, for example: 'A flock of sparrows — some of them juveniles — alighted and sang.' A dash also indicates a break in thought, for example: 'An indicator — a flashing light or an alarm — signals danger,' and 'Rashid, how long do you think — Oh God, what's that?'

mcqs.q: What is the meaning of the entry word 'journey' in the dictionary work?
options: An act of travelling from one place to another, especially a long distance
A line or surface that bends gradually without sharp angles
A tall plant grown for its large yellow grains
The pointed top of a mountain
mcqs.why: The notes define 'journey' as an act of travelling from one place to another, especially over a long distance.

mcqs.q: What is the pronunciation of the word 'curve'?
mcqs.why: The notes give the pronunciation of 'curve' as 'kurv'; the other pronunciations belong to journey, maize and peak.

mcqs.q: In the lesson, the word 'suspend' is linked with which thing at Balakot?
options: A suspended train over the lake
A suspended road over Malika Parbat
A suspended bridge over the River Kunhar
A suspended boat over the valley
mcqs.why: The notes explain that Salma's family crossed the River Kunhar over a suspended bridge at Balakot.

mcqs.q: What does 'maize' mean?
options: A large mass of ice formed by snow on mountains
The place where an animal is normally found
A line that bends without sharp angles
A tall plant grown for its large yellow grains, also called corn
mcqs.why: The notes define maize as a tall plant grown for its large yellow grains, also called corn, eaten as food.

mcqs.q: What is the pronunciation of 'habitat'?
mcqs.why: The dictionary work in the notes gives the pronunciation of 'habitat' as 'hab-i-tat', and it is a noun.

mcqs.q: Which word is a synonym of 'amazing'?
mcqs.why: The thesaurus work lists astonishing, surprising, wonderful, remarkable and incredible as synonyms of 'amazing'.

mcqs.q: Which word is a synonym of 'severe', as in the severe heat wave in Peshawar?
mcqs.why: The notes list harsh, intense, extreme, serious and strict as synonyms of 'severe', used for the heat wave in Peshawar.

mcqs.q: Which meaning best matches 'livelihood'?
options: Land that plants grow well in
The way a person earns money to live
mcqs.why: The thesaurus work explains livelihood as a living or means of support: the way a person earns money to live.

mcqs.q: How is a motel different from a hotel, according to the notes?
options: A motel is a small hotel on or near a main road for motorists, with rooms opening towards parking
A motel is a large area of water surrounded by land
A motel is a tall building only inside a village
A motel is a hotel with no rooms for travellers
mcqs.why: The notes contrast a hotel in a town with a motel on or near a main road where motorists can park near their rooms.

mcqs.q: How is a stream different from a lake?
options: A stream is a large still lake, while a lake is a narrow flowing river
A stream is a small, narrow river that flows continuously, while a lake is a large area of water surrounded by land
A stream is frozen snow, while a lake is moving ice
A stream is a group of houses, while a lake is a low valley
mcqs.why: The notes define a lake as a large area of water surrounded by land and a stream as a small, narrow flowing river.

mcqs.q: Which sentence correctly uses the difference between 'snow' and 'glacier'?
options: A glacier is soft flakes that fall for one night only
Snow is a solid base that stays in a valley for centuries
A glacier is a large mass of ice formed by snow on mountains that moves very slowly down a valley
Snow and glacier mean exactly the same thing
mcqs.why: The glossary and difference work define a glacier as a large mass of ice formed by snow that moves very slowly down a valley.

mcqs.q: How is 'instruction' divided at the end of a line?
options: instruct- / ion at the hyphen only
It can never be divided at all
mcqs.why: The notes divide 'instruction' between its syllables as instruc- / tion, with the hyphen at the end of the line.

mcqs.q: Why can 'Peshawar' not be divided at the end of a line?
options: Proper nouns and proper adjectives are never divided at the end of a line
One-syllable words are never divided at the end of a line
Hyphenated words are divided only at their own hyphen
Compound words are divided between their two parts
mcqs.why: The notes state the rule directly: proper nouns like Peshawar are never divided, so the whole word goes to the next line.

mcqs.q: How is the hyphenated word 'father-in-law' divided at the end of a line?
options: father-in- / law at the second hyphen
It is split in the middle of 'father'
mcqs.why: A hyphenated word is divided only at the hyphen already in the word, so 'father-in-law' breaks as father- / in-law.

mcqs.q: What does a dash denote in a sentence, according to the notes?
options: The end of every formal letter
The division of a one-syllable word
A break in a sentence or a break in thought
The pronunciation of an entry word
mcqs.why: The notes explain that a dash, longer than a hyphen, denotes a break in a sentence or a break in thought.

lessons.title: Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Writing A — Write a letter to your cousin and discuss how human activities are destroying natural beauty of your city / village

  • Q: Write a letter to your cousin and discuss how human activities are destroying the natural beauty of your city / village.
    Ans: House # 166A, Phase V, Hayatabad, Peshawar. 10th March 2017. Dear Cousin Ahmed, I hope this letter finds you in good health and lots of happiness. I am writing to share a sad change that I have noticed in our city. Day by day, human activities are destroying its natural beauty. People are cutting down trees to build houses and shops, so the green areas are disappearing. Smoke from vehicles and factories has made the air dirty, and people throw plastic bags and garbage into the streams and on the roadsides. The clear water of the streams has become polluted, and birds and animals are losing their natural habitat. If we do not stop this carelessness, our city will lose all its beauty and healthy atmosphere. We should plant more trees, keep our surroundings clean and avoid throwing waste in water. I hope you will also play your part in protecting nature in your area. Convey my regards to uncle and aunt. Your loving cousin, Salma Khan.

Writing B — Write your cousin's address on envelope clearly and in proper format

  • Q: Write your cousin's address on the envelope clearly and in proper format.
    Ans: On the front of the envelope, the receiver's address is written in the centre in clear block letters, with a postage stamp fixed at the top right corner: To, Mr. Ahmed Khan, House # 25, Street # 4, Gulberg, Lahore. The sender's name and address are written at the back (or at the bottom left on the front) of the envelope: Sender's name and address: Salma Khan, House # 166A, Phase V, Hayatabad, Peshawar.

Writing C — Descriptive composition of a place (as guided in the Teacher's guideline)

  • Q: Write a descriptive composition of a place, giving general and finer details, defining characteristics, atmosphere, correct verb forms and vivid adjectives and adverbs.
    Ans: Lake Saif-ul-Malook is one of the most beautiful places in Pakistan. It lies 10 km away from Naran in the Kaghan Valley, and visitors hire jeeps to reach it because the road is rough and steep. The lake is large and its clear, calm water shines brightly in the sunlight. All around it stand tall, majestic mountains, and it provides a marvellous view of Malika Parbat, the highest peak of the valley. The atmosphere of the place is pleasant, peaceful and refreshing, and the cool breeze blows gently over the water. The local people narrate the famous tale of fairies associated with the lake, which makes the visit more interesting. The lake is also the habitat of large brown Trout fish weighing up to 7 kilograms. Truly, its mesmerizing beauty makes every visitor feel close to nature.

mcqs.q: In the model letter in Writing A, to whom is the letter addressed?
mcqs.why: The model letter begins 'Dear Cousin Ahmed' and is signed 'Your loving cousin, Salma Khan'.

mcqs.q: What sad change does the model letter to the cousin discuss?
options: Examinations are becoming harder every year
Human activities are destroying the natural beauty of the city
The river water has become warm in summer
New motels are opening near the lake
mcqs.why: The writer says she is sharing a sad change: day by day, human activities are destroying the city's natural beauty.

mcqs.q: According to the model letter, why are the green areas disappearing?
options: People are planting trees along every road
Rivers are covering the green areas with water
People are cutting down trees to build houses and shops
Birds are eating all the green plants
mcqs.why: The letter states that people are cutting down trees to build houses and shops, so the green areas are disappearing.

mcqs.q: What has made the air dirty in the city, according to the model letter?
options: Dust from the mountains of Naran
Steam from the cold river water
Smoke from cooking fires in villages only
mcqs.why: The model letter says smoke from vehicles and factories has made the air dirty in the city.

mcqs.q: How have the streams been harmed, according to the model letter?
options: People throw plastic bags and garbage into the streams, polluting the clear water
People have built bridges over every stream
Factories have covered the streams with ice
Fish have left the streams for the lake
mcqs.why: The letter says people throw plastic bags and garbage into the streams and on roadsides, so the clear water has become polluted.

mcqs.q: What does the writer advise people to do to protect nature?
options: Cut more trees and build more shops
Plant more trees, keep the surroundings clean and avoid throwing waste in water
Throw all waste into the streams
mcqs.why: The model letter advises planting more trees, keeping surroundings clean and avoiding throwing waste in water.

mcqs.q: In Writing B, how is the receiver's address written on the envelope?
options: At the back of the envelope in small letters only
At the bottom left corner with no stamp
In the centre of the front, in clear block letters, with a postage stamp at the top right corner
Across the top left corner in joined writing
mcqs.why: The notes say the receiver's address goes in the centre of the front in clear block letters, with a stamp at the top right.

mcqs.q: Where is the sender's name and address written on the envelope?
options: In the centre of the front over the receiver's address
Only inside the letter, never on the envelope
At the top right corner over the stamp
At the back of the envelope, or at the bottom left on the front
mcqs.why: Writing B states the sender's name and address are written at the back, or at the bottom left on the front of the envelope.

mcqs.q: In the descriptive composition, how do visitors reach Lake Saif-ul-Malook and why?
options: They hire jeeps because the road is rough and steep
They walk because the road is smooth and flat
They take a train because the track is straight
They use boats because there is no road at all
mcqs.why: The composition says visitors hire jeeps to reach the lake because the road is rough and steep.

mcqs.q: How is the atmosphere at Lake Saif-ul-Malook described in the composition?
options: Noisy, crowded and full of smoke
Pleasant, peaceful and refreshing, with a cool breeze blowing gently over the water
Hot, dry and dusty all day
mcqs.why: The composition describes the atmosphere as pleasant, peaceful and refreshing, with a cool breeze over the water.

chapters.title: Unit 16: The Life We Build for Ourselves

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-reading

  • Q: Q1. How can you perform your role in life effectively?
    Ans: We can perform our role in life effectively by doing every duty honestly, sincerely and with our best effort, without deceit or carelessness. The story of Amjad teaches us that whatever work we do, we should do it with full integrity, because in the end we ourselves have to live with the results of our own choices and actions.
  • Q: Q2. How do you perform your duties as a student?
    Ans: As a student, I perform my duties by attending school regularly and punctually, listening to my teachers attentively, completing my homework and classwork honestly and on time, revising my lessons daily, and respecting my teachers and classmates. I try to give my best effort in every task instead of doing it carelessly.
  • Q: Q3. Why is quality of work important?
    Ans: Quality of work is important because poor and careless work harms its maker in the end. Amjad built his last house with inferior material and shoddy workmanship, and he himself had to live in that badly built house for the rest of his life. Good quality work brings satisfaction, trust and lasting benefit, while dishonest work brings shame and loss.

Comprehension A — Answer the following questions

  • Q: Q1. Write the character sketch of Amjad, keeping in mind his motives, actions and emotional responses.
    Ans: Amjad was a gifted carpenter who built most of the houses in his village, yet he himself could never afford a home of his own. His motive throughout life was to earn a living for his family, and at retirement he wished to build a house for himself and live a leisurely life. When his boss asked him to build one last house, greed overcame him: he used inferior material, cut corners and did shoddy work to pocket the leftover money. When the house turned out to be a gift for himself, he felt deeply shocked, ashamed and remorseful, because he had betrayed his boss's trust and compromised on his own integrity and honesty. In the end he had to live in the carelessly built house, so his actions show how dishonesty finally harms the dishonest person himself.
  • Q: Q2. Why did Amjad agree to build the last house for his boss?
    Ans: Amjad agreed to build the last house because his boss requested it as a personal favour. The boss was sorry to see his good worker go, and Amjad could not refuse him. The boss also told him to build the finest house he was capable of and to spare no expense, as he intended to give the house to a dear friend.
  • Q: Q3. What is the theme and setting of the story?
    Ans: The setting of the story is the towns and villages where Amjad built houses, especially his own village, in the last days of his working life before retirement. The theme of the story is honesty and integrity in work: we build our lives by our own choices and actions, so deceit and dishonesty damage our own character and future, just as inferior material damaged Amjad's house.
  • Q: Q4. What is the explicit and implied meaning of the story?
    Ans: The explicit meaning of the story is the literal account of a carpenter who built a poor-quality house and then had to live in it himself for the rest of his life. The implied meaning is deeper: each person is the carpenter and his or her life is the house. Our character is built by our choices and actions, so if we build our lives carelessly with deceit, fraud and dishonesty, the result will be a weak life with a creaky floor, a leaky roof and a fragile foundation, and we ourselves will suffer its consequences.
  • Q: Q5. Why did Amjad compromise on quality of the house?
    Ans: Amjad compromised on the quality of the house because of greed and selfishness. He thought the wealthy boss already had a few houses while he himself had none, so he decided to use inferior material, cut a few corners and do a quick job, make the house look nice from outside and charge the full amount. In this way he wanted to pocket the leftover money and finally afford a house of his own.
  • Q: Q6. Do you like the story? Why?
    Ans: Yes, I like the story very much because it teaches a great life lesson in a simple and interesting way. It shows that honesty and integrity always benefit us, while deceit finally harms the deceitful person. The surprising ending, in which the badly built house becomes Amjad's own home, makes the moral unforgettable: we build our lives by our own choices and actions.
  • Q: Q7. Suggest a new ending for the story.
    Ans: Suggested new ending: When Amjad unfolded the paper and found the deed of the house in his own name, he fell at his boss's feet with tears in his eyes and confessed everything honestly. The kind boss forgave him and said that a lesson learnt is better than a house lost. Amjad then repaired the house with his own savings, used the best material, and made it strong and beautiful. He lived in it happily for the rest of his life and became famous in the village for his honesty, teaching every young carpenter never to compromise on quality and integrity.

Glossary — Word Meanings

  • Q: What does 'betrayed' mean?
    Ans: To hurt somebody who trusts you, especially by not being loyal or faithful to them.
  • Q: What does 'misjudge' mean?
    Ans: To form a wrong opinion about a person or situation, especially in a way that makes you deal with them or it unfairly.
  • Q: What does 'remorseful' mean?
    Ans: Feeling extremely sorry for something wrong or bad that you have done.
  • Q: What does 'leaky' mean?
    Ans: To allow liquid or gas to get in or out through a small hole or crack.
  • Q: What does 'excellence' mean?
    Ans: The quality of being extremely good.
  • Q: What does 'consequence' mean?
    Ans: A result of something that has happened.
  • Q: What does 'shoddy' mean?
    Ans: Made or done badly and with not enough care.
  • Q: What does 'foundation' mean?
    Ans: A layer of bricks, concrete, etc. that forms the solid underground base of a building.
  • Q: What does 'disdainful' mean?
    Ans: The feeling that somebody or something is not good enough to deserve your respect or attention.

mcqs.q: How can we perform our role in life effectively, according to the pre-reading answers?
options: By doing every duty honestly, sincerely and with our best effort, without deceit or carelessness
By doing every duty quickly, even if the work is careless
By letting others do our duties for us
By working only when someone is watching us
mcqs.why: The pre-reading answer says we perform our role effectively by doing every duty honestly and sincerely with our best effort.

mcqs.q: Why is quality of work important, according to the notes?
options: Because poor work always earns more money
Because poor and careless work harms its maker in the end
Because quality matters only for the boss, not the worker
Because careless work is finished in less time
mcqs.why: The notes explain that Amjad's poor-quality house harmed Amjad himself, showing that careless work harms its maker in the end.

mcqs.q: Who was Amjad, and what was his difficulty in life?
options: A wealthy boss who owned many houses in the village
A young student who could not finish his homework
A gifted carpenter who built most of the houses in his village but could never afford a home of his own
A farmer who built only one house in his life
mcqs.why: The character sketch calls Amjad a gifted carpenter who built most village houses yet could never afford a home of his own.

mcqs.q: Why did Amjad agree to build the last house for his boss?
options: He wanted to earn double payment for the house
His boss ordered him and threatened to dismiss him
He hoped the boss would give him the leftover money
His boss requested it as a personal favour and he could not refuse him
mcqs.why: The notes say Amjad agreed because his boss, sorry to see him go, requested the last house as a personal favour.

mcqs.q: What did the boss tell Amjad about building the last house?
options: To build the finest house he was capable of and spare no expense, as it was for a dear friend
To build the cheapest house as quickly as possible
To build the house with inferior material and save money
To build a small house that only looked nice outside
mcqs.why: The boss told Amjad to build the finest house he was capable of, sparing no expense, for a dear friend.

mcqs.q: Why did Amjad compromise on the quality of the last house?
options: The boss asked him to use inferior material
Greed and selfishness: he wanted to pocket the leftover money for a house of his own
He had forgotten how to build good houses
Good material was not available in the village
mcqs.why: The notes say greed overcame Amjad: he used inferior material and cut corners to pocket the leftover money.

mcqs.q: How did Amjad actually build the last house?
options: He used the best material and worked with great care
He built it slowly with excellent workmanship
He used inferior material, cut corners and did shoddy work, making it only look nice from outside
He hired the finest workers and spared no expense
mcqs.why: Comprehension answers state Amjad used inferior material, cut a few corners and did a quick, shoddy job.

mcqs.q: What is the theme of the story 'The Life We Build for Ourselves'?
options: The importance of retiring as early as possible
How to become wealthy by saving leftover money
Why bosses should never trust their workers
Honesty and integrity in work, because we build our lives by our own choices and actions
mcqs.why: The notes give the theme as honesty and integrity in work: deceit damages our own character and future.

mcqs.q: What is the implied meaning of the story?
options: Each person is the carpenter and his or her life is the house, built by that person's choices and actions
Every carpenter should build at least one house
A house with a leaky roof can never be repaired
Retirement is the happiest time of a worker's life
mcqs.why: The implied meaning is deeper than the literal story: each person is the carpenter and his life is the house he builds.

mcqs.q: How did Amjad feel when he learnt the house was his own gift?
options: Proud and pleased with his clever plan
Deeply shocked, ashamed and remorseful, because he had betrayed his boss's trust
Angry with his boss for hiding the gift
Happy that his shoddy work had succeeded
mcqs.why: The character sketch says Amjad felt shocked, ashamed and remorseful because he had betrayed his boss's trust and his own integrity.

lessons.title: Language Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary A — Use dictionary to find the meaning of the following words. Also find guide and entry words

  • Q: Word: 'leisure' — give its meaning and guide and entry words.
    Ans: Entry word: leisure. Guide words: it appears in the 'L' section of the dictionary, among entries beginning with 'lei-'. Meaning: time when you are not working and can relax and do things you enjoy. Pronunciation: 'lezh-er'. Amjad wanted to live a more leisurely life with his family after retirement.
  • Q: Word: 'deserve' — give its meaning and guide and entry words.
    Ans: Entry word: deserve. Guide words: it appears in the 'D' section, among entries beginning with 'des-'. Meaning: to be worthy of something because of what you have done or how you are. Pronunciation: 'di-zurv'. The boss said his dear friend deserved a house like the one Amjad had built.
  • Q: Word: 'wonderful' — give its meaning and guide and entry words.
    Ans: Entry word: wonderful. Guide words: it appears in the 'W' section, among entries beginning with 'won-'. Meaning: extremely good; very pleasant and enjoyable. Pronunciation: 'wun-der-ful'. The boss said that the house looked wonderful.
  • Q: Word: 'quick' — give its meaning and guide and entry words.
    Ans: Entry word: quick. Guide words: it appears in the 'Q' section, among entries beginning with 'qui-'. Meaning: done in a short time; fast. Pronunciation: 'kwik'. Amjad decided to do a quick job on the house.
  • Q: Word: 'expense' — give its meaning and guide and entry words.
    Ans: Entry word: expense. Guide words: it appears in the 'E' section, among entries beginning with 'exp-'. Meaning: the money spent on something; a cost. Pronunciation: 'ik-spens'. The boss asked Amjad to spare no expense in building the finest house.
  • Q: Word: 'crooked' — give its meaning and guide and entry words.
    Ans: Entry word: crooked. Guide words: it appears in the 'C' section, among entries beginning with 'cro-'. Meaning: not straight, bent or twisted; also dishonest. Pronunciation: 'krook-id'. The story calls Amjad the crooked carpenter because he cheated his boss.
  • Q: Word: 'retire' — give its meaning and guide and entry words.
    Ans: Entry word: retire. Guide words: it appears in the 'R' section, among entries beginning with 'ret-'. Meaning: to stop working permanently, usually because of old age. Pronunciation: 'ri-tyer'. It was time for the elderly carpenter Amjad to retire from the company.

Grammar — Quotation Marks: Add quotation marks to each sentence, keeping in mind the rules for quotation marks

  • Q: 1. Add quotation marks: There's a fifty percent chance of rain this afternoon, reported Tahira.
    Ans: "There's a fifty percent chance of rain this afternoon," reported Tahira.
  • Q: 2. Add quotation marks: Azra asked, Do you think I should take my new umbrella to school?
    Ans: Azra asked, "Do you think I should take my new umbrella to school?"
  • Q: 3. Add quotation marks: Of course you should take it to school, answered Javed.
    Ans: "Of course you should take it to school," answered Javed.
  • Q: 4. Add quotation marks: If it starts raining, Kiran added, you will be nice and dry.
    Ans: "If it starts raining," Kiran added, "you will be nice and dry." (The second part of the interrupted quotation is not capitalized because the quotation continues the same sentence.)
  • Q: 5. Add quotation marks: Asma squealed, I see dark gray storm clouds rolling in.
    Ans: Asma squealed, "I see dark gray storm clouds rolling in!"

Grammar — Direct and Indirect Speech: Change the following into indirect speech

  • Q: 1. Change into indirect speech: The girl said, "It gives me great pleasure to be here this evening."
    Ans: The girl said that it gave her great pleasure to be there that evening. ('This evening' changes to 'that evening', and the present tense changes to the past tense.)
  • Q: 2. Change into indirect speech: The man said, "I must go as soon as possible."
    Ans: The man said that he had to go as soon as possible. ('Must' changes to 'had to' in indirect speech.)
  • Q: 3. Change into indirect speech: She said, "I don't want to see any of you; go away."
    Ans: She said that she did not want to see any of them and told them to go away. (The statement is reported with 'did not want', and the order 'go away' is reported with 'told them to go away'.)
  • Q: 4. Change into indirect speech: The teacher says, "If you work hard, you will pass."
    Ans: The teacher says that if we work hard, we will pass. (There is no change of tense because the reporting verb 'says' is in the present tense.)
  • Q: 5. Change into indirect speech: He asked, "Have you won?"
    Ans: He asked if I had won. (A yes/no question is reported with 'if' or 'whether', and the present perfect changes to the past perfect.)
  • Q: 6. Change into indirect speech: He said, "Let's wait for her return."
    Ans: He suggested that they should wait for her return. ('Let's' is reported as a suggestion with 'suggested that they should'.)
  • Q: 7. Change into indirect speech: Alice said, "How clever I am!"
    Ans: Alice exclaimed that she was very clever. (An exclamatory sentence is reported with 'exclaimed that', and 'How clever I am' becomes 'she was very clever'.)

mcqs.q: What does the entry word 'leisure' mean?
options: Time when you are not working and can relax and do things you enjoy
Money spent on something; a cost
The quality of being extremely good
A result of something that has happened
mcqs.why: The dictionary work defines 'leisure' as time when you are not working and can relax and do things you enjoy.

mcqs.q: What is the pronunciation of 'deserve'?
mcqs.why: The notes give the pronunciation of 'deserve', meaning to be worthy of something, as 'di-zurv'.

mcqs.q: What does 'wonderful' mean, as the boss used it for the finished house?
options: Done in a short time; fast
Extremely good; very pleasant and enjoyable
Made badly and with not enough care
mcqs.why: The dictionary work defines 'wonderful' as extremely good and very pleasant, which is how the boss described the house.

mcqs.q: What does 'expense' mean in 'spare no expense'?
options: Time free from work and duty
A solid underground base of a building
A feeling of being extremely sorry
The money spent on something; a cost
mcqs.why: The notes define 'expense' as the money spent on something, so 'spare no expense' means do not hold back the cost.

mcqs.q: What does 'crooked' mean when the story calls Amjad the crooked carpenter?
options: Not straight, bent or twisted; also dishonest
Free from work and able to relax
mcqs.why: The notes give both meanings of 'crooked' — bent or twisted, and dishonest — and Amjad is called crooked because he cheated.

mcqs.q: What does 'retire' mean?
options: To hurt somebody who trusts you
To stop working permanently, usually because of old age
To form a wrong opinion about a person
To allow liquid to get out through a crack
mcqs.why: The dictionary work defines 'retire' as stopping work permanently, usually because of old age, as Amjad was about to do.

mcqs.q: Which sentence has the quotation marks placed correctly?
options: There's a fifty percent chance of rain this afternoon, reported Tahira."
"There's a fifty percent chance of rain this afternoon" reported, Tahira
"There's a fifty percent chance of rain this afternoon," reported Tahira.
There's "a fifty percent chance of rain this afternoon, reported Tahira.
mcqs.why: The notes punctuate it with opening marks before 'There's', a comma inside the closing marks, then 'reported Tahira'.

mcqs.q: Which sentence has the quotation marks placed correctly?
options: Azra asked, Do you think I should take my new umbrella to school?"
"Azra asked, Do you think I should take my new umbrella to school?
Azra asked "Do you think, I should take my new umbrella to school"?
Azra asked, "Do you think I should take my new umbrella to school?"
mcqs.why: The question Azra speaks is placed inside quotation marks after 'Azra asked,' exactly as the notes punctuate it.

mcqs.q: In '"If it starts raining," Kiran added, "you will be nice and dry."', why is 'you' not capitalized?
options: Because the second part continues the same sentence of the quotation
Because 'you' is never capitalized in English
Because Kiran is starting a completely new quotation
Because quotation marks remove all capital letters
mcqs.why: The notes explain that in an interrupted quotation the second part is not capitalized because it continues the same sentence.

mcqs.q: Change into indirect speech: The girl said, "It gives me great pleasure to be here this evening."
options: The girl said that it gives me great pleasure to be here this evening.
The girl said that it gave her great pleasure to be there that evening.
The girl said that it gave her great pleasure to be here this evening.
The girl said that it gives her great pleasure to be there that evening.
mcqs.why: In indirect speech 'this evening' becomes 'that evening' and the present tense changes to the past tense, as the notes show.

mcqs.q: Change into indirect speech: The man said, "I must go as soon as possible."
options: The man said that he must go as soon as possible.
The man said that I must go as soon as possible.
The man said that he had to go as soon as possible.
The man said that he has to go as soon as possible.
mcqs.why: The notes state the rule used here: in indirect speech 'must' changes to 'had to'.

mcqs.q: Why is there no change of tense in 'The teacher says that if we work hard, we will pass'?
options: Because the sentence contains the word 'if'
Because 'work hard' is a command, not a statement
Because indirect speech never changes any tense
Because the reporting verb 'says' is in the present tense
mcqs.why: The notes explain there is no tense change because the reporting verb 'says' is in the present tense.

mcqs.q: Change into indirect speech: He asked, "Have you won?"
options: He asked if I had won.
He asked that have you won.
He asked if I have won.
He said if you had won.
mcqs.why: A yes/no question is reported with 'if' or 'whether', and the present perfect changes to the past perfect: 'had won'.

mcqs.q: Change into indirect speech: He said, "Let's wait for her return."
options: He said that let's wait for her return.
He suggested that they should wait for her return.
He ordered that they must waited for her return.
He asked if they wait for her return.
mcqs.why: The notes report 'Let's' as a suggestion: 'suggested that they should wait for her return'.

mcqs.q: Change into indirect speech: Alice said, "How clever I am!"
options: Alice exclaimed that how clever I am.
Alice said that she is how clever.
Alice exclaimed that she was very clever.
Alice asked that she was very clever.
mcqs.why: An exclamatory sentence is reported with 'exclaimed that', and 'How clever I am' becomes 'she was very clever'.

lessons.title: Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Writing A — Write the story 'The Life We Build for Ourselves' in first person describing events and incidents

  • Q: Write the story 'The Life We Build for Ourselves' in first person describing events and incidents.
    Ans: I am Amjad, a carpenter who built houses in towns and villages, and I built most of the houses for the people of my own village. I was a gifted carpenter, but unfortunately I was never able to afford a home of my own. When it was time for me to retire, on my last working day my boss asked me about my plans. I told him that after leaving the house-building business, I wanted to build a house for myself and live a more leisurely life with my family, though I would miss the paycheck. My boss was sorry to see me go and asked me to build just one more house as a personal favour, the finest house I was capable of, sparing no expense, because he intended to give it to a dear friend. I agreed, but then a wicked thought struck me: this wealthy man already had a few houses, while I had none, so I decided to use inferior material, cut a few corners, do a quick job, make the house look nice and pocket the leftover money to build my own house. I resorted to shoddy workmanship and finished the house carelessly. My boss was impressed because it looked beautiful from a distance, shook my hand, and gave me an envelope with a thank-you card and the deed of the very house I had just built. He handed me the keys and said it was his gift to me for my long service. I was shocked and ashamed of myself, repenting that I had betrayed my friend and compromised on my integrity and honesty. Now I have to live for the rest of my life in the house I built so carelessly, and I have learnt that we build our lives by our own choices and actions.

Writing C — Expository Essay: Using conventions of expository essay, describe three things you would like to change in the world and explain why

  • Q: Using conventions of expository essay, describe three things you would like to change in the world and explain why you would change them.
    Ans: Three Things I Would Like to Change in the World. Thesis: If I could change the world, I would end dishonesty, spread free education to every child, and make our environment clean and green, because these three changes would make human life happier, fairer and safer. First, I would change dishonesty and corruption because deceit is like the inferior material in Amjad's house: it weakens the foundation of society, and in the end everyone suffers its consequences, just as Amjad had to live in his own badly built house. Secondly, I would give free and quality education to every child, because an educated person builds his life and his country with knowledge and skill, while ignorance keeps people poor and dependent. An educated nation can solve its own problems instead of asking what its country can do for it. Thirdly, I would make the world clean and green by stopping pollution and planting more trees, because polluted air and water make people ill and destroy the natural beauty that our health depends on. In conclusion, these changes are connected: honest people value education, and educated people protect their environment. If we start these changes from our own lives and homes, we will truly be building a better world, because we build our world by our own choices and actions.

mcqs.q: In the first-person retelling, how does the narrator introduce himself?
options: As Amjad, a carpenter who built houses in towns and villages and most of the houses in his own village
As the boss who owned the house-building company
As a young carpenter building his first house
As a dear friend who received the house as a gift
mcqs.why: The first-person story begins with Amjad telling that he built houses in towns and villages, most of them in his own village.

mcqs.q: What did Amjad plan to do after retirement, in the first-person story?
options: Build houses for the company for ten more years
Build a house for himself and live a more leisurely life with his family, though he would miss the paycheck
Leave his family and travel to another country
Sell his tools and open a shop in the village
mcqs.why: Amjad tells his boss he wants to build his own house and live a more leisurely life with his family after retiring.

mcqs.q: What reason did the boss give for wanting one more finest house, in the retelling?
options: He intended to sell the house at a high price
He intended to keep the house empty for guests
He intended to give the house to a dear friend
He intended to give the house to another company
mcqs.why: In the retelling, the boss asks for the finest house, sparing no expense, because he intends to give it to a dear friend.

mcqs.q: What wicked thought struck Amjad in the first-person story?
options: The boss had no house at all, so Amjad would build him two
The boss planned to dismiss him, so he would work slowly
The dear friend deserved a poor house, so quality did not matter
The wealthy boss already had a few houses while Amjad had none, so he would pocket the leftover money
mcqs.why: Amjad narrates the wicked thought himself: the wealthy man had a few houses while he had none, so he would keep the leftover money.

mcqs.q: What did the boss hand to Amjad when the house was finished?
options: An envelope with a thank-you card and the deed of the very house he had just built, and the keys
An envelope with his last paycheck and a retirement letter
The deed of a different house in another village
A new set of carpentry tools and a thank-you card
mcqs.why: The retelling says the boss gave an envelope with a thank-you card and the deed of the house, and handed Amjad the keys.

mcqs.q: What did the boss say the house was, when he gave it to Amjad?
options: His payment for building one more house
His gift to Amjad for his long service
A loan that Amjad must repay in a year
A prize for finishing the work quickly
mcqs.why: The boss said the house was his gift to Amjad for his long service, which is why Amjad felt shocked and ashamed.

mcqs.q: What lesson does Amjad say he learnt at the end of the first-person story?
options: A worker should never trust his boss
Cheap material is enough for a strong house
We build our lives by our own choices and actions
Retirement should come as early as possible
mcqs.why: The story ends with Amjad's lesson: we build our lives by our own choices and actions, just as he built his house.

mcqs.q: Which three changes does the expository essay choose to make in the world?
options: Build more houses, open more shops, and cut more trees
End examinations, close all schools, and stop all work
Make everyone rich, famous, and free from all duties
End dishonesty, spread free education to every child, and make the environment clean and green
mcqs.why: The essay's thesis names exactly three changes: end dishonesty, free education for every child, and a clean, green environment.

mcqs.q: Why does the essay compare dishonesty to inferior material in Amjad's house?
options: Because deceit weakens the foundation of society and in the end everyone suffers its consequences
Because dishonesty makes society stronger and richer
Because inferior material is easy to repair later
Because society has no foundation to weaken
mcqs.why: The essay says deceit is like inferior material: it weakens society's foundation and everyone suffers, as Amjad suffered in his own house.

mcqs.q: According to the essay, why should every child get free and quality education?
options: Because education removes the need for honesty in life
Because an educated person builds his life and country with knowledge and skill, while ignorance keeps people poor and dependent
Because educated people never face any problem at all
Because schools can then solve the problem of pollution alone
mcqs.why: The essay argues that education lets a person build his life and country with knowledge, while ignorance keeps people poor and dependent.

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-reading

  • Q: Study the pictograph and predict the content of the lesson.
    Ans: The pictograph is a wheel of human feelings and emotions. It shows six groups of feelings: excited, tender, scared, angry, sad and happy, with words of different strength for each feeling, such as ecstatic, loving, terrified, furious, heartbroken and fulfilled. From this we can predict that the lesson is about human emotions and feelings, and about how a person should receive and deal with every feeling that comes to him in life, whether it is pleasant or painful.

Reading — Deduce the meaning of the following words

  • Q: What does 'arrival' mean in the poem?
    Ans: Arrival means the act of coming to a place. In the poem, every morning brings a new arrival, which means a new feeling or emotion comes to the human heart every day.
  • Q: What does 'joy' mean in the poem?
    Ans: Joy means a feeling of great happiness and pleasure. In the poem, joy is one of the unexpected visitors, that is, one of the pleasant emotions that come to a person.
  • Q: What does 'shame' mean in the poem?
    Ans: Shame means a painful feeling of guilt, embarrassment or dishonour for having done something wrong. In the poem, shame is one of the dark feelings that we are told to meet at the door and invite in.
  • Q: What does 'guide' mean in the poem?
    Ans: A guide is a person who shows the way and gives direction to others. In the poem, every feeling is called a guide from beyond because each emotion comes to teach us something and to lead us towards a better life.
  • Q: What does 'beyond' mean in the poem?
    Ans: Beyond means on the farther side, or from a place that is outside our ordinary world. In the poem, the feelings are sent as guides from beyond, that is, from God and the unseen spiritual world.

Glossary

  • Q: What does 'depression' mean?
    Ans: Depression is a medical condition in which a person feels very sad and anxious and often has physical symptoms such as being unable to sleep, etc.
  • Q: What does 'meanness' mean?
    Ans: Meanness means unkind behaviour.
  • Q: What does 'momentary' mean?
    Ans: Momentary means lasting for a very short time.
  • Q: What does 'awareness' mean?
    Ans: Awareness means knowing something; knowing that something exists and is important; being interested in something.
  • Q: What does 'unexpected' mean?
    Ans: Unexpected means regarded as not likely to happen; something that comes suddenly and without warning.
  • Q: What does 'entertain' mean?
    Ans: To entertain means to invite people to eat or drink with you as your guests, especially in your home.
  • Q: What does 'violently' mean?
    Ans: Violently means with great energy or strong movement, especially caused by a strong emotion such as fear or hatred.
  • Q: What does 'treat' mean?
    Ans: To treat means to behave in a particular way towards somebody or something.
  • Q: What does 'honorably' mean?
    Ans: Honorably means in a way that is deserving of respect and admiration; in a way that shows high moral standards.
  • Q: What does 'grateful' mean?
    Ans: Grateful means feeling or showing thanks because somebody has done something kind for you or has done as you asked.

Comprehension A — Answer the following questions

  • Q: Q1. Who are the guests in Rumi's 'The Guest House'?
    Ans: The guests in the poem are our feelings and emotions. Every day a new feeling arrives in the human heart like a guest, for example a joy, a depression, a meanness, a dark thought, shame and malice. Rumi calls all these emotions guests because they come to us for a short time and then leave, just as guests stay in a guest house for a while.
  • Q: Q2. What message does the poet convey through the poem 'The Guest House'?
    Ans: The poet conveys the message that we should welcome and accept every feeling and experience of life, both pleasant and painful. We should not reject sorrows and dark thoughts, because every experience is sent by God as a guide. Even painful feelings clear us out and prepare us for some new delight, so we should be grateful for whatever comes to us.
  • Q: Q3. What two things does Rumi compare in the first two lines of 'The Guest House'?
    Ans: In the first two lines Rumi compares being a human being with a guest house. Just as new guests keep arriving at a guest house every day, in the same way new feelings and emotions keep arriving in the life and heart of a human being every morning.
  • Q: Q4. How might you apply the message of 'The Guest House' to your everyday life?
    Ans: In everyday life I can apply this message by accepting my feelings instead of fighting them. When I feel happy, I should be thankful, and when I feel sad, angry or worried, I should bear it patiently and try to learn from it. I should remember that hard times do not last forever and that they often make room for better things, so I should face every situation with courage and gratitude.
  • Q: Q5. Read the line 'This being human is a guest house' and tell whether it is a simile or metaphor. Give reason for your answer.
    Ans: This line is a metaphor, not a simile. In a simile two things are compared with the help of the words 'like' or 'as', but here the human being is directly called a guest house without using 'like' or 'as'. The poet directly identifies the human heart with a guest house because feelings keep arriving in it like guests.

Comprehension B — Choose the correct option

  • Q: Q1. What does the word 'furniture' mean in the lines 'who violently sweep your house / empty of its furniture'?
    Options: happiness / equipment / people / instruments
    Ans: equipment
  • Q: Q2. What comes as an unexpected guest in the poem 'The Guest House'?
    Options: emotions and feelings / friends and family / human beings / visitors and guests
    Ans: emotions and feelings
  • Q: Q3. In the poem the poet suggests to _____.
    Options: face the painful thoughts with rejection and refusal instead of delight / face the uncomfortable thoughts with acceptance and courage instead of contempt / face the painful thoughts with denial and cowardice instead of approval / face the comfortable thoughts with acceptance and courage instead of admiration
    Ans: face the uncomfortable thoughts with acceptance and courage instead of contempt

mcqs.q: What does the word 'furniture' mean in the lines 'who violently sweep your house / empty of its furniture'?
mcqs.why: The book keys 'furniture' in these lines as equipment — the things that fill a house and can be swept away.

mcqs.q: What comes as an unexpected guest in the poem 'The Guest House'?
mcqs.why: The book keys this answer: the unexpected guests in the poem are our emotions and feelings, arriving every morning.

mcqs.q: In the poem the poet suggests to _____.
options: face the painful thoughts with rejection and refusal instead of delight
face the painful thoughts with denial and cowardice instead of approval
face the uncomfortable thoughts with acceptance and courage instead of contempt
face the comfortable thoughts with acceptance and courage instead of admiration
mcqs.why: The book keys this option: Rumi advises facing uncomfortable thoughts with acceptance and courage, not contempt.

mcqs.q: Who are the 'guests' in Rumi's 'The Guest House'?
options: The poet's relatives visiting his house
Travellers staying in a real guest house
The students reading the poem in class
Our feelings and emotions, such as a joy, a depression, a meanness, shame and malice
mcqs.why: Comprehension A states the guests are our feelings and emotions, which arrive in the heart like guests and then leave.

mcqs.q: What two things does Rumi compare in the first two lines of the poem?
options: Being a human being and a guest house
A guest house and a school
mcqs.why: The notes say Rumi compares being human with a guest house: new feelings keep arriving in the heart as guests arrive daily.

mcqs.q: 'This being human is a guest house' is a metaphor, not a simile, because _____.
options: The human being is compared using the word 'like'
The human being is directly called a guest house without using 'like' or 'as'
The line describes a real building with rooms
The poet gives the reason with the word 'because'
mcqs.why: The notes explain a simile uses 'like' or 'as'; here the human being is directly identified as a guest house, so it is a metaphor.

mcqs.q: What does 'arrival' mean in the poem?
options: The act of leaving a place forever
A feeling of great happiness and pleasure
The act of coming to a place; a new feeling comes to the human heart every day
A person who shows the way to others
mcqs.why: The reading work defines 'arrival' as the act of coming to a place; every morning a new feeling arrives in the heart.

mcqs.q: What does 'shame' mean in the poem?
options: A feeling of great happiness and pleasure
Knowing that something exists and is important
Behaviour that is unkind to others
A painful feeling of guilt, embarrassment or dishonour for having done something wrong
mcqs.why: The notes define shame as a painful feeling of guilt or dishonour, one of the dark feelings we must invite in.

mcqs.q: Why is every feeling called 'a guide from beyond' in the poem?
options: Because each emotion comes to teach us something and lead us towards a better life, sent from God
Because every feeling shows us the road to the guest house
Because feelings come from other countries to visit us
Because a guide is a guest who stays only one night
mcqs.why: The notes explain each feeling is a guide from beyond — sent from God — to teach us and lead us towards a better life.

mcqs.q: What should we do even when painful feelings clear us out, according to the poem's message?
options: Reject them and refuse to feel anything
Be grateful, because they may be preparing us for some new delight
Complain that life has treated us unfairly
Hide them from everyone and feel ashamed
mcqs.why: The message answer says even painful feelings clear us out for some new delight, so we should be grateful for whatever comes.

lessons.title: Sounds and Speaking
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary A — Pronunciation, syllable division and stress pattern

  • Q: Give the pronunciation, syllable division and stress pattern of 'guest'.
    Ans: Guest is pronounced 'gest'. It has one syllable only: guest. Being a one-syllable word, the whole word carries the stress.
  • Q: Give the pronunciation, syllable division and stress pattern of 'thought'.
    Ans: Thought is pronounced 'thawt'. It has one syllable only: thought. Being a one-syllable word, the whole word carries the stress.
  • Q: Give the pronunciation, syllable division and stress pattern of 'laughing'.
    Ans: Laughing is pronounced 'laaf-ing'. It is divided into two syllables: laugh-ing. The stress falls on the first syllable: LAUGH-ing.
  • Q: Give the pronunciation, syllable division and stress pattern of 'beyond'.
    Ans: Beyond is pronounced 'bi-yond'. It is divided into two syllables: be-yond. The stress falls on the second syllable: be-YOND.
  • Q: Give the pronunciation, syllable division and stress pattern of 'clearing'.
    Ans: Clearing is pronounced 'kleer-ing'. It is divided into two syllables: clear-ing. The stress falls on the first syllable: CLEAR-ing.
  • Q: Give the pronunciation, syllable division and stress pattern of 'furniture'.
    Ans: Furniture is pronounced 'fur-ni-cher'. It is divided into three syllables: fur-ni-ture. The stress falls on the first syllable: FUR-ni-ture.
  • Q: Give the pronunciation, syllable division and stress pattern of 'empty'.
    Ans: Empty is pronounced 'emp-ti'. It is divided into two syllables: emp-ty. The stress falls on the first syllable: EMP-ty.

mcqs.q: How is 'guest' pronounced, and how many syllables does it have?
options: Pronounced 'gest'; it has one syllable only
mcqs.why: The notes give 'guest' as pronounced 'gest' with one syllable only, so the whole word carries the stress.

mcqs.q: How is 'thought' pronounced, and how many syllables does it have?
options: Pronounced 'thawt'; it has one syllable only

lessons.title: Language Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary B — Find words in the poem which mean the same as

  • Q: Find a word in the poem which means the same as 'despair'.
    Ans: The word in the poem is 'depression'. Despair is deep sadness and loss of hope, and the poem uses 'depression' for this sad and hopeless feeling that arrives as a guest.
  • Q: Find a word in the poem which means the same as 'cruelty'.
    Ans: The word in the poem is 'malice'. Malice means the wish to harm others, which is a form of cruelty. The poem also uses 'meanness', which means unkind behaviour.
  • Q: Find a word in the poem which means the same as 'brief'.
    Ans: The word in the poem is 'momentary'. Brief means lasting for a very short time, and the poem speaks of 'some momentary awareness'.
  • Q: Find a word in the poem which means the same as 'brush'.
    Ans: The word in the poem is 'sweep'. To sweep is to clean with a brush, and the poem says the sorrows 'violently sweep your house empty of its furniture'.
  • Q: Find a word in the poem which means the same as 'sudden'.
    Ans: The word in the poem is 'unexpected'. Sudden means happening without warning, and the poem says awareness comes 'as an unexpected visitor'.
  • Q: Find a word in the poem which means the same as 'respectably'.
    Ans: The word in the poem is 'honorably'. The poem advises us to 'treat each guest honorably', that is, in a respectable and worthy manner.

Grammar — Kinds of Adverbs: underline the adverbs and state their kind

  • Q: Q1. The girl sang sweetly. Identify the adverb and state its kind.
    Ans: The adverb is 'sweetly'. It tells us how the girl sang, so it is an adverb of manner.
  • Q: Q2. What is he doing outside? Identify the adverb and state its kind.
    Ans: The adverb is 'outside'. It tells us where he is doing something, so it is an adverb of place.
  • Q: Q3. We visit them frequently. Identify the adverb and state its kind.
    Ans: The adverb is 'frequently'. It tells us how often we visit them, so it is an adverb of frequency.
  • Q: Q4. I look forward to hearing from you soon. Identify the adverb and state its kind.
    Ans: The adverb is 'soon'. It tells us when I look forward to hearing from you, so it is an adverb of time.
  • Q: Q5. The old woman was walking slowly. Identify the adverb and state its kind.
    Ans: The adverb is 'slowly'. It tells us how the old woman was walking, so it is an adverb of manner.
  • Q: Q6. The kittens are playing there. Identify the adverb and state its kind.
    Ans: The adverb is 'there'. It tells us where the kittens are playing, so it is an adverb of place.
  • Q: Q7. He did not work hard, therefore, he failed. Identify the adverb and state its kind.
    Ans: The adverb is 'therefore'. It gives the reason for his failure, so it is an adverb of reason.
  • Q: Q8. The girls danced gracefully. Identify the adverb and state its kind.
    Ans: The adverb is 'gracefully'. It tells us how the girls danced, so it is an adverb of manner.
  • Q: Q9. You are absolutely right. Identify the adverb and state its kind.
    Ans: The adverb is 'absolutely'. It tells us to what degree or extent you are right, so it is an adverb of degree.
  • Q: Q10. We have been living here for several years. Identify the adverb and state its kind.
    Ans: The adverb is 'here'. It tells us where we have been living, so it is an adverb of place.

Grammar — Position of Adverbs: rewrite the sentence using the adverb in brackets in its correct position

  • Q: Q1. He listens to the radio. (often)
    Ans: He often listens to the radio.
  • Q: Q2. They read a book. (sometimes)
    Ans: They sometimes read a book.
  • Q: Q3. Palwasha gets angry. (never)
    Ans: Palwasha never gets angry.
  • Q: Q4. Tehmina is very friendly. (usually)
    Ans: Tehmina is usually very friendly.
  • Q: Q5. I take sugar in my coffee. (sometimes)
    Ans: I sometimes take sugar in my coffee.
  • Q: Q6. Rashid and Farukh are hungry. (often)
    Ans: Rashid and Farukh are often hungry.
  • Q: Q7. My grandmother goes for a walk in the evening. (always)
    Ans: My grandmother always goes for a walk in the evening.

Grammar — Which of the following sentences is correct according to position of Adverbs?

  • Q: Q1. Never — which sentence is correct?
    Options: I have never seen a whale. / I never have seen a whale. / Never I have seen a whale.
    Ans: I have never seen a whale.
  • Q: Q2. Rarely — which sentence is correct?
    Options: I am rarely late for work. / Rarely I am late for work. / I rarely am late for work.
    Ans: I am rarely late for work.
  • Q: Q3. Always — which sentence is correct?
    Options: I get up early always. / Always I get up early. / I always get up early.
    Ans: I always get up early.
  • Q: Q4. Sometimes — which sentence is correct?
    Options: It sometimes gets very windy here. / Sometimes it gets very windy here. / Both sentences are correct.
    Ans: Both sentences are correct.
  • Q: Q5. Often — which sentence is correct?
    Options: My boss is often bad-tempered. / My boss often is bad-tempered. / My boss is bad-tempered often.
    Ans: My boss is often bad-tempered.

Grammar — Degrees of Comparison: fill in the blank with the correct comparative / superlative form of the adverb in brackets

  • Q: Q1. He arrived _____ than expected. (early)
    Ans: earlier
  • Q: Q2. I speak English _____ now than last year. (fluent)
    Ans: more fluently
  • Q: Q3. We walked _____ than the rest of the people. (slowly)
    Ans: more slowly
  • Q: Q4. They called us _____ in the afternoon. (late)
    Ans: the latest
  • Q: Q5. My mother and my sister talked _____ than the other guests. (loudly)
    Ans: more loudly
  • Q: Q6. He hit his arm _____ than before. (hard)
    Ans: harder
  • Q: Q7. He had an accident last year. Now, he drives _____ than before. (careful)
    Ans: more carefully
  • Q: Q8. Jabbar can run _____ than Asim. (fast)
    Ans: faster
  • Q: Q9. Our team played _____ of all. (bad)
    Ans: the worst
  • Q: Q10. He worked _____ than ever before. (hard)
    Ans: harder

Grammar — Adverbial Phrase: underline the adverbial phrase and write the question it answers

  • Q: Q1. We raced our toy cars on the playground. (Example as printed in the book)
    Ans: The adverbial phrase is 'on the playground'. It answers the question: Where did you race your cars? We raced our toy cars on the playground.
  • Q: Q2. We expect our grandparents to arrive in about an hour. Identify the adverbial phrase and the question it answers.
    Ans: The adverbial phrase is 'in about an hour'. It answers the question: When do you expect your grandparents to arrive? It is an adverbial phrase of time.
  • Q: Q3. My cousin watches television almost as much as you do. Identify the adverbial phrase and the question it answers.
    Ans: The adverbial phrase is 'almost as much as you do'. It answers the question: How much does my cousin watch television? It shows degree or extent.
  • Q: Q4. The weatherman says it will rain all day. Identify the adverbial phrase and the question it answers.
    Ans: The adverbial phrase is 'all day'. It answers the question: When, or for how long, will it rain? It is an adverbial phrase of time.
  • Q: Q5. Your brother plays soccer better than my brother does. Identify the adverbial phrase and the question it answers.
    Ans: The adverbial phrase is 'better than my brother does'. It answers the question: How does your brother play soccer? It is an adverbial phrase of manner.
  • Q: Q6. Our friend drives on Mondays. Identify the adverbial phrase and the question it answers.
    Ans: The adverbial phrase is 'on Mondays'. It answers the question: When does our friend drive? It is an adverbial phrase of time.
