lessons.title: Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Writing — Paraphrase and Summary

  • Q: Paraphrase the first stanza of the poem (model paraphrase as printed in the book).
    Ans: Rumi uses metaphors in this poem. Rumi says that being a human being is like being a guest house and your guests are your emotions. They are all unexpected guests. These guests may even sweep your furniture away, but then you will be cleared out for new furniture. No matter if these guests are good or evil, they may have come for a good reason.
  • Q: A. Paraphrase the second stanza of the poem.
    Ans: The poet says that we should welcome all our feelings and give them a good reception. Even if the feelings are a crowd of sorrows that enter our heart by force and take away everything we love and value, we should still treat every feeling with honour and respect. The reason is that such a painful feeling may be emptying our heart only to make room for some new happiness that is about to come into our life.
  • Q: Paraphrase the third stanza of the poem.
    Ans: The poet says that we should not run away from bad feelings like dark thoughts, shame and ill will. Instead, we should meet them cheerfully at the door of our heart and invite them inside. We should be thankful for every feeling that comes to us, because every feeling has been sent by God as a guide to show us the right way.
  • Q: B. Write the summary of the poem.
    Ans: In the poem 'The Guest House', Maulana Jalaluddin Rumi compares a human being to a guest house and his feelings to guests. Every morning a new feeling arrives, such as joy, sadness, unkindness or a sudden awareness. The poet advises us to welcome and entertain all these feelings. Even a crowd of sorrows, which sweeps our heart empty, should be treated honourably, because it may be clearing us out for some new delight. Dark thoughts, shame and malice should also be met laughing at the door and invited in. In short, we should be grateful for whatever comes, because every feeling is a guide sent by God from beyond.

mcqs.q: According to the model paraphrase of the first stanza, what are the guests in the poem?
options: Our emotions, and they are all unexpected guests
Our relatives, and they are all invited guests
Our neighbours, and they are all welcome guests
Our friends, and they are all permanent guests
mcqs.why: The printed paraphrase says Rumi's guests are our emotions, and they are all unexpected guests in the guest house of being human.

mcqs.q: According to the first stanza's paraphrase, what may happen even when guests sweep our furniture away?
options: We will lose our house forever
We will be cleared out for new furniture
We will never feel any emotion again
We will be punished for our evil deeds
mcqs.why: The paraphrase explains that guests may sweep the furniture away, but then we will be cleared out for new furniture.

mcqs.q: According to the paraphrase of the second stanza, how should we receive all our feelings?
options: Drive them away and lock the door of the heart
Welcome only happy feelings and refuse sorrows
Welcome them and give them a good reception, even a crowd of sorrows that enters by force
Ignore them until they leave on their own
mcqs.why: The second stanza's paraphrase says we should welcome all feelings and give them a good reception, even sorrows entering by force.

mcqs.q: Why, in the second stanza's paraphrase, should a painful feeling still be treated with honour?
options: It will bring us money and fame in return
It proves that we have done something wrong
It will never come back once it is honoured
It may be emptying our heart only to make room for some new happiness about to come
mcqs.why: The paraphrase gives the reason: a painful feeling may empty the heart to make room for new happiness about to come into our life.

mcqs.q: According to the paraphrase of the third stanza, what should we do with dark thoughts, shame and ill will?
options: Meet them cheerfully at the door of our heart and invite them inside
Run away from them and hide in fear
Fight them with anger and hatred
Pretend they have never come to us
mcqs.why: The third stanza's paraphrase says we should not run away but meet bad feelings cheerfully at the door and invite them in.

mcqs.q: Why should we be thankful for every feeling, according to the third stanza's paraphrase?
options: Because every feeling brings us worldly success
Because every feeling has been sent by God as a guide to show us the right way
Because feelings never cause us any pain
Because a guide always stays with us forever
mcqs.why: The paraphrase states we should be thankful because every feeling has been sent by God as a guide to show us the right way.

mcqs.q: Whom does the summary name as the poet of 'The Guest House'?
mcqs.why: The summary begins by naming Maulana Jalaluddin Rumi as the poet who compares a human being to a guest house.

mcqs.q: Which feelings does the summary say arrive every morning?
options: Feelings such as hunger, thirst and tiredness only
Only feelings of happiness and delight
Feelings that stay in the heart forever
Feelings such as joy, sadness, unkindness or a sudden awareness
mcqs.why: The summary lists the morning arrivals as joy, sadness, unkindness or a sudden awareness — a new feeling every morning.

mcqs.q: According to the summary, why should even a crowd of sorrows be treated honourably?
options: Because it may be clearing us out for some new delight
Because sorrows bring furniture into the house
Because it will make us famous among people
Because sorrows are the only true feelings
mcqs.why: The summary states a crowd of sorrows sweeping the heart empty should be treated honourably, as it may clear us out for new delight.

mcqs.q: How does the summary say dark thoughts, shame and malice should be met?
options: They should be met with tears and turned away
They should be met laughing at the door and invited in
They should be hidden so no one sees them
They should be fought until they disappear forever
mcqs.why: The summary says dark thoughts, shame and malice should also be met laughing at the door and invited in, with gratitude.

lessons.title: Practice Activities
lessons.notes_html:
Listening and Speaking

  • Q: In pairs discuss 'Ups And Downs of Life'. Present your ideas in front of the class. (Model response)
    Ans: Life is full of ups and downs, just as a road goes up and down over hills. Sometimes we are happy and successful, and sometimes we face sorrow, failure and difficulty. We should enjoy the good days with gratitude and face the bad days with patience and courage. The downs of life teach us lessons that the ups can never teach us, and they make us stronger. A wise person welcomes both, because after every down there comes an up, just as after every night there comes a morning.

chapters.title: Unit 18: Cleanliness is Next to Godliness

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-reading

  • Q: How can we create a clean living environment?
    Ans: We can create a clean living environment by keeping ourselves and our surroundings clean. We should not throw garbage in streets, roads and parks, but always use dustbins. We should clean our homes and shops without throwing the garbage outside, plant trees, save water and use eco-friendly things. We should also raise awareness in our society and work with volunteers to clean litter, so that our environment stays healthy and free from diseases.

Glossary

  • Q: What does 'evident' mean?
    Ans: Evident means clear; easily seen.
  • Q: What does 'littering' mean?
    Ans: Littering means small pieces of rubbish or garbage such as paper, cans and bottles, that people have left lying in a public place.
  • Q: What does 'implications' mean?
    Ans: Implications means a possible effect or result of an action or a decision.
  • Q: What does 'imperativeness' mean?
    Ans: Imperativeness means relating to, or constituting, the grammatical mood that expresses the will to influence the behavior of another; expressive of a command, entreaty, or having power to restrain, control, and direct.
  • Q: What does 'dump' mean?
    Ans: To dump means to get rid of something you do not want, especially in a place which is not suitable.
  • Q: What does 'eco-friendly' mean?
    Ans: Eco-friendly means not harmful to the environment.
  • Q: What does 'provoke' mean?
    Ans: To provoke means to cause a particular reaction or have a particular effect.
  • Q: What does 'sanitation' mean?
    Ans: Sanitation means the equipment and systems that keep places clean, especially by removing human waste.

Comprehension A — Answer the following questions

  • Q: Q1. In Islam 'cleanliness is half of faith', explain why?
    Ans: In Islam cleanliness is called half of faith because Islam gives it the highest importance in the life of a Muslim. Islam instructs Muslims to keep themselves, their roads and their streets clean, and removing dirt and filth from the streets is counted as charity. Cleanliness is the pathway to health and strength, and Islam wants a healthy and strong Muslim society which is safe from infectious diseases. A clean person is also spiritually pure and better able to understand and apply the message of God, so cleanliness stands next to faith itself.
  • Q: Q2. Explain the proverb 'Cleanliness is next to godliness'.
    Ans: The proverb means that cleanliness comes immediately after godliness, that is, after devotion to God. A person who keeps his body, clothes, home and surroundings clean is very close to being truly religious and pure. Cleanliness keeps us healthy, keeps diseases away and makes our life happy, and Islam also teaches it as a religious duty. So a clean life is a sign of a pure and God-fearing life.
  • Q: Q3. How can we guard ourselves against the germs and bacteria?
    Ans: We can guard ourselves against germs and bacteria by keeping ourselves and our surroundings clean. We should keep our surroundings clean and avoid littering in public, always use dustbins, and never throw garbage in streets, roads or parks. We should plant trees, save water, use eco-friendly things and keep our homes and streets free from dirt and filth, because a clean environment keeps us safe from diseases like dengue, swine flu and jaundice.
  • Q: Q4. How can we keep our surrounding clean?
    Ans: We can keep our surroundings clean in several ways. We should not litter in public places and roads, and we should set a good example for others. We should use dustbins, because they help in keeping the society clean. If the society is plagued by litter, we should consult society members and other authorities to raise awareness, and work with them and with volunteers to clean the litter. We should also plant trees and take care of them to control pollution.
  • Q: Q5. How can we be eco-friendly?
    Ans: We can be eco-friendly by doing things that do not harm the environment. We should restore and save water, use eco-friendly things, and not dump electronic gadgets carelessly. We should use a bicycle instead of cars, because cars make a lot of noise and increase pollution. We should also plant trees, because trees give us fresh air, control pollution and keep the society green and healthy.
  • Q: Q6. What is the main idea of the lesson?
    Ans: The main idea of the lesson is that cleanliness is one of the most important practices of life and a religious duty in Islam. We must keep ourselves, our homes, streets and whole surroundings clean, avoid littering, plant trees and be eco-friendly. By keeping ourselves and our surroundings clean, we keep our loved ones away from deadly diseases and help everyone live a happy and healthy life.

Vocabulary B — Use the following phrases related to environment in sentences of your own

  • Q: Use the phrase 'back to nature' in a sentence of your own.
    Ans: After a long busy life in the city, my grandfather decided to go back to nature and live a simple life in his village among green fields and trees.
  • Q: Use the phrase 'global warming' in a sentence of your own.
    Ans: Global warming is increasing day by day because of smoke from vehicles and factories, and it is melting the ice at the poles.
  • Q: Use the phrase 'balance of nature' in a sentence of your own.
    Ans: Cutting down forests and killing animals disturbs the balance of nature and harms all living things.
  • Q: Use the phrase 'climate change' in a sentence of your own.
    Ans: Climate change has made the summers hotter and the rains uncertain in many parts of the world.

Vocabulary C — Dictionary meanings, parts of speech, guide words and entry words

  • Q: Find the meaning and part of speech of 'preservation', and give its entry word and guide words.
    Ans: Preservation is a noun (abbreviation 'n.'). It means the act of keeping something safe and in good condition, or protecting something from damage. Its entry word is 'preservation' itself, and in a dictionary it is found on a page whose guide words begin before and after it alphabetically; the exact guide words depend on the dictionary used.
  • Q: Find the meaning and part of speech of 'environment', and give its entry word and guide words.
    Ans: Environment is a noun (abbreviation 'n.'). It means the natural world around us, including land, water, air and living things, in which people, animals and plants live. Its entry word is 'environment' itself, and its guide words are the first and last entry words printed at the top of its dictionary page; the exact guide words depend on the dictionary used.
  • Q: Find the meaning and part of speech of 'benefit', and give its entry word and guide words.
    Ans: Benefit can be a noun (abbreviation 'n.') and also a verb (abbreviation 'v.'). As a noun it means an advantage or a good effect gained from something, and as a verb it means to gain advantage from something or to help someone. Its entry word is 'benefit' itself, and its guide words are the first and last entry words printed at the top of its dictionary page; the exact guide words depend on the dictionary used.
  • Q: Find the meaning and part of speech of 'plantation', and give its entry word and guide words.
    Ans: Plantation is a noun (abbreviation 'n.'). It means the growing of trees and plants on a large scale, or a large area of land where trees or crops are grown. Its entry word is 'plantation' itself, and its guide words are the first and last entry words printed at the top of its dictionary page; the exact guide words depend on the dictionary used.
  • Q: Find the meaning and part of speech of 'adapt', and give its entry word and guide words.
    Ans: Adapt is a verb (abbreviation 'v.'). In the lesson it is used in the sense of adopting and taking care of something; in general it means to change or adjust something to suit a new purpose or new conditions. Its entry word is 'adapt' itself, and its guide words are the first and last entry words printed at the top of its dictionary page; the exact guide words depend on the dictionary used.
  • Q: Find the meaning and part of speech of 'volunteer', and give its entry word and guide words.
    Ans: Volunteer can be a noun (abbreviation 'n.') and also a verb (abbreviation 'v.'). As a noun it means a person who offers to do work without being paid, and as a verb it means to offer to do something willingly. Its entry word is 'volunteer' itself, and its guide words are the first and last entry words printed at the top of its dictionary page; the exact guide words depend on the dictionary used.

Grammar — Punctuation and Capitalization

  • Q: Punctuate and capitalize where necessary in the following paragraph: 'once there was a little boy his name was hashir when he was of a year his father brought him toys he played with toys for sometimes then broke them the toys he broke were helicopter aero-plane a variety of motorcars and animals these toys were very costly his father bought them during his stay in china.'
    Ans: Once there was a little boy. His name was Hashir. When he was of a year, his father brought him toys. He played with toys for sometimes, then broke them. The toys he broke were helicopter, aero-plane, a variety of motorcars and animals. These toys were very costly. His father bought them during his stay in China.

Grammar — Decide whether the sentences are written in Active or Passive

  • Q: Q1. They often listen to music. Is this sentence Active or Passive?
    Ans: This sentence is in the Active voice, because the subject 'They' performs the action of listening.
  • Q: Q2. She is reading the newspaper now. Is this sentence Active or Passive?
    Ans: This sentence is in the Active voice, because the subject 'She' is performing the action of reading.
  • Q: Q3. These cars are produced in Japan. Is this sentence Active or Passive?
    Ans: This sentence is in the Passive voice, because the subject 'These cars' receives the action and the doer is not mentioned.
  • Q: Q4. Alan teaches geography. Is this sentence Active or Passive?
    Ans: This sentence is in the Active voice, because the subject 'Alan' performs the action of teaching.
  • Q: Q5. The bus driver was hurt yesterday. Is this sentence Active or Passive?
    Ans: This sentence is in the Passive voice, because the subject 'The bus driver' receives the action of being hurt.

Grammar — Change these active sentences to passive

  • Q: Q1. Change into passive: The Government is planning a new road near my house.
    Ans: A new road is being planned near my house by the Government.
  • Q: Q2. Change into passive: My grandfather built this house in 1943.
    Ans: This house was built by my grandfather in 1943.
  • Q: Q3. Change into passive: The cleaner has cleaned the office.
    Ans: The office has been cleaned by the cleaner.
  • Q: Q4. Change into passive: He had written three books before 1867.
    Ans: Three books had been written by him before 1867.
  • Q: Q5. Change into passive: Jameela will tell you later about the plan.
    Ans: You will be told later about the plan by Jameela.

lessons.title: Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Writing

  • Q: A. Write a paragraph on 'Clean and Green Surroundings'.
    Ans: Clean and green surroundings keep us healthy, happy and safe. We can keep our environment at school and home healthy by never littering and by always throwing wrappers and waste into dustbins. At school we should keep our classroom and playground neat, and at home we should clean our rooms and not throw garbage into the street. Moreover, we should plant trees in our school, homes and neighbourhood and water them regularly, because trees control pollution and give us fresh air. We should also save water and use eco-friendly things instead of harmful plastic. If every student sets a good example and works with others to clean litter, our surroundings will stay clean and green, diseases will stay away, and everyone will enjoy a fresh and beautiful environment.
  • Q: B. With the help of the mind map, write an essay on 'Personal Hygiene'.
    Ans: Personal hygiene means keeping our own body clean so that we stay healthy, fresh and free from germs. First of all, we should take a shower once a day and use soap and shampoo to remove all the dirt and bad odour, so that we smell good and fresh. Secondly, tooth brushing is very important: we should brush our teeth twice a day, use mouthwash after brushing, and do flossing to prevent gum disease. Thirdly, hand washing protects us from sickness, because it removes dirt and avoids germs; we should rub our hands with soap and hot water properly so that our hands smell good and look fresh. Finally, we should wear clean clothes and keep our hair clean, because bacteria curl up in used clothes if they are not washed, so parents should wash clothes frequently and we should always wear neat and clean dress. In this way, by showering daily, brushing our teeth, washing our hands and wearing clean clothes, we can smell good, look clean and live a healthy life.

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-reading

  • Q: Q1. Have you ever been on a bus or train and had to listen to someone obnoxiously chatting on his cell phone?
    Ans: Model answer: Yes, I have often travelled by bus, and sometimes a passenger talks loudly on his cell phone for a long time. It disturbs all the other passengers, because everyone is forced to listen to his conversation. A polite traveller holds off long cell phone conversations until he reaches his stop, or speaks in a low voice.
  • Q: Q2. Have you ever been pushed to the side or trampled on by rude passengers?
    Ans: Model answer: Yes, at busy bus stops passengers sometimes push each other while getting on the bus. This is rude and can hurt elderly people and children. Passengers should wait for their turn, stand in a queue, and let others get down before they get on.

Comprehension A — Answer the following questions

  • Q: Q1. How can we live responsibly in the society?
    Ans: We can live responsibly in society by following the rules of etiquette and showing good manners in our daily life. We should behave in a way that is socially acceptable and respectful, be considerate of other people's wishes and feelings, and show good manners even when others do not. Good manners, dignity and a calm attitude make life comfortable for us as well as for others.
  • Q: Q2. What is meant by the phrase "mirroring bad behaviour"?
    Ans: Mirroring bad behaviour means copying the bad behaviour of others and behaving badly in return, just as a mirror reflects an image. The lesson says there is no point in mirroring bad behaviour; instead, we should keep showing good manners even when others do not.
  • Q: Q3. Why shouldn't one bring food and drink on public transportation?
    Ans: One should not bring food and drink on public transportation because smells travel and intensify in small spaces and disturb other passengers. There is also a risk of spilling the food or drink, which can cause a dangerous environment where people may slip and fall.
  • Q: Q4. What are some good manners a person should possess?
    Ans: A person should greet the driver when he gets on a bus or taxi and thank him when he leaves, offer his seat to the elderly, the disabled, the blind or anyone on crutches, and keep his belongings under the seat or on his lap instead of occupying another seat. He should not make noise, should use ear buds for music at a low volume, should not smoke, should not drop trash on the floor, and as a pedestrian should stay to the right and be considerate of disabled people and people with children.
  • Q: Q5. What is the theme of the lesson?
    Ans: The theme of the lesson is that good manners and rules of etiquette must be followed while travelling, especially on public transportation. Following these rules creates favourable conditions for travelling and increases the chance of comfort for ourselves as well as for others, because good manners convey respect to the people we interact with.
  • Q: Q6. How do you travel from home to school? How do you follow travel etiquettes?
    Ans: Model answer: I travel from home to school by bus. I follow travel etiquettes by waiting for my turn to get on, greeting the driver, and keeping my school bag on my lap so that it does not take another passenger's space. I offer my seat to elderly or disabled passengers, I do not talk loudly or play music without ear buds, and I never drop wrappers on the floor of the bus.

Comprehension B — Choose the correct option for the following sentences

  • Q: Q1. We show good manners and etiquettes when we __________
    Options: do not talk with a full mouth / do interrupt, or cut into a line / do not say thank you or sorry / fight with each other
    Ans: do not talk with a full mouth
  • Q: Q2. Good manners have been developed __________
    Options: to give people more rules to learn / for no good reason / because people are mean / to make living together easier
    Ans: to make living together easier
  • Q: Q3. We show good manners and etiquettes when we __________
    Options: do not wait for our turn / give someone else our seat on a crowded bus / do not hold the door open for another person to walk through / do not knock before opening the closed door of a room
    Ans: give someone else our seat on a crowded bus
  • Q: Q4. If I meet someone new and I want to show good manners, I should __________
    Options: smile and say "hello" / pretend I don't see him / her / stare at that person / say nothing to him / her
    Ans: smile and say "hello"
  • Q: Q5. If I'm sitting on a crowded bus or train and someone older than I comes, I should __________
    Options: do nothing / get up and give that person my seat / stare at him / make fun of him
    Ans: get up and give that person my seat

Vocabulary — Glossary (meanings as printed in the book)

  • Q: What does "overwhelming" mean?
    Ans: Very great or very strong; so powerful that you cannot resist it or decide how to react.
  • Q: What does "recreation" mean?
    Ans: Activity done for enjoyment when you are not working.
  • Q: What does "blazing" mean?
    Ans: Extremely hot.
  • Q: What does "interconnected" mean?
    Ans: To connect similar things; to be connected to or with similar things.
  • Q: What does "inflict" mean?
    Ans: To make somebody or something suffer something unpleasant.
  • Q: What does "crutches" mean?
    Ans: One of two long sticks that you put under your arms to help you walk after you have injured your leg or foot.
  • Q: What does "receptacle" mean?
    Ans: A container for putting something in.
  • Q: What does "possession" mean?
    Ans: Something that you own or have with you at a particular time.
  • Q: What does "considerate" mean?
    Ans: Always thinking of other people's wishes and feelings; careful not to hurt or upset others.
  • Q: What does "continent" mean?
    Ans: One of the large land masses of the earth such as Europe, Asia or Africa.
  • Q: What does "mirroring" mean (as printed in the glossary)?
    Ans: As printed in the book's glossary: a piece of special flat glass that reflects images, so that you can see yourself when you look in it. In the lesson, "mirroring bad behaviour" means copying the bad behaviour of others.
  • Q: What does "attitude" mean?
    Ans: The way that you think and feel about somebody or something; the way that you behave towards somebody or something that shows how you think and feel.
  • Q: What does "etiquette" mean?
    Ans: The formal rules of correct or polite behaviour in society or among members of a particular profession.
  • Q: What does "pedestrian" mean?
    Ans: A person walking in the street and not travelling in a vehicle.
  • Q: What does "underneath" mean?
    Ans: Under or below something else, especially when it is hidden or covered by the thing on top.
  • Q: What does "elderly" mean?
    Ans: (Of people) used as a polite word for 'old'.
  • Q: What does "adhere" mean?
    Ans: To stick firmly to something.
  • Q: What does "intensify" mean?
    Ans: To increase in degree or strength; to make something increase in degree or strength.
  • Q: What does "aisle" mean?
    Ans: A passage between rows of seats in a church, theatre, train, etc., or between rows of shelves in a supermarket.

lessons.title: Language Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar — The First Conditional and the Second Conditional

  • Q: Q1. What is the form of the first conditional? What is it used for?
    Ans: The first conditional has the present simple after 'if', then the future simple in the other clause: if + present simple, ... will + infinitive. It is used to talk about things which might happen in the future; it describes possible things which could easily come true. Example from the book: "If it rains, I won't go to the park."
  • Q: Q2. What variations of the first conditional are given in the book?
    Ans: Instead of if + present + will, we may have: (1) if + present + may/might for possibility, e.g. "If the climate keeps warming, the Arctic might be warm enough for swimming"; (2) if + present + may (permission) or can (permission or ability), e.g. "If your documents are in order, you may/can leave at once" and "If it stops raining, we can go out"; (3) if + present + must, should or any expression of command, request or advice, e.g. "If you want to look slim, you must/should eat less meat."
  • Q: Q3. What variations of the if-clause are given in the book?
    Ans: Instead of if + present simple, we can have: (1) if + present continuous, to indicate a present action or a future arrangement, e.g. "If you are waiting for a bus, you'd better join the queue" and "If you're staying for another night, I'll ask the manager to give you a better room"; (2) if + present perfect, e.g. "If you have finished dinner, I'll ask the waiter for the bill" and "If she has written the letter, I'll post it."
  • Q: Q4. What is the form of the second conditional?
    Ans: The second conditional uses the past simple after 'if', then 'would' and the infinitive: if + past simple, ... would + infinitive. We can use 'were' instead of 'was' with 'I' and 'he/she/it'; this is mostly done in formal writing. Its first use, as printed in the book, is to talk about things in the future that are probably not going to be true.
  • Q: Note: Missing pages in the scanned copy
    Ans: Book pages 193 and 194 are missing from the scanned copy (the scan jumps from book page 192 to book page 195). Because of this, the remaining explanation of the second conditional and any grammar exercise printed on book page 193 could not be solved here, and nothing has been invented in its place. Only the conditional rules and examples actually printed on book pages 191-192 are solved above.

If + present perfect for a finished action

lessons.title: Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Writing A — With the help of the mind map write an essay on "Types of Etiquettes"

  • Q: Write an essay on "Types of Etiquettes" using the mind map (eating, meeting, travel, telephone, social, business).
    Ans: Types of Etiquettes Etiquette means the formal rules of correct and polite behaviour in society. Good manners are an important thing to learn, because having good manners means acting in a manner that is socially acceptable and respectful. Excellent manners help us to have better relationships with the people we know and those we meet. There are many types of etiquettes, and each type guides our behaviour in a different situation of daily life. Eating etiquette is about our manners at the table. We should not talk with a full mouth, we should wait for our turn to be served, and we should not make noises while eating. We should thank the person who serves the food and should never waste it. Meeting etiquette is followed when we meet people. When we meet someone new, we should smile and say hello. We should listen carefully, not interrupt others, knock before opening the closed door of a room, and hold the door open for another person to walk through. Travel etiquette is observed on public transportation. We should greet the driver, offer our seat to elderly and disabled passengers, keep our belongings on our lap or underneath the seat, and not inflict our noise on others. We should not bring food and drink on the bus, should not smoke, and should never drop trash on the floor. Telephone etiquette requires us to speak politely and in a low voice on the phone. We should not chat loudly and obnoxiously on a cell phone in public, and we should hold off long conversations in crowded places. When we call someone, we should introduce ourselves and not call at odd hours. Social etiquette covers our general behaviour in society. We should say thank you and sorry at the right time, give others their turn, help people in need, and be considerate of everyone's wishes and feelings. Business etiquette is followed at work and in offices. We should be punctual, dress properly, speak respectfully to colleagues and customers, and keep our promises. In a meeting we should listen to others and present our views politely. In conclusion, all these types of etiquettes have been developed to make living together easier. A person who follows eating, meeting, travel, telephone, social and business etiquettes earns respect everywhere, because good manners convey respect to those we interact with.
  • Q: Write a paragraph on travelling etiquette with a clear topic sentence.
    Ans: Good travelling etiquette makes a journey comfortable for ourselves and for everyone travelling with us. A polite passenger greets the driver when he gets on the bus and thanks him when he leaves. He offers his seat to an elderly, disabled or blind passenger and keeps his bags underneath the seat or tightly on his lap so that others are not disturbed. He does not talk loudly, listens to music only through ear buds at a low volume, and never brings smelly food or drops trash inside the vehicle. In this way, dignity, good manners and a calm attitude increase the chance of comfort for all passengers.

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-reading

  • Q: Q1. Do you have a pet? If so, what kind of pet do you have? Is it very old?
    Ans: Model answer: Yes, I have a pet cat at home. It is not very old; it is about two years old. I feed it daily and play with it, and it is a friendly member of our family.
  • Q: Q2. What about an animal that is used for work, maybe a horse or dog?
    Ans: Model answer: A working animal, such as a horse or a dog, helps its master in his daily work. A dog guards the house and the flock, and a horse carries loads and pulls a cart. Such animals earn their livelihood by their service, so they deserve good food and kind treatment.
  • Q: Q3. Should a working animal be treated differently?
    Ans: Model answer: No, a working animal should not be treated differently in kindness; in fact it should be treated even more carefully, because it serves its master faithfully for many years. Like the farmer's wife says about Motti, a faithful animal ought to be given a livelihood for the rest of its days, even when it grows old and can no longer work.

Comprehension A — Answer the following questions

  • Q: Q1. How does the author describe the character of the dog, Motti?
    Ans: The author describes Motti as a faithful dog who had served his master well for a great many years. He had grown very old and had lost all his teeth, so he could no longer frighten the thieves. Yet he remained true and loyal to his master till the end, and this faithfulness is the main feature of his character.
  • Q: Q2. What was the motive of the wolf behind helping Motti?
    Ans: The wolf's help was not sincere friendship only; he had a selfish motive behind it. After Motti was saved, the wolf expected a favour in return: he wanted Motti to turn his head the other way when the wolf came to taste one of the old farmer's fine fat sheep. In other words, he helped Motti so that he could steal the farmer's sheep without being stopped.
  • Q: Q3. How did Motti and the cat manage to defeat the wolf and the bear?
    Ans: Motti took the farmer's old three-legged cat with him as his second, and as the poor cat limped along, she stuck her tail straight up in the air. From a distance the wolf and the bear thought the cat was carrying a sword for Motti, and every time she limped they thought she was picking up a stone to throw at them, so they became frightened. The bear hid behind a bush and the wolf jumped up into a tree; then the cat, thinking the bear's moving ear was a mouse, sprang upon it and bit and scratched it, and the bear ran away. In the end the wolf was called a coward and had to promise to be good friends again with old Motti.
  • Q: Q4. Why did the farmer want to get rid of Motti?
    Ans: The farmer wanted to get rid of Motti because the dog had grown very old and had lost all his teeth. He was of no use now, the thieves did not care for him at all, and the farmer thought he had only worked to earn his livelihood. So the farmer decided to abandon old Motti at the train station the next morning.
  • Q: Q5. How did Motti manage to stay at the farmer's, despite the fact that the farmer wanted to get rid of him?
    Ans: Motti overheard his master's plan and went to his friend the wolf, who advised him to pretend to guard the farmer's child in the field. The wolf carried the child away, Motti ran after him, and the wolf let the child drop, so Motti carried the child back to his master and mistress. The farmer believed Motti had saved their child from the wolf, so he patted him on the head and promised that Motti would live with them, be well taken care of, and have plenty to eat for the rest of his life.
  • Q: Q6. What is the theme and setting of the story?
    Ans: The theme of the story is faithfulness and gratitude: a faithful servant should be valued and cared for in old age, and true loyalty, like Motti's loyalty to his master, is always rewarded. The setting is a countryside farm near a wood; the farmer and his wife work in the field, keep sheep, a dog and a cat, and the wolf lives in the nearby woods.
  • Q: Q7. Who is your favourite character in the story? Why?
    Ans: Model answer: My favourite character in the story is Motti, the old dog. Although the wolf had saved his life, Motti refused to betray his master and informed him about the wolf's plan to steal the sheep. His faithfulness, honesty and gratitude make him the most admirable character in the story.
  • Q: Q8. Suggest a new ending for the story.
    Ans: Model new ending: After the wolf promised to be good friends again with old Motti, he kept his promise and never came near the farmer's sheep again. Motti spent the rest of his days in comfort on the farmer's old cushion, and the farmer, who had learned his lesson, never again thought of abandoning a faithful animal. He told his neighbours, "Never throw away those who have served you faithfully, for faithfulness is worth more than strength."
  • Q: Q9. Find at least two anaphoric and two cataphoric references in the text.
    Ans: Cataphoric references (the description comes before the name, as explained in the book): (1) "A farmer had a faithful dog, Motti..." — the description 'faithful dog' is given in advance of the name Motti. (2) "...he went to his good friend the wolf" — the description 'his good friend' comes before the name 'the wolf'. Anaphoric references (the expression refers back to an earlier expression): (1) "Poor Motti, who was lying close by them..." — 'who' refers back to Motti, mentioned earlier. (2) "he has not a tooth in his mouth" — 'he' refers back to Motti, who has already been introduced in the story.

Vocabulary — Glossary (meanings as printed in the book)

  • Q: What does "dainty" mean?
    Ans: Small and delicate in a way that people find attractive.
  • Q: What does "cudgel" mean?
    Ans: A short thick stick that is used as a weapon.
  • Q: What does "rogue" mean?
    Ans: A person who behaves badly, but in a harmless way.
  • Q: What does "swore" mean?
    Ans: To make a serious promise to do something.
  • Q: What does "limped" mean?
    Ans: To walk slowly or with difficulty because one leg is injured.
  • Q: What does "espied" mean?
    Ans: To see somebody or something suddenly.
  • Q: What does "morsel" mean?
    Ans: A small amount or a piece of something, especially food.
  • Q: What does "stout" mean?
    Ans: Strong and thick.
  • Q: What does "abandon" mean?
    Ans: To leave somebody, especially somebody you are responsible for, with no intention of returning.
  • Q: What does "livelihood" mean?
    Ans: A means of earning money in order to live.
  • Q: What does "hedge" mean?
    Ans: A row of bushes or small trees planted close together, usually along the edge of a field, garden, yard or road.
  • Q: What does "patted" mean?
    Ans: To touch somebody or something gently several times with your hand flat, especially as a sign of affection.
  • Q: What does "scratched" mean?
    Ans: To rub your skin with your nails, usually because it is itching.
  • Q: What does "heartily" mean?
    Ans: With obvious enjoyment and enthusiasm.
  • Q: What does "ashamed" mean?
    Ans: Feeling shame or embarrassment about somebody or something, or because of something you have done.
  • Q: What does "sprang" mean?
    Ans: To move suddenly and with one quick movement in a particular direction.

options: Faithfulness and gratitude: a faithful servant should be valued and cared for in old age
Strength is more important than loyalty

options: A countryside farm near a wood where the farmer keeps sheep, a dog and a cat
A school in a large town
A train station in winter only

lessons.title: Language Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary A — Use dictionary to find the meaning of the following words; also find guide and entry words

  • Q: Find the meaning, guide word and entry word for: scratch
    Ans: Meaning: to rub your skin with your nails, usually because it is itching; to make a mark on a surface with something sharp. Entry word: scratch. Guide words: the guide words at the top of its dictionary page depend on the dictionary used; in a school dictionary 'scratch' is found on the page whose guide words begin with words like 'scrape' and end with words like 'scream' — students should note the guide words of their own dictionary.
  • Q: Find the meaning, guide word and entry word for: sprang
    Ans: Meaning (as printed in the glossary): to move suddenly and with one quick movement in a particular direction; it is the past tense of 'spring'. Entry word: sprang (entry is given under 'spring'). Guide words: depend on the dictionary used; 'sprang' appears on the page listing words around 'sprain' to 'spread' in most school dictionaries — students should note the guide words of their own dictionary.
  • Q: Find the meaning, guide word and entry word for: locks
    Ans: Meaning: locks of hair are curls or pieces of hair; in the story the farmer's cudgel 'combed his locks' means it beat the wolf's hairy back. 'Lock' can also mean a device that fastens a door with a key. Entry word: lock (plural: locks). Guide words: depend on the dictionary used; 'locks' is found on the page around 'lobster' to 'logic' in most school dictionaries — students should note the guide words of their own dictionary.
  • Q: Find the meaning, guide word and entry word for: plenty
    Ans: Meaning: as much as is needed or wanted; a large amount. In the story the farmer promises that Motti will 'have plenty to eat', that is, more than enough food. Entry word: plenty. Guide words: depend on the dictionary used; 'plenty' is found on the page around 'pledge' to 'plot' in most school dictionaries — students should note the guide words of their own dictionary.
  • Q: Find the meaning, guide word and entry word for: sword
    Ans: Meaning: a long sharp weapon with a handle, used in the past for fighting. In the story the wolf and the bear wrongly thought the cat was carrying a sword for Motti. Entry word: sword. Guide words: depend on the dictionary used; 'sword' is found on the page around 'switch' to 'symbol' in most school dictionaries — students should note the guide words of their own dictionary.
  • Q: Find the meaning, guide word and entry word for: pretend
    Ans: Meaning: to behave as if something is true when it is not, in order to deceive others or as part of a game. In the story Motti had to pretend to be watching the child. Entry word: pretend. Guide words: depend on the dictionary used; 'pretend' is found on the page around 'pressure' to 'prevent' in most school dictionaries — students should note the guide words of their own dictionary.
  • Q: Find the meaning, guide word and entry word for: livelihood
    Ans: Meaning (as printed in the glossary): a means of earning money in order to live. Entry word: livelihood. Guide words: depend on the dictionary used; 'livelihood' is found on the page around 'little' to 'load' in most school dictionaries — students should note the guide words of their own dictionary.

Vocabulary B — Direct quotations enclosed in quotation marks from the text

  • Q: Direct quotation — words of the farmer about abandoning Motti
    Ans: "I will abandon old Motti at the train station tomorrow morning, for he is of no use now."
  • Q: Direct quotation — words of the farmer's wife defending Motti
    Ans: "No! Let the poor faithful creature live with us; he has served us well a great many years, and we ought to give him a livelihood for the rest of his days."
  • Q: Direct quotation — words of the wolf comforting Motti
    Ans: "Make yourself easy," said the wolf, "I will give you some good advice."
  • Q: Direct quotation — words of the farmer after the child was brought back
    Ans: "Old Motti has saved our child from the wolf, and therefore he shall live and be well taken care of, and have plenty to eat."
  • Q: Direct quotation — words of Motti refusing the wolf's demand
    Ans: "No," said Motti; "I will be true to my master."

Grammar — Punctuation: Parenthesis (use parentheses where needed in these sentences)

  • Q: Q1. Use parentheses where needed: I'll get back to you tomorrow Friday.
    Ans: I'll get back to you tomorrow (Friday).
  • Q: Q2. Use parentheses where needed: Which country countries do you want to visit?
    Ans: Which country (countries) do you want to visit?
  • Q: Q3. Use parentheses where needed: You put fifty-four 54 books on that shelf.
    Ans: You put fifty-four (54) books on that shelf.
  • Q: Q4. Use parentheses where needed: If you want to be healthy, you must 1 eat good food, 2 get sufficient exercise, and 3 get adequate sleep.
    Ans: If you want to be healthy, you must (1) eat good food, (2) get sufficient exercise, and (3) get adequate sleep.
  • Q: Q5. Use parentheses where needed: We are going to visit Brazil I don't know where this spring.
    Ans: We are going to visit Brazil (I don't know where) this spring.
  • Q: Q6. Use parentheses where needed: I need seven 7 dollars for tonight.
    Ans: I need seven (7) dollars for tonight.

Grammar — Ellipses

  • Q: Q1. What is an ellipsis? Give the example printed in the book.
    Ans: An ellipsis is a set of three periods (. . .) indicating an omission. Each period should have a single space on either side, except when adjacent to a quotation mark, in which case there should be no space. The book's example is: "If only she had . . . Oh, it doesn't matter now." Here the ellipsis shows that the speaker's words break off and something is left unsaid.
  • Q: Note: Missing pages and end of the book
    Ans: Book pages 193 and 194 are missing from the scanned copy (the scan jumps from book page 192 to book page 195), so Unit 20's title and SLOs page could not be transcribed. This (book page 201) is the last page of the book in the scan; it ends with the Ellipses explanation and its example, and there is no separate ellipses exercise printed after it. Nothing has been invented for the missing pages.

We are going to visit Brazil (I don't know where this spring.
We are going to visit Brazil (I don't know where) this spring.
mcqs.why: The aside 'I don't know where' is placed in parentheses in the middle of the sentence as shown in the notes.

mcqs.q: What is an ellipsis?
options: A pair of brackets for extra numbers
A capital letter at a sentence start
A set of three periods indicating an omission, where words break off or are left unsaid
A stick used as a weapon
mcqs.why: The book defines an ellipsis as a set of three periods indicating an omission, shown in the example where the speaker's words break off.

lessons.title: Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Writing

  • Q: Write the story "The Farmer's Dog" in first person describing events and incidents.
    Ans: The Farmer's Dog — told by Motti himself I am Motti, the faithful old dog of a farmer. I served my master well for a great many years, but I grew very old and lost all my teeth. One day I was lying close by the house when I heard my master say to his wife that he would abandon me at the train station the next morning, for I was of no use now. His wife begged him to let me live with them, but he refused and said that tomorrow would be my last day. I was very much frightened. In the evening I went to my good friend the wolf, who lived in the woods, and told him all my sorrows. He comforted me and gave me good advice. The next morning, when my master and his wife went to the field and laid their little child behind the hedge, I lay down close by the child and pretended to watch it. The wolf came out of the wood and ran away with the child; I ran after him as fast as I could, and he let the child drop. I carried the poor little thing back to my master and mistress. My master patted me on the head and promised that I would live with them, be well taken care of, and have plenty to eat, and that I would sleep on his old cushion as long as I lived. Soon afterwards the wolf came to me and asked me to turn my head the other way when he came to taste one of my master's fine fat sheep. I refused and said that I would be true to my master. I even told my master what the wolf meant to do, and he lay in wait behind the barn door and beat the wolf with a stout cudgel. The angry wolf then sent the bear to challenge me to a fight in the wood. I took the farmer's old three-legged cat as my second. The wolf and the bear mistook her upright tail for a sword and her limping for picking up stones, so they hid in fear. The cat scratched the bear's ear, thinking it was a mouse, and the bear ran away, while the wolf was shamed as a coward and had to promise to be good friends with me again. From that time I lived happily and faithfully with my master.
  • Q: Write a story with the following beginning and give it a suitable title: "A fisherman catches a golden fish. When the fish announces that he is a prince under an evil spell, the fisherman throws him back into the sea. On his return __________"
    Ans: Title: The Golden Fish and the Kind Fisherman A fisherman catches a golden fish. When the fish announces that he is a prince under an evil spell, the fisherman throws him back into the sea. On his return home, he told his wife all that had happened. At first she was surprised, but then she said, "You have done a kind and noble deed. A life is worth more than all the gold in the world." The next morning, as the fisherman walked along the shore, he heard a voice calling his name. It was the golden fish. "Kind man," said the fish, "your goodness has broken the evil spell. I am a prince again, and I have come to thank you." Saying this, the fish changed into a tall young prince before his eyes. The prince rewarded the fisherman with a bag of gold coins and promised that his family would never be poor again. The fisherman thanked the prince and returned home happily. He and his wife lived comfortably for the rest of their lives, and the fisherman always told his children: "Kindness is never wasted; a good deed always comes back to reward us."

mcqs.q: In the first-person retelling, who is the narrator of 'The Farmer's Dog'?
options: Motti himself, the faithful old dog
mcqs.why: The writing task retells the story in first person by Motti himself, beginning 'I am Motti, the faithful old dog of a farmer'.

mcqs.q: In Motti's retelling, what did he overhear his master say?
options: That Motti would get a new cushion daily
That he would abandon Motti at the train station the next morning, for he was of no use now
That the wolf would live on the farm
That the cat would guard the sheep
mcqs.why: Motti lying close by heard his master say he would abandon him at the train station the next morning because he was of no use now.

mcqs.q: In the retelling, what happened when the farmer's wife begged for Motti?
options: The master gave Motti plenty to eat
The master refused and said tomorrow would be Motti's last day
mcqs.why: The first-person story says the wife begged him to let Motti live with them, but he refused and said tomorrow would be his last day.

mcqs.q: In Motti's story, where did the farmer and his wife lay their child in the field?
mcqs.why: Motti recounts that his master and wife went to the field and laid their little child behind the hedge while he pretended to watch it.

mcqs.q: In the retelling, what did the master promise after Motti brought the child back?
options: That Motti would live with them, be well taken care of, have plenty to eat and sleep on his old cushion
That Motti would be abandoned next morning
That Motti would get no food
That the wolf would be rewarded
mcqs.why: After carrying the child back, Motti says his master patted his head and promised he would live with them, be well cared for, have plenty to eat and sleep on the old cushion.

mcqs.q: In Motti's account, what did the wolf ask him to do about the sheep?
options: Turn his head the other way when the wolf came to taste one of the master's fine fat sheep
Tell the master at once about every sheep
mcqs.why: Motti recounts the wolf asked him to turn his head the other way when he came to taste one of his master's fine fat sheep, which he refused.

mcqs.q: How did the farmer beat the wolf, according to Motti's retelling?
options: He chased the wolf with a sword
He set the cat on the wolf
He lay in wait behind the barn door and beat the wolf with a stout cudgel
He threw stones from a tree
mcqs.why: Motti told his master the wolf's plan, and the master lay in wait behind the barn door and beat the wolf with a stout cudgel.

mcqs.q: In the retelling, who did Motti take as his second for the fight in the wood?
mcqs.why: Motti says he took the farmer's old three-legged cat as his second, whose tail and limping frightened the wolf and the bear.

mcqs.q: In the golden fish story, why did the fisherman throw the fish back into the sea?
options: Because the fish announced he was a prince under an evil spell
Because the fish was too small to eat
Because his wife told him to sell it
Because the fish offered him gold at once
mcqs.why: The story beginning says when the fish announced he was a prince under an evil spell, the fisherman threw him back into the sea.

mcqs.q: What is the moral at the end of the golden fish story?
options: Gold is worth more than a life
Kindness is never wasted; a good deed always comes back to reward us
A prince should never be trusted
mcqs.why: The fisherman always told his children that kindness is never wasted and a good deed always comes back to reward us, as the story ends.

lessons.title: Practice Activities
lessons.notes_html:
Listening and Speaking — Conversation using prepositions (Alian and Zain)

  • Q: Which prepositions are used in the conversation between Alian and Zain?
    Ans: The prepositions used in the dialogue are: at (a football match at the stadium), for (fun for us), by (go there by bus), in (in my own car), along with (along with my brother), between (the match will be between HBL Karachi and PAF Peshawar; competition between them), and with (trophy with them; good players with them). Students should practise the dialogue with a partner, noting how each preposition shows place, means, company or relation.
